Tea a la Sir Andrew Clarke,
For years. whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China whic h I keep, end the advice has been appreciated.

It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an intereting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: " Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido au/ know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representatlfin of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consults- tiona here and there, and about five o'cLock, when I get into a place, the lady of the holm, will say to me: 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup ot tea.' I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a clip and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecrueity to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always sets Our face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Tea the. Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powertni in its effects upon the nervons system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produCes a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will no injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each parson and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, am o necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. The colour of the tea after it is ti'ewed will be found tube much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its oPixifent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system. and if, Inn week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. TIT-BITS.
THE CHILD AND THE TIGER.

In the far east, "on a stern and rook-bonna coast," the encroaching waters of the ever-restless ocean have formed an estuary, separating from the mainland a bold and beautiful promontory, called, from its singular appearance, "The Dolphin's Nose," on whose green and richly-wooded summit man, with good taste, has erected a castellated building, with turrets and towers overlooking the sea. A covered way leads from the house to a detached building, surrounded by a high wall, by way of pro- tection from beasts of prey. This formed the apartment of the widowed master of the mansion, and in an inner room was the little bed on which reposid his son and heir, a lovely boy. A lamp was burning, and the light fell on a mirror which stood opposite the door, the only article of furniture to mark that woman once "had part and portion there." It was midnight—the infant. slept "calm as a child's repose"; but the father could not sleep— fast-thronging memories of by-gone days, the . thoughts of that dear partner separated from him by the hand ef death, anxieties regarding the wel-. fare of his child, and official duties, stole over him and combined to keep him watchful. The weather was oppressive, though every door and window was open to woo each passing breeze. His child awakes and cries, and the attention of the lonely watcher is at once wrested ;.suddenly he observes a dim and shadowy form creep by him, with stealthy step into the room that held his child. Is it a dream or phantom conjured up by the memories of the past? The light of a solitary lamp swung from above, and glanced upon the coat of a huge royal tiger, which, impelled by hunger, and attracted by the' cries of the child, had sprung over the protecting wall. The royal brute sees his own image reflected in the ruirroz, to him as the image of an enemy; scowl reflects scowl, and as be crouches for a spring, his silent enemy is prepared also; one wave of his snaky tad, one indignant growl, one bound, and the rnitror fal:s clashing around him in countless glittering fragments. Scarce two more bounds, the first through the suite of chambers, the second over the wall, and he sped far away to the solitary lair; and the father kneels with clasped hands over the hod of his unharmed child.

div.head: GOOD RULES FOR WINTER
div.p: GOOD RULES FOR WINTER

The following rules are worth heeding by who believe that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure: Never lean with the back upon anything that is cold. Never begin a journey until the breakfast has been eaten. Never take warm drinks and then immediately go out into the cold. Keep the back, especially between the shoulder- blades, well covered; also the chest well protected. In sleeping in a cold room establish the habit of breathing through the nose, and never with the month open. Never go to bed with cold or damp feet. , Never omit regular bathing, for unless the skin is in active condition the cold will close the pores, and favour congestion and other diseases. After exercise of any kind, never ride in an open carriage or near the window of a car for a moment; it is dangerous to health and even to life. When hoarse, speak as little as possible until the hoarseness is recovered from, else the voice may be permanently lost, or difficulties of the throat be produced. Merely warm the back by a fire, and never con- tinue keeping the back exposed to heat aft& it has become uncomfortably warm. To so expose the back is debilitating. When going from a warm atmosphere into a cooler one keep the mouth closed, so that the air may be warmed by its passage through the nose ere it reaches the lungs. Never stand still in cold weather, especially after having taken a slight degree of exercise; and always avoid standing on ice or snow, or whet e the person is exposed to a cold wind.

div.head: DON'T JUDGE A MAN BY HIS COAT.
div.p: DON'T JUDGE A MAN BY HIS COAT.

This story comes from the "Peak Cori The great cavern at Castleton attracts large num- bers of tourists every year, and ram and then notabilities visit the place. A visitor somewhat shabbily dressed presented himself before the guide, an official employed by the Duke of Devon- shire, and asked what it woald cost to see the sights. " &wen shillings," was the man's reply. "It seems a lot of money," said the inquirer. But the guide, with a glance at the man's gar- ments, deigned no answer. The visitor however resolved to go in. Emerging into the light of day again, he entered his name in the visitor's book, and said.: "There's seven shillings for your master and something for yourself." The "something" was a sovereign. The guide, staggered by the magnitude of the gratuity, hastily scanned the visitors' book, and found the signature of a well-known millionaire duke. He looked the surprise he felt. "Yendidn't expect that, did you?" drolly asked thallake. "No, your grace, I did not," said the guide honeetly. Auci you thought, now, I was scarcely good for the seven shillings?" persisted the duke. The thought, from the guide's frank admission, certainly had crossed his mind. "Well," said his grace smilingly, "never in future judge a man by the coat he wears."

div.head: OLD AGE.
div.p: OLD AGE.

Apedical man compares az old man to an old waggon; with light loading and careful usage it will last for years, but one heavy load or sudden strain will break it and ruin it for ever. Many people reach the age of fifty or sixty or seventy measur- ably free from most of the pains and infirmities of age, cheery in heart and round in health, ripe in wisdom and experience, with sympathies mellowed by age, and with reasonable prospects and opportunities for continued usefulness in the world for a considerable time. Let such persons be thankful; but let them also be careful. An old constitution is like an old bone, brcken with ease, mended with difficulty. A young tree bends to the gale, an old one snaps and falls before the blast. A single hard lilt, an hour of heating work, an evening of exposure to rain or damp, a severe chill, an excess of food, the unusual indulgence of an appetite or passion, a sudden fit of anger, an improper dose of medicine—any of these or similar other things may out of a valuable life In an hour, and leave the fair hopes of usefulness and enjoyment but a shapeless wreck.

div.p: THE GHOSTS AND THE GAME OF FOOTBALL. There was once a poor widow woman's son that was going to look for service, and one winter's even- he came to a strong farmer's,house, and this house was very near an old castle. "God save all here." says he, when he got inside the door. " God save you kindly," says the farmer. "Come to the fire." "Could you give me a night's lodging ?" says the boy. "That we will, and welcome if you will only sleep in a comfortable room in the old castle above there; and you must have a fire and candlelight, and whatever you like to drink; and if you're alive in the morning I'll give you ten guineas." " Sure ill be 'live enough if you send no one to kill me." "I'll send no one to kill you, you may depend. The place is haunted ever since my father died, and three or four people that slept in the same room were found dead next Morning. if you can banish the spirits I'll give you a good farm and my daughter, so that you like one another well enough to be mar- ried." " Never say't twice. I've, a middling safe conscience, and don't fear any evil spirit that ever smelled of brimstone." Well and good, the boy got his supper, and then they went up with him to the old castle, and showed him into a large kitchen, with a roaring fire in the • grate, and a table, with a bottle and a glass, and a tumbler on it, and the kettle ready on the hob. They bade him good-night and God speed, and I went off as if they didn't think their heels were half swift enough. " Well," says he to himself," if there's any danger this prayer-book will be usefuller than either the glass or tumbler." So he kneeled down and read a good many prayers, and then sat by the fire and I waited to see what would happen. In about a I quarter of an hour, he heard something bumping ' along the floor overhead till it came to a hole in the ceiling. There it stopped, and cried out," I'll fall, I'll fall." " Fall away," says Jack, and down came a pair of legs on the kitchen floor. They walked o one end of the room, and they stood, and Jack's hair had like to stand upright on his head along with them. Then another crackling and whacking came to the hole, and the same words passed be- tween the thing above and Jack, and down came a man's body and went and stood upon the legs. Then comes the head and shoulders, till the old man,with buckles in his shoes and knee-breeches, and a big flapped waistcoat and a three-cocked hat, was standing in one corner of the room. ',Not to take up your time for nothing, two more men, more old- fashionedly dressed than the first,were soon standing in two other corners, Jack was a little cowed at first ; but found his courage growing stronger every moment, and what would you have of it, the three old gentlemen began to kick a puekeen (football) as fast as they could, the man in the three-cocked hat playing again' the other two. "Fair play is bonny play," said Jack, as bold as bold as he could; but the terror was on him, and the words came out as if he was frightened in his sleep: "so I'll help you, sir." Well and good, he joined the sport, and kicked away till his shirt was wringing wet, savin' your presence, and the ball flying from one end of the room to the other like thunder, and still not a word was exchanged. At last day began to break, and poor Jack was dead beat, and he thought, by the way the three ghosts began to look at himself and themselves, that they wished him to speak. So, says he, "Gentlemen, as the sport is nearly over,and I've done my best to please you,would you tell a body what is the reason of your coming here night after night, and how could I give you rest, if it is rest you want ?" "Them is the wisest words," • says the ghost with the three-cocked hat, " you ever said in your life. Some of those that came before you found courage enough to take a part in our game, but no one had inienacti (energy) enough to speak to us. I am father of the good man of next house, that man in the left corner is my father, and the man on my right is my grandfather. From father to son we were too fond of money. We lent it at ten times the honest interest it was worth ; we never paid a debt we could get over, and almost, starved our tenants and labourers, "Here," says he,lugging a large drawer out of the wall ; " here is the gold and notes that we put together, and we were not honestly entitled to the one-half of it; and here," says he, opening another drawer, "are bills and memorandums that'll show who were wronged, and who are entitled to get a ' great deal paid back to them. Tell my son to saddle two of his best horses for himself and yourself, and keep riding day and night, till every man and woman we ever wronged be rightified. W hen that is done come here' again some night ; and if you don't hear or see anything, we'll be at rest, and you may marry my granddaughter as soon as you please." Just as he said these words, Jack could see the wall through his body, and. when he winked to clear his sight, the kitchen was as empty as a noggin turned upside down. At the very moment the farmer and his daughter lifted the latch, and both fell on their knees when they saw Jack alive.. He soon told them everything that happened, and for three days and nights did the farmer and himself ride about, till there wasn't a. single wronged person left without being paid to the-last farthing. The next, night Jack spent in the kitchen he fei asleep. Before he was after sitting a quarterof al hour at the fire, and in his sleep, he thought he- SfLW three white birds flying up to. heaven from, the steeple of the next church. Jack got the daughter for his wife, and they lived comfortably in the old castle; and if ever he was tempted to hoard up gold, orkeep for a minute a guinea or a shilling from the man that earned it through the nose, he bethought him of the ghosts and the game of foothall.—Legewekry Fictions of Me ..trisbCedi, by Patrick Kennedy.

LONG, referring to the matting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce, at 'Dublin, said their Irish 'friths& were, s usual,i qlospitality itself. There was a very interesting discussion on the question of imperial federation, and there was a. feeling throughout , that if such a thing 'could be brought about it might possibly work well. He added that he believed the meetings of the Associated Chambers of Commerce had great weight with the government of the day in commercial matters. —The Chairman agreed with this opinion, and said he looked forward with very great pleasure to being able to participate in those meetings. The meetings were much more interesting than an ordinary meeting of Par- liament. ' Be added that the Chamber had been able to do something useful with regard to the rivers and the Ship Canal.—Mr. Fleming asked if anything more could be done with regard to the Ship Canal.—Mr. Tunstall said he did not think it would be necessary to do any- thing. He was told that the Canal Company did not propose to make any material alteration.—Mr..Fairclough thought it would be better to leave the matter, over till. the Bill was published.—Mr. Tunstall said they would no doubt be hearing from the Corporation. , The subject then dropped and the meeting terminated.

, . , ACTION UNDER, EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT AT WIDNES. Yesterday week, at Widnes County Court, before his honour Judge Collier, the administrators (father and mother) of the late David Lunt, of Garston, brought an action under the employers' Liability Act, against the London and Manchester Plate Glass Coy., Sutton, for compensation for the death of their son,who was killed at the defendants' works, it was alleged through the negligence of the defendants or of some one in their employ.—Mr. Pickf 3rd, barrister (instructed by Mr. W. T. Hus- band), represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland barrister, (instructed by Mr. Brewis, St. Helens;) the defendants. It appeared that the works were divided into two parts and connected by a line of railtin which there was a sharp curve,at which,point there was a.set.pf points. There was a lever to open the points, but they were 'So constructed tinit•tfie wagon could open them without the aid of the lever. On the 7th October last year, the deceased was assisting in taking a wagon of glass along the line, when one of the wheels caught the points, throwing the wagon. off the points, and causing ,the glass pa be throwh oft the "horse," the wooden structure on which the glas&was placed. 35 cwt. of glass fell upon the deceased, breaking his back, and he died in a few moments. L quantity of glass also fell upon a man named Twist, who was at the lever, with such a force that the handle of the lever went right through his body, and he died immediately. It was alleged that, wazons frequently came off, at this spot, there being a defect in the lapag of .the' metals.— After the evidence had been given, Mr. Mulhol- land contended that there was no., case proved at all. His Honour said the fact that the wagon had frequently coma off the line was printa-facie evidence of a defect.—Rebutting evidence was then called, Mr. Smith, the manager of the works, being the first witness. He examined the line immediately after the acoident, and found no defect except a little move- ment in the "heel chair," and this might have contri- buted to the accident, but he thought there must have been other causes at work. Other' witnesses were Ultimately the judge gave a verdict for the -Ilaintiff for £5O, the £l5 paid by defendants for the uneral expenses to be deducted from this amount.

-- With reference to the recent severe mortality here are two significant facts :—A firm of under- takers in North London announce that no more orders can be taken for a fortnight, and brown horses have had to be called into use for funeral purposes.

Dr. Frederick Leighton, the father of the dis- tinguished Presidet of the Royal Academy, died on Sunday night at 11, Kensington-Park-gardens, at the age of ninety-three. His son, Sir Frederick Leighton, and daughter, Mrs. Sutherland-Orr, were at his bedside when he expired.

Cardinal Al anning's burial place at Kensal Green, was on ',Sunday visited by thousands of people. At the head of the grave is placed a large knot If violets with a small cross of lilies of the valley, sent by the Queen, and amongst the other floral tributes are wreaths from Mr. A.lichael Davitt andothers.

A characteristic story is told of the late Cardinal :Manning. A lady in deep distress called on him. He was in bed sick at the time, but knowing her distressing story, he got up and, afterdressing, saw her. He heard the painful history of her life's trouble repeated, and then lie sent, her to one of his secretaries with instructions that she "should not want for protection and the necessaries of life." After the interview the Cardinal was so prostrated 1 that he panted with exhaustion.

The funeral of Mr. William May, the ornithologist whose death we announced the other day, was largely attended, and it was noted that all those at the graveside kept their hats on. In this, among other matters, it is well to imitate the example of the Jews, who always remain covered at their \ prayers.

Sir John Swinburne, Bart., of Capheaton, New- castle-on-Tyne, is engaged to be married to Miss Cullen, daughter of Dr. Dorsey Cullen, of Richmond, Virginia. Sir John Swinburne met his finance while he was in America representing English interests in the adjustment of the Virginia debt. The Swin- borne baronetcy was created in 1660, and the present baronet is sixty-one years old, and a widower. _His prospective bride is only nineteen. She is not an heiress.

The Middlesex Hospital has a sdandalOns record of deaths from chloroform—three in five months. In August last a porter named Frank Alder, in December a carman named John Coster, and this month a hammerrnan named John Porter have died in the same hospital from the effects of the anesthetic. The inquests in each case have been held by Coroner Danford Thomas, and the verdict has always been "death from misadventure." But there is a terrible reponsibility attaching to such frequ- ent and fatal misadventure.

The mortality among the Tory papers is some— thing fearful. The "St. Stephen's Review" disap- peared on Saturday. Within a week three promi- nent organs of the party have gone to their long homes—the "Anti-Jacobin," the "New York Herald," and the "St. Stephen's Review." In addition to these casualties in the enemy's ranks there have been one or two desertions. It is not long since the "Whitehall ReView " came over to Liberalism, and the "Newspaper Review" has since followed suit. All signs of the flowing tide!

Lady Mary Howard, the sister of the Duke of tiorfolk,is a Sister of Charity of St. Vincent of Paul. The institution over which she presides at Mill Hill is one of the most beautifully situated and com- plete if its kind in the country. There the sisters have from four to five hundred little boys under their charge, all rescued either from East-end work houses or the still more sordid and evil surround- inffs of their own homes. The little fellows are dressed, cared for, and educated by the good Sis- ters until they reach the age of twelve, when they are transferred to homes under the guardianship of priests.

-- Lord Beamont, who escaped many dangers in Zululand and Spain only to succumb to a London fog, was of a restless, romantic, and adventurous disposition. Some years ago he incurred much unpopularity through claiming £20,000 for an acre and an eighth of land at Fulham which was required by the District railway. The jury awarded £7,250. 1.7,rd Beamont was the son-in-law of Mr. F. W. Isaacson, the member for Stepney, but leaves no family, so the title ',asses to his brother, Colonel Stapleton, who is a bachelor, and has surveyed mankind from almost as many points of view as the , late peer.

In well-infamed Catholic circle-s Dr. Yanghan's appointment to the vacant archbishopric is nut now considered probable. The rumor that he would he supported by the Duke of Norfolk is without found- ation, as the Duke's influence.—such as it is—wilLit is stated, be exercised in favour of Dr. Butt, Bishop of Southwark. Dr. Butt, who was a Catholic chap- lain to the forces during the Crimean War,is a Tory, though he never concerts himself in the politics of his priests, the vast majority of whom are Liberals. Re is a native of Richmond, having been born there in 182 G, and since his appointment seven year. ago to Southwark he has managed the affairs of the diocese with great success.

The judges quashed the Old Bailey conviction and censured the Eastbourne bigots. he point to decide was whether the Salvationists had the in- tention to commit a breach of the peace. Justice Hawkins, speaking for himself and kis four col- leagues, said they had come to the unanimous con- clusion that the Salvationists did nothing that could in the least lead any human being to suppose that they intended a breach ot the peace_ They coo- -1 ducted themselves as quietly as they could do. They did play their instruments and beat their drums on the waste land, where they might lafuhly have done so. This decision we hope carries costs with it. It would be manifestly unjust to make the Sal- vationists pay the expenses of a case which ought I never to have been brought._

A most curious coincidence with regard to the death of the late Duke of Clarence has just, come under notice. It is as follows :—There is, it seems. a superstition that when " Big Ben," the clock at Westminster, strikes irregularly at midnight evil, will befall the Royal house within three months. At twelve o'clock on the night of November 14, the members of a political club within a stoue's throw of the Houses of Parliament were astonished to hear the quarter chimes sounding simultaneously with the hour strokes, and to note that Big Ben struck thirteen times. The event was commented on. and the day being a critical one in the illness of Prince George, his name was, happily incorrectly. associated with the evil omen. Two months later, to the very day, his elder brother died.

Some burglars who have continued to elude the researches of the Birmingham police are at this moment in possession of an article which from a professional point of view must be regarded by them as eminently disappointing. It consists of a magnificeat chain of state, originally manufac- tured for the purpose of decorating the person of an African prince, which was stolen by them the other night from the warehouse of a dealer in brie- ti-bric in that town. Its stately appearance and massive form doubtless satisfied the thieves who made off with it that they haoksecured a precious booty ; but unluckily for OM the bric-a-bric dealer reports that instead of being silver it is only nickel-plate of little value. The practical mind of the African prince, it appeared, did not value what was precious so much as what would dazzle the eyes of his simple subjects. -- John Henry Maden, the hero of more than the hour, is one of the best-known manufacturers in Lancashire. Liberal in nature as in name he sue- creded to a large fortune from his father and a great reputation for generosity and kindness of heart. "Mester Madin " is what Rossendalians call him before strangers, but in his presence and to each other his emplo3'6s speak of him as "John Henry." He is not quite twenty-nine years old, and his ap- pearance, save for the abence of clerical attire, is that of the traditional curate. He is pale, fair- haired, slightly built, of moderate height, rather nervous in manner, and wears pince-nez. Before the cares of cottol manufacture and politics claimed his whole attention he was a keen footballer. Ile has lately married a wife, and his house at Bacup is among the best in the County Palatine.

KAY'S COMPOUND, for Coughs and Colds. Asthma, and Bronchitis are immediaeely relieved by It.—Adrt. A Hong Kong telegram reports the safety of the Rev. J. Parker, of the London Missionary Society, regarding whom much anxiety had been felt during the recent attacks on Christians in China. The same telegram re- ports the beheading of 200 straggling and private looters after the defeat of the rebels at Clutoyung.

div.head: YOU MUST HAVE A GOOD STOVE.
div.p: YOU MUST HAVE A GOOD STOVE.

You can't have a fire without burning some kind of fuel. You agree to this? Why, of course. Well, now suppose you had bought a stove in which no fuel what- ever would burn, what would you do ? Throw it back on the dealer's hands and get another ? To be sure.
Now, fancy you had— But let us have the story first and draw the conclusion
afterwards.

A woman tells this bit of experience : It was in 1882," she says, " when I began to feel ill and out of sorts. I did not know what was the matter with me. In the morning I was tired and languid, and _ . _

was constantly spitting and belching up a clear fluid like water. My appetite gradually left me, and I had great pain after every morsel I ate. I had great pain at the chest, which at times seemed to strike through to the back and shoulders. I lost a good deal of sleep at niiht owing to spasms and to wind that appeared to gatherin my sides. No food, however simple, agreed with me. For three years I suffered like this, and could take no solid food, such as a meat dinner. "Now, as I had always been of an active disposition, I strove hard to do my work and attend to my shop, but in April, 1885, .1 got so bad that I sent for my
, daughter, who was living at Priest Hutton, near Carn- forth, and she returned home. Whilst away she had been under a doctor for weakness and neuralgia, but getting

no better she had been recommended to take a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and this cured her ; so she insisted upon my taking the same medicine. I got a bottle from Messrs. Needham Bros., chemists, Brighouse, and began t 3 take it. In a day or two I found relief. Soon all my pains leec me, and I gradually gained strength. I could eat my food, and after having used two bottles I found myself completely cured. " I have recommended this medicine to many of my friends and customers who come to my shop, and it has done them good ;so 1 think it right that its virtues should be made as widely known as possible."
(Signed) Mrs. Coiling; grocer, Rastrick, Brighouse, near Halifax. •

Another woman says :—ln December, 1835, after my 1 confinement, I began to have a poor appetite and much 1 pain and sickness after eating. My food seemed to turn to wind, and I suffered from fulness in the chest and pain in the stomach. I gradually lost my strength, and fell into adow, desponding state of mind. However light food I took! had pain, so that I became afraid to eat. I lost a deal of sleep, and got so weak I was frequently obliged to lie down on the couch and rest. At times the pain was almost more than I could bear, and I had to go to bed and have hot salt applied to my chest and stomach, for when those attacks came on I felt as if I was dying. The doctor who attended me said! was suffering from Chronic indigestion, and that something was wrong with the " upper stomach." What a strange statement for a doctor to make ! He did all he could to relieve me, but without success, and I lingered on in this way for twelve months. About this time Mr. Connor, Stevedore, living at Dennison Street, told my father of the great benefit he had de- rived from taking Mother Seigel's Syrup, and I sent at once and got a bottle, and after taking three bottles all pain left ins. I got strong and could eat anything,and from that time to this I have never been ill. I keep the ' medicine in the house, and if any of the family all any- thing a dose or two of Mother seigelss Syrup sets them right. (Signed) Mrs. Reid, 12, Galton-st., Great Howard-st., Liverpool. We said you cannot have a fire without burning some kind of fuel. The human stomach is a stove, and food is the fuel we put into it. If the food is consumed, or digested, the body 14 nourished and built up, and we en- joy health and stterigth ; but if otherwise we quickly waste away and perish. Now, when the stomach re- fuses to digest, burn, or consume food, we have what is called indigestion and dyspepsia, the most common and dangerous of all diseases. This is what ailed these two women, and what ails millions more in this country The conclusion is plain enough :—The remedy which cured them will cure others. Then (the fire burning well) we shall have heat, which is life and' power.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL, AND THE DEATH OF THE DUKE OF CLARENCE.

On Saturday, at floors, a meeting of the Warring- ton Town Council was held at the Town Hall,having been specially convened for the purpose.of consider- ing a proposal with reference to the death of the Duke of Clarence. The. Mayor (Alderman Greenall) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Burgess, Francomb, Harrison, and Wright; Coun- cillors Hepherd, R. T. Fhirclough, Ashton, Bolton, Bonen, Muir, Hill, Dixon, FL Roberts, F. W. Monks, and Brown; Mr. J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk.)—The - 'Nall said that, as they all knew, they had been tansoned there that day to express their sympathy with the Royal_ Family.. Ile would move " That addresses of condolence be presented to her alajesty the queen and their Royal Hignesses the Plince and Princess of Wales, on the occasion of the lamented death of 11.R.H. the Duke of Clarence and Avondale." —261631:man FaiNcoun said it-was with feelings of the deepest sorrow that he rose 'so second the proposition. At their last meeting it was decided that they should at a very early date adopt some method of showing the loyalty of their ancient borough for Her Majesty the Queen,.and also of expressing their love for the prince and his young bride. Since then death had removed from amongst them the Duke. of Clarence, and he was sure he was only expressing the feelings of the Council and of his fellow townsmen when he said that they deeply deplored the death of the young prince. Lie was also deeply grieved at the sad fate which had 'I befallen the Princess May. (Hear, hear.)—Akierman Bcaosse expressed his pleasure at seeing the Mayor again equal to taking the chair after his severe 'illness. (Hear, hear.) It was a painful sul4-et that had called them together, and they felt very acutely for her Majesty, who had occupied the throne for more than half a century-. It must have been a blow of a very serious character at her advanced period of life. So far as the parents of the young Prince were concerned they had had to go through an ordeal of so • I trying a character that only those who had gone- through the seine domestic affliction could realise it. Fie hoped that they might be sustained in their great affliction, and it might be something to them to know,.and for the Queen herself to know, that the sympathies a the en- tire peopleof the country were flowing out to them in a way he had never witnessed before. So far as the Princess May was concerned her affliction was of the most trying kind and could not easily be realised. Time alone could wear out the painful result of the blow that had fallen upon her, and he hoped that she too might have& sustaining power. He trusted that so far as he was concerned he should never again be called upon to to take the part he was taking in that meeting. (Hear, hear.)—Alderman HARRISON also spoke to, the proposi- tion, which was then passed.

div.head: _ 4. WARRINGTON" CHAMBER OF COMORO E.
div.p: _ 4. WARRINGTON" CHAMBER OF COMORO E.

The annual meeting of this Chamher of Commerce was held at the Chamber, Bewsey-street, Warring- on Monday morning). Mr. W. Pierpoint pre- sided, and there were also present, Councillor J. H. Fleming, Mr. W. Long, Mr. J. Fairolough, Mr. J. L. Tunstall (hon. secretary) and Mr, C. Lae (collector). -

div.head: ERECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ERECTION OF OFFICERS.

Mr. W. Pierpoint was elected president, and Councillor J. FL Fleming vice-president ; hon., treasurer, Mr. John Dun ; hon. secretaries, Mr. J. Davies and Mr. J. L. Tunstall ; auditors, Mr. Z. Armitage and Mr. T. Tunstau, F.C.A. ; collector, Mr. C. Lee. The Council was also re-elected. THE REPC4I.I% The Council report of the Council for the past year was as follows :—" Messrs. William Long and Jcseph Davies attended, on behalf of the Chamber, the Autumnal meet- ing of the Association of Chambers of Commerce, when resolutions were passed in favour of :—lmperial Federa- tion; amendment of the law as to rating machinery ; amendment of the Companies Act ; codification of the law ; extension of County Court Jurisdiction ; iin- provement of the system of private bill legisla- tion ; improvement of Parliamentary procedure by the continuance of hills in succeeding sessions ; improvement of the American mail service; postal re- forms; increasing the facilities for the delivery of tele- grams; regulation of the telephonic system ; telegraphic and telephonic communication with light-houses and light-ships ; registration of firms; and the adoption of the decimal system. In order to facilitate tenders by the local tanners, the Admiralty, in the spring of last year, exhibited at the Warrington Chamber samples of heavy leather goods, and the Council have since been , favoured with an interview with the Director of Navy Contracts for the discussion generally of the facilities given to manutacturers who tender for Admiralty Con- tracts. The chief manufacturers in the district have since been invited to send in their names for submission to the Admiralty, so that forms of tender may in future I be supplied to them. div.head: HOW JACK CAME HOME,
div.p: HOW JACK CAME HOME,

Four long years had Jack the sailor been away,,, and his ship was reported "lost, with all on board."' The news seemed to pile years CAI his father's bent , shoulders ; his mother's smile faded out, and, wrinkles seamed her cheeks. One summer day, however, as the two came slowly out of church with their pretty daughters —all three scarcely balancing the loss of the one dear son—a shabby, bronzed, and handsome fellow rushed up to the group, and took his mother in his arms. " It's my boy I my own boy !" cried she,. throwing her arms about him and smothering him with kisses, while the father managed to get possession of one brown, sinewy hand. "Come, mother,give as a chance cried the girls in chorus, and by this time the entire- congregation had surrounded the wanderer, and claimed his greeting. " But you were drowned; Jack !" exclaimed the youngest sister, and J laughed as he explained: "No, only partly. TN. of Us floated for days, reached an island in the Pacil- fic, fell in with friendly savages, and then—waited for a ship. Got my belt full of money, father, but couldn't wait to buy a rag of decent clothes." Then the minister said solemnly, "-Let us pray," and there under the trees, with uncovered head, he offered thanks for the wanderer's return. When he had finished every one was softly weeping, and not a soul dreamed that the tragic joy of the occasion could be turned into mirth. Suddenly Jack's mother, wrought up beyond endurance, opened her lips and spoke. "Jack," said she, sharply, "aint you as- hamed to come to meetin with such a ragged oM hankercher as that ?" Jack roared, and so did the neighbours. Tears were wiped away, and laughter reigned.

THE Ronnoits OF THE RUSSIAN FAMINE. TERRIBLE MORTALITY. A St. Petersburg correspondent says tht? most distress- ing accounts continue to come in from the extreme Eastern districts. At Tumen, a great centre for emi- grants on their way to Siberia, the ravages of disease, especially influenza and various forms of typhus, have reduced the population by one-half. The emigrants being poor, the priests in many cases refuse to bury the dead, pretending that they do not belong to the parish. It is not uncommon to see families wandering about with a cart full of coffins from church to church until they find a priest who will perform the last rites.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT

ROMANCE. An old man nam.d 111• Kenna, living at Deptford, has just had a remarkable experience of the vicissitudes of fortune. He and his dacv,hter, aged 18, caught influenza, and, the girl dying, M.Kenna was left to shift for himself, with only a few shillings between him and starvation. One day last week a fashionably,dressed lady drove up to the house and asked for M•Kenna. She was shown into his room, and at the sight of him she dropped on her knees and exclaimed Oh, Jack, forgive me !" it I was his wife. Twenty years ago she eloped with his best friend to California, where her paramour made a huge fortune in the gold fields. He died recently, and the woman returned to England to find M'Kepaa. The pathetic part of the romance is, that in nursing the old fellow back to health she herself caught influenza, and just died of pneumonia, leaving him £62,000.

div.head: MEETING OF WARRINGTON. SHOP
div.p: MEETING OF WARRINGTON. SHOP

ASSISTANTS. ' FORMATION OF AN ASSOCIATION. On Tuesday evening a well attended meeting o' shop assistants was held in the rooms in Bold-street, lately occupied by the . Young Men's Christian Association. Mr. Cummings prestded. The CHAIRMAN explained that the'object of the meet- ing was,in the first place,to consider as to the desirability of reducing the number of hours worked by shop assist- , ants in the town. He said Mr. Powell, one of Messrs. Melia's assistants, sent circulars out to from 20-ttf 30 assistants, asking them, to meet, him in the a.djiiiiing room. They met him, and he (Mr. Cummings) was chairrnan of the meeting; - and it was urianittrously resolved tolortn a small Committee-pro tem, to try the feelings of the shop-keepers, with regard to adopting either early closing in the evening or a half-holiday in the week. Al. certain number of the Committee were selected to visit the tradesmen. ' On the part of a very large majority of all classes of tradesmen there was a desire to make some concession. The Comniittee had called the present meeting to consider the matter, and had obtained the services of &gentleman from Liverpool, of large and varied experience in these matters, to addrdss them. The hours of assistants in Lixerpool had been greatly reduced, while in other towns shorter hours or the half holiday were being granted, but in Warring- ton the "shop assistants had been putting in unreason- ably long boors) andkthings were growing worse. At one time nearly all the grocers in the town closed at o'clock; now a 'great many of them kept open, till eight or nine. It was also thought desirable that the shop assistants- of Warrington should form themselves into an association, whether they now obtained any concessions or. not. (Applause.) Had there been such. an association in Warrington years ago to have acted as other associations had done, informed new tradesmen coming to the town of the adoptioh of early closing, the privilege would pot have - come 3 to an end througn the new corners keeping Open later. The Chairman read a resolution by a meeting of the Evan- gelical Nonconformist MinistereAssociation instructing the secretary to, write to the local press in favour of the agitation. (Applause.) The Chairman expressed him- self in favour of asking for early closing rather than the half holiday at present, and was met with some excla- mations of dissent, but assured the meeting that what- ever it decided should have his support. Mr. KAY proposed a motion that they apply for the half holiday. (Loud applause.), He argued that this Would benefit both those who worked late, and those who worker( shorter hours, and would allow them an opportunity of going out of the-Itown to enjoy them- selves. If they worked with a will they would get both early closing and the half holiday in time. Mr. Pncrciresnoseconded. Mr. McDovar,n, proposed an amendment in favour of applying for closing at seven o clock instead of for the half holiday. He thought if they got the latter passed it was extremely probable they would get back to later hours on other days. (Cries oi "No.") He strongly advocated earlier closing on Saturday night. Mr. A. Caaves seconded the amendment. Mr. Revs 31aotes, secretary of the- Liverpool Grocers' Association, then addressed the meeting. He commenced by deploring the manner in which the movement was hindered by the want of unanimity among the shop assis- tants. As to taking excursions from the town on a half holiday, he questioned whether the- assistants if no bet- ter paid than in Liverpool, and especially if married could afford this. Early closing in the evening would give them time for recreation and self improvement in the evenings. The half holiday would come later on. When working-men were agitating. for eight hour's wont a day, surely shop,assistants would not be content to work 16 to 18 hours, a day, provided they only got a half holi- day. But if, they did not form, an organisation they would never accomplish their obiects. The advantages of combination were strongly urged by the speaker. It would for instance not only be the means of reduchig the hours he said, but also of putting an end to the dis- placement of men of age-and experiencehy their juniors in shops, as the result of which.there was scarcely an aged man to be found in the grocery and provision trade in Liverpool. Early closing, was going to be triea at 150 shopsin the south of Liverpool. and if it took well there it would soon'be adopted in the north of the city. Mr. STLI2IIE advocated the half holiday, and another speaker early closing. The amendment and original motion were pot, when the original motion was carried by a considerable majority. ' It was unanimously decided to form an Association, aad .a provisional committee was afterwards appointed. -
THE QUEEN AN]) ZEE _DITEE OF
_ CLARENCE'S DEATH. A supplement to the "London Gazette " of Wednesday night publishes the following letter from the queen, which has been received by the Home Secretary :

" Osborne, January 26, 1892. "I must once again give expression to my deep sense of the loyalty and affectionate sympathy evinced by my subjects in every part of my empire on an occasion more sad and tragical than any but one which has befaJlen me and mine, as well as the nation. The overwhelming misfortune of my dearly-beloved grandson having been thus suddenly nit off in the flower of his age, full of promise for the future,amiable and gentle,and endearing himself to all, ;enders it hard for his sorely-stricken par- ents, his dear young bride, and his fond grandmother, to bow in submission to the inscrutable decrees of Pro- vidence. The sympathy of millions, which has been so touchingly and visibly expressed, is deeply gratifying at such a time, and I wish, both in my own name and that of mty children, to express from my heart my warmest gratitude for all these testimonies of sympathy with us and appreciation of my dear grandson,whorn I loved as 44 son, and whose devotion to me was as groat as that of a son. It will be a help and consolation to ine and mine ill our affliction. My bereavements during the last 30 years of my reign have indeed been heavy. Though the labours, anxieties, and responsibilities inseparable from my posi- tion have been great, yet it is my earnest prayer that God may continue to give me health and strength to work for the good and happiness of my dear country and empire while life lasts.
66 vlcrolus, R. 1."

33y LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," " Where. the North Wind Blows,"--thc., the.

BELL WIDDRINGTON'S SWEETHEART. Like the generality of fisher dwellings in the vicinity, that of the Widdringtons had capabili- ties for the safe and secret stowage of goods which 'did not pay duty. Free-trading was not considered a crithe by those who spoke of it under that 'euphemistic term. Even though not actively en- gaged in it himself, every. man had a sneaking sympathy for it, and disdained not the comfortable 'luxuries it provided, at a very moderate cost. .Farmers left their stable doors unlocked at nights, and were in nowise dismayed when they found their horses wearied and in a lather of sweat of 'mornings; magistrates winked at the illegal doings, ,in consideration ,of the excellent quality of the Cognac or Hollands, contraband but cheap; brought to their cellars without any, trouble or expense on their own parts. The smugglers ran the risk of being shot or hanged indeed, but when fate over- took them there were always others ready to fill their places, and keep up the supply. They had many difficulties to contend with, and dangers to brave, but then they were favourites while the Excise officers were the objects of favourites, and derision with the public, especially those who were strict in the performance of their duty. People were heavily taxed, and considered themselves justified in evading the law, and supplying their wants in a cheap and ready manner. So it came to pass that the old houses and fisher cottages on the coast are fitted with all sorts of queer contrivances, mementos of past times, re- maining after the need for them is over. Perhaps the owner would not object, even in the present day, to evade the law in this respect, for smuggling is like consumption, difficult to get out of a race, and 'lingers. in the blood for generations; but at least they do not proceed :to such extreme measure- as formerly, when a revenue officer:was considere quite as fair game for a stray shot as a rabbit or seagulL Window seats 'are hollow, there are.re* ceases behind fireplades and in chimneys, and unsuspected- 'cellars lurking under flooring of apparent solidity. Many a valuable bale of goods has,been seeurely hidden welder, a, pile of nets, and , barrels of salted fish have been known tO containf tobacco, while even the big homely cottage hid has shown a'decided tendency to run to ?minable lace and silk hose in its interior in place of crumb. But, much to the disgust of Bill, her twin , brother, and still more so of old Nanny in the chimney corner, Bell Widdrington had set her face against any active participation in the profitable game of smuggling, and would not allow the lockers and hiding-places in their cottage ta, be used for storage. In this'respect she was upheld by Cuddy, the eldest Widdrington, a guiet,/mther dour. of twenty-four, who had. " experienced religion 'I short time previously from the sermons and minis- trations Of an itinerant Methodist preacher, and who gave up his share in the quick sailing sloop Bonny Bess to his younger brother in conOtinence- He could not reconcile, the free trading with ins aroused.and sensitive conscience, and.yet was loth that such a lucrative investment shinild go 'out of the family altogether, so, he ,effected,acompromise. But he did not wish his sister to hold a candle to the devil, and was glad when she declared for ,neutral dealing. He sometimes feared that her heart was enlisted, against her conscience, on the side of the smugglers. It was well known that she loved Dickag.lish,_ the most reckless and daring of the crew,. and Cuddy lived in fear of her casting her lot amongst them for the sake of Dick. As it happened, he did not give Bell credit for as much firmness and self-possession as she really DoftgeSPlA4.- - any connectron with smuggling must needs be concealed, there Was no similar reason why the waifs and strays that came legitimately in the shape of wreckage should also be hidden. There- fore the cottage was decorated with some strange memorials of the sea. A figure-head of the Medusa with entwining snakes, snakes once bright and picked out with gold, but from which the constant washing of wave and spray had worn away the gilding, and embel- lished with a decided and terrible squint, adorned .the wall above the fireplace; while two really charming panels with pastoral landscapes, a la, Watteau, must have originally formed part of the decorations of the cabin of,some gay pleasure craft. Amongst the coarse delft and china on a rude shelf was a metal casket of rare and delicate workman- ship, most probably of Indian origin; and a brass hanging lamp, exquisitely carved and fretted, from; some Eastern mosque or temple, was used as a reCeptacle for netting needles, twine and spare fines. , ,The effect of this incongruity was strange, bizarre yet not wholly unpleasing at least it formed a picturesque background for the splendid' figure of the fisher-lass, Bell, as she moved about,. prepariagtfor the return of her brothers., Bill; the younger of them, canto in first. He was generally ahead of Cuddy, who took deliberate. step!, audit must be confessed in justice, generally carried the heavier load. ' • Bill wet twin brother to Bell, and had no small share Of her 'g9od looks. They were, in fact, so. much alike that, had they been both. habited in either masculine or feminine garb, it would have been difficult to distinguish them. Bell was tall for a woman, Bill was, if anything, short for a man. It was only after careful study and long acquaintance that Bell's eyes were seen to be calmer and graver in expression, and her lips firmer in outline, than those of her merry twin brother. Bill was in a boisterous mood. "We're gaun to hey a game on the neet, Bell,. and get rid o' th' liquor that's stored away—ye know where? So I maim ha' ma supper and be off in a jiffey, lass! Mebbe yell see yer sweetheart afore theneet's over. He'll never ride by without_ a lbok at ye?" " What ? Is Dick cumin'?" Bill nodded. He was already seated at the. table, and devouring, a huge bowl of porridge at double quick speed, all scalding hot as it was. At it descended, he tempered its heat with great draughts of milk. Old Nanny's ears were quick to,catch the intima- tion Of eomoing mischief, although she had been nodding over the fire's moment before. "Ay, ay, ma bonny lad, thotell beat them all for pluck and. cumin', aw'se warrant.' It wasn't for nowt aw dreamt thou was- hung on a high gallows the neet afore thou was born -If. that stands for bad luck, thou needn't fetch me either 'Jamey or Holism& from the Bonny Bess next run she makes." Bill's hearty laugh rang through the room. "Ch, granny, ye beat th' warld for bad dreams wi' good meaning to them. An' would sooner be promoted i' SCUM other fashion than that, if it's all the same to. yen" "Dreams go.bycontraries, ma canny Bill!" "All the 'inkier for me, then! But ye shall yer baccy and yer gin, granny, until the noose is round ma throttle. Bell! war Cuddy'll gotten a sweetheart at last in " Hand yer tongue! None o' yer lees,. lad !" " True's death! It's Jinny Dodd, Matthe Ogle's widow woman, her wi' six bairns, and a deevil of a temper into th' bargain I" " Yer jokin' ?" Bill's eyes twinkled with merriment. He had finished his supper, and felt dying to tell his news,, so lingered, spite of his professed haste. "It's the grandest fun! She's been made a saint on too, and though it's not improved her temper, she sings hymns and makes pious exclamations during her, fits o' passion. As we went by this morn, she was giver' young Mat his licks, and calm' him, all the time. 'Wad ye disobey yer Mother, yer gobby young toad, ye, and set up your sauce, forbye ? Glory, Glory, Hallelujah ,ve a mansion in the sky !—Let me get hand on ye, aw'll tan yes hide, if ever it was tanned !—Glory, Glory, Hallelujah What a humble worm ain r Here's wor Criddy ! Diarvent tell on us !" And off the narrator bolted, leaving Bell and old Nanny convulsed with suppressed laughter, which they did not dare to indulge in before the morose and austere Cuddy. Bell wondered whether the said Cuddy who really smitten with the widow, who was rather a comely personage, half a dozen years older than himself, Iput could not summon sufficient courage to ask him the question. Certainly he spruced himself up more than he was wont to do when he went to the village of a night And since he had given up the drink, he could not go to the public on these occasions. Where, then, did he spend the time? After he had gone as usual to the village, all was very 'quiet Bell had just got her' granny safely tucked into bed, and was sitting by the fire looking into the dying embers, when suddenly her quick ears detected the sound of a horse's hoofs in the distance. She started up, and her face &rew full of

eager rongfng, as sne put more ruei on tne tire, talc! stirred it into a cheerful blaze. Thea she listened again. Yes it stopped before the door, and a low - melodious Yes, imitating closely the notes Of thrush, came stealing in at the door. 134 gave a laugh, brimful of happineinkliftgss and de- -- . light, and was out of the cottage in a. horseman, who was standing there, leapt to the griound, and was by her side as quickly. "Is the e 1 e st clear, lass ?" he asked, in a low voice, "lßill t ed me he'd had to dodge the coast-g,uard , t night., and he wasn't sure which way theY'd . gdne.' ." Aw've seen none o' them !" replied Bell. The min thereupon led his horse into a shed, tied it 1117,' , by the reins, and followed Bell into the kitchen 01 . the cottage. As he stood by the fire, vvhidi Ivo . n#w burning brightly, and throwing a ruddY glow 1 over the room, he showed to great advantagfo ""' "j, - fine well-built man, of perhaps thirty years of age'. ' with a good ,natured bronzed face, curling darli hair, and merry black eyes. Bell looked at hinz , with pride and pleasure, but shook her head. , i "ye shouldn't ha' come the nest, when them , fellows are on th' look cot 1" she said in f 0314 ' reproof. ' ' Oh, never lash about them! ma bonn7 J''-'' , • ': ir4 Aw've led them a dance afore, and can dee it aga 4 . lif needs be! An' how d'ye think aw can live with: ' out a look at you, ma darlin' ?" As he spoke he drew her to him, and for just a ' i moment she yielded herself to his embrace. Then 1 she sighed : I " Dick, ma canny man, aw wish thou'd give 1-11't this game, and settle down. There's many a need ' aw canna a sleep a wink for thinking o' thee, an:-',' , the narrow escapes thou's had! Oh, Dick lad, 1' they took thee it would be the death. o' me too! .L 1 "No fear, Bell! Wi' ma good mare Gir! . , ea:Leath me, aw can leave th' best on them far De' 1 bind! Wait a bit, aw'm not tired o' th' game yet. 1 Its very' danger helps th' fun on't. Not that there's much o' danger either," went on Dick, suddenlY ve' membering'Bell's fears. "There's only one thing , makes me tired on't 1" " Ah' what's that, Dick?" asked the girl seftlY ' " His arms were round her, and his eyes burnt into hers, and filled her with delicious tremors. "Thou knows reet well! It's thysel;my beau* Ye've sod ye winna wed me till aw leave it off, ye're as obstinate as a mule when once yer miati'• made up. Bell, aw'm tired o' livin' without Ye? that's the long an' the short on't 1 Aw want ye fc'r ma wife, lass." , " Wey, wey, them's nowt but words. Ye 10°,1'd the terms, an' ,ye can do as ye like, aw show g 5, y. , 7 As he held her tightly to him, she could. feel his heart beat tumultuously against her own, and this moved her strongly. She loved him, body and seall she loved him more than anything in the world, longed to be his. But he was quite correct in wl'' he had stated, for all that! la -, Poverty she did not dread, hardships she vvo", endure right willingly, if he were only with be'ri f` but this perpetual evasion of the law on the Pa of the free traders entailed penalties she did are*, aad would not willingly endure. Her mind Iva! made up, and on this subject she was firm. Ali th.e : influeribe she possessed should be used against the ; illegal proceedings. " But she was a woman, and a passionate one lar_ the bargain, and her resolution was not held vf , without a struggle. Dick knew perfectly well thati'' . d o she was very fond of him, and tried, as he ha ftee .! tried before, to use that fondness as a lever to Oa" her from her fixed determination. • • He could feel her thrill and tremble in hi ' arms, and this gave him a triumphant sense victory,' His kisses grew more frequent upon he' ! lips. , "Don't be cruel, &din'," he whispered pa: ately, ", think better on't an' let me call yorlr'_,,,aiir" 11 Why should we keep apart when our whole ow. , .* are crying out for one another? • Be 4 " lit *, altogether, Bell lass, for aw canna live withoer, ~ , any longer ! " use If he expected her to lower her colours heea • ' her heart fought on his side he was doomed- to appointment, for in a moment she wrenched free, and stood aloof; panting but resolute., 1 "If y, loved me as much as ye pretend to, 1 1 ye would give up the smugglin' for ma sake. 1 telled ye yea mind. once and for all, Ind it's do right cruel on ye to, tempt ma" Dick laughed, with the bitter acorn born of rin, "It's precious little aw- can do to tempt 7,3,17,-,, woman, it appears to ma If yer blood was h‘°'' ,0 through yer veins, like mine is, ye wouldn't P°' '- mighty stand-offish, aw'l warrant ! ' "Dick, how dare ye speak to me like cried Bell, stamping her foot, and. her eyes a.'_,„"iii, with sudden anger "ye forget yersel', ay* to"' or else ye forget Who ye're talkin' to 1r Dick hung his head sheepishly for a while, theli as his grew calmer, he held out his hand. '; " Dinna be angry with me, sweethesirt,7 he 6-00 "there's whiles aw think ye dinna care abbat, to' since ye can keep so calm, and it makes me Ma"' , Bell laid her soft arms round his neck. "Never think 'that, lad. Ye vex me, wri ,it ma temper gets the better on me, but Dick, la'-",,i1l love ye mair than anything in the world, and a prove it to ye some day!" "That's ma own canny Bell! But, ma conscieh:isZ' thou is a spitfire when thoo's vexed.," he „5,.,j, * teasing her. She only smiled. 4)11 ye'd wall.; milk-and-water one ye wouldn't ha chosen rre " Ye're reet there, lass 1 Aw never love Ye '-aad than when ye get. into one o' yor tantraraa,ro ! make me frightened ye'll stick a knife jut% But then aw know it's always when awdeseVol te, ' Noo lass, aw must be off. Awm gannin 40°,„,a1el the, Point, an' then off over the moors to P`"ajle,4lo Farm wi' a barrel ,slung on either side of in etier. . Wish me good luck o th' ride. IS BRIGHT'S DISEASE CURABLE? (" Family Doctor," November 7, 1851.) As showing the increased attention which the public htinvr evince in such matters, the London "Evening News and Post" " devoted a whole column of its issue of August, ±neh to a résumé of the opinions of English and foreign Specialists on the important question" Is Bright's Disease curable ? ' In view of the generally accepted opinion and belief that there is no help for a patient whose case has bees ngnesed as Bright's disease, and which opinion and ..'ll,q is, we make bold to say, fostered by the medical prosession, it must have been with surprise that the readers of that most interesting article learned that such atilniOg lights as Sir Morell Mackenzie, Dr. Madlagan, Physician to the Princess Christian and other members Of. the Royal Fa nily, Dr, Samuel Mills, Dr. Herbert 'l.ffihes and other medical men of prominence in Lon- don, express the opinion that while some phases are incurable, others are certainly curable, or that life may be at least prolonged for a longer or shorter period. This Opinion is also held by Doctors Dujardin, Beaumetz, Paris, Labadie-Lagrave, and Professor of Paris, Professor Senator of Berlin, and Professors Noth- naiel, Schroetter, and Winternitz of Vienna. One eminent gentleman, Professor Gerinain Lee, of the fact de Medicin, of tans, callsaltention to the fact that the presence of albumen in the urine does not necessarily:denote Bright's disease—a mistake that is too frequently made by the ordinary practitioner. It must be a matter of self-commendation to the pro- qirietors of Warner's " Safe" Cure to note that in ex- 'Pressing the opinions referred to, the medical gentlemen Mentioned but line out the arguments and mode of treat- Merit followed by Messrs. Warner With such wonderful 11.nceess for some years. There can be no doubt that to .weesrs. Warner's persistent efforts to educate the people as to the functions and importance ot those great organs. the kidneys and the liver, considerable attention has 'been directed to them, and as such knowledge is of a' most desirable character, we cannot but sympathise with the result of their efforts. That they are successful we cannot doubt, when we notice the reference to them that has recently appeared in the flnancial j.,urnals. 'While on the subject of Bright's disease, we reproduce a testimonial of recent date, the original of which we have seen, and which we have every reason to believe is genuine. Birley Carr, Wadsley Bridge, Sheffield, October 3rd, MIL I will relate just the bare facts of my case, and will SaY that no swearing to statement will be necessary, for enme hundreds of people can bear witness as to its truth. Three years ago fever brake out in our neighbour- hood and my children were attacked by it. An anxious ti,nie followed—night and day I nursed them till my Strength gave way. My legs swelled with the constant 'Wear upon them, and a large abscess forming *von one, ~ was obliged to take to my bed. Whilst lying there typhoid fever attacked me., and I was unconscious for ions weeks. When the fever left me I was informed by the doctor that Bright's disease had 'settled in my system --then dropsy set in. From that time life was a tor- 'inent, and not to be desired. My body swelled to an enormous size. I was tortured with excruciating pains. Although swollen to such a size, the doctors (I had now two in attendance)would not tap me. " It Was no use," they said, " the kidneys ibeing entirely useless. I would make water as fast as it was drawn frons ray body." Then I begged my old doctor to tell me the worst, so he told me there was no possible hope, I had but a few days to live, and all he could co now was to make them Pass as easily as possible. .Day by day he said the end Vas nearer, and I was glad, for two of my children had flied whilst I lay there, and I did not want to live. At last but one more day's "life seemed left to me. Both doc- tors had tried everything in their power, and both said that 24 hours must see the end. Still, I was to have eam more chance. Taking my husband aside, my old doctor said, " Thereisan American named Warner.who advertises that he can cure cases of Bright's disease by rnea as of his "Safe. Cure. He had not inucli faith in it, but we could try it if we liked ; it could do no harm, and it might do good. But there was no time to lose, and in the meantime he would send round some Medicine. The doctorthen loft, and my husba.nd rushed off to Sheffield to get the "Safe" Cure. 'Presently the doctor's man came with two bottles of medicine, with instructions to take some at once. I was still living when my husband returned, and gradually improved. My husband having ,compared the dectar's medicine With the "Safe" Cure obtained from Sheffield found them to be alike. Speaking of this to my nurse, she told me that there were three empty Warner's " Safe" Cure bottles in the doctor's house. So we knew for a fact that the doctor himself had as a last. chance given me that " Safe " Cure. My recovery was slow, but sure. And at the end of two weeks the abscess burst. 'First matter and then clear water flowed, and continued to flow until my body regained its usual size, and I had no return of the dropsy. Three months eterwards 1 went down to Sheffield market. In eight months I was entirely recovered. Since then I have been to America arid back. Such is my statement, and freely do I give 7°ll Permission to publish it. MRS. LOUISA VireODFIELD. Witnesses { JassEs W °ODE lELD. • HENRY NATHAN.

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The adjourned annual meeting of the members of this Society was hetd in the Co-operative Sankey-et., on Monday evening. There was a very large attendance. The Prtsident (Mr. T. Birchall) occupied the chair, and in his opening remarks he Mentioned that that was the 31st annual meeting of the Society. le also referred to the steady pro- gress the Society had made, and to its almost pre- eminent position amongst similar societies. Ile believed that the reserves standing to the credit of the Society were larger than those of any other society of equal size. He then referred to the new check system, and dealt with some criticisms that had been made at the previous meeting upon the management of the Society.—The minutes of the Committee of Management were submitted to the meeting and unanimously adopted. It was re- ported by Mr. Rath bone, the managing secretary, that during the past quarter 615 new members had joined, while there had been 110 withdrawals. The balance shest showed that, during the past quarter, the total sales had amounted to £22,034 Is. Bd. which was very largely in excess of any previous quarter. The committee recommended that a dividend of 3s. 2d. in the £ be paid upon purchases amounting to £25,188. It was explained that the excess of purchases upon which dividend had to be raid over the sales, was due to the calling in of all the old metal cheques, owing to the adoption of the new cheque system. The balance sheet was adopted unanimously. The following officers were re-elected without opposition :—President, Mr. T. , Birchall; treasurer, Mr. W. Ford : auditor, Mr. J. Shaw Green ; members of committee, Messrs. R. Cook, S. Dunbobbin, W. Jeffrey, and T. Critchley. Mr. Shaw Green, in acknowledging his re-election, remarked upon the splendid financial position of the Society, and upon the fact that since he was appointed auditer,a few years ago,the capital had been almost doubled. Mr. F. Monks C.C., who was present also spoke, and referred in com- plimentary terms to the successful management of Mr. Rathbone. It was decided, on the suggestion of the chairman, to appoint a sub-committee to revise the rules of the Society, and the Chairman (Zr. Birchall), Mr. W. Jeffrey, Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. Shaw Green ' were appointed for that purpose. WARRINGTON LIBE RAL ASSOCIATION.

div.head: MEETING OF GENERAL COUNCIL.
div.p: MEETING OF GENERAL COUNCIL.

- - On Monday evening, a meeting o! the General Council of the WarringtoiLLiberal Association, was held in the Liberal Clab. There was a fair atten- dance of members. In the absence of Mr. John Ryland% Councillor F. A. Roberts, C.C., was elected to preside. He stated that,the first business was to consider and, if approved of, to proceed to the elec- tion of an honorary secretary of the Association as recommended by the exeeutive. He then called upon Mr. W. Pierpoint; as chairman of the eitectitive, to lay the matter before the meeting. Mr. Pierpoint ,said it had been felt that, as they were on Use eve of a General Election, and would have a great deal of work of all kinds to do, it would be helpful to him as Chairman if there was somebody to assist him as hon. secretary. There was plenty of work or the agent te do, and plenty of work for an honorary secretary. Under the circumstances it was thought advisable that the council should be consulted in the matter, as it amounted practicalls? to the appointment of another officer of the Associa- tion.Re wished the meeting to discuss it thoroughly, and if they saw any difficulty in the way, to state it, so that they might he perfectly satisfied that the right course was being taken. He concluded by moving the recommendation of the executive that an hon. secretary should be appointed. This was seconded by Mr. D. Tinnion, and after some discussion, in which the Chair- man, 9r. .Gornall, Mr. F. Loughlin, Mr. J. Walker, Mr. C. J. Holmes, and others, took part, the resolution was adopted. Afterwards, on the motion of Mr. Lawrence Weir, it was unanimously resolved that Councillor IL Roberts be asked to accept the post of hon. secretary. Mr. Roberts consented to do so, intimating that he had no interest to serve in that matter beyond the interests of the party, and he was anxious that they should all do everything they could to win Warrington at the next election. He thought he could be of some service as hon. secretary, and there would be a great deal of work for everybody to do. Mr. PIERPOINT next proceeded to state what arrange- ments were in progress with a view to holding public meetings in support of the eandidature of Dr. Houston. He added that announcements would be made public as soon as dates could be fixed and rooms secured. He pointed out that they were getting near the time when the County Council elections would again take place, the elections being fixed for an early day in March. As they had Councillor F. A. Roberts present he thought they could not do better than move that he be thanked for his services as county councillor in the past, and be requested to allow himself to be again mominated for the portion of the town he already represented. This motion was seconded, and unanimously adopted. Mr. ROBERTS intimated that he found it a great tax upon his time, and he was desirous of retiring if they could find some one to take his place. Still, he left himself in their hands. He then proceeded to give some account of the work that had been done, and also pointed out

several defects in the County Government measure which had been passed by the present Government, and which needed remedying in a democratic direction. He referred in particular to the appointment of aldermen as a blot upon the Act. On the motion of Councillor H. ROBERTS it was resolved that a letter of congratulation be sent to Mr. Maden upon the magnificent victory which had been achieved in Rossendate. A vote of thanks to the Chair- man concluded the proceedings.
