div.head: EXAMINER, SATTiRDAY, JANUARY 30, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATTiRDAY, JANUARY 30, 1892.
SIR JOHN GORST AT ST. HELENS.

Sir John E. Gorst, Q.C., M.P., Financial Secretary to the Treasury, visited St. Helens, on Tuesday afternoou for the purpose of re-opening the Conser- vative Club, Hall-street, which for the past twelve months has been closed for alteration and redecora- tion. During that period the club has been con; verted into a liability company, and the first direc- tors are Messrs. W. L. Pilkington (chairman). W. J. Thomson,J. Robinson, B. B. Glover, J. Massey, 11. S. Oppenheim, and John Green, with Mr. J. 0. Swift as the bon. sec. The alterations have been carried out at a cost of nearly £2,000, and have been un- der the charge of Messrs. Waizbom & Sons. Mr. R. NNelly has done the painting and decorations. There were present at the re-opening proceedings, in ad- dition to Sir John Gorst, Mr. W. L. Pilkington, J.P., who presided, Mr. H. Seton-liarr,M.P. for St. Helens; Mr. 1. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division ; Colonel Windus, Major M'Tear, Councillors Urmson, Massey, Morgan. and Brooks; Messrs. Joseph Robinson, W. J. Thomson, B. B. Glover, B. S. Biram, E. Biram . E. Grimshaw, J. 0. Swift (secretary), W. Loader, H. S. Oppenheim, T. H. Pearson (Newton-le-Willows), John Hamelin, James Crooks, Joseph Wallace. John Pritc- hard, kc.—The Chairman alluded at some length to the changes in the management of the club during the period it had been closed, and accorded a hearty welcome to Sir John Gorst, who had kiadly promised to re-open the premises.—Sir John Gorst, M.P., who was warmly received, said he was glad to be the medium of declaring the .club open. The establishment of political clubs in the large centres of population was of the very greatest service, both to the country at large and to the inhabit- ants of the particular districts where those clubs were promoted. The existence of the clubs, quite ,-respective of the political party which had established them, tended to promote intelligence and an active and energetic ,public opinion in the country, and tended to promote that common feeling so useful to all, and raised thcir lives and the public and political institutions above the level of common selfishness and common self-seeking. (Cheers.) Mr. J. 0. Swift moved a vote ofthanks to .Sir John Gorst for his services, and Mr. H. Stton-Karr, M.P., briefly seconded the compliment.

PUBLIC MEETING. A public meeting was held in the Volunteer Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr. Wm. Pilkington, J.P.;D.L., pre- sided, and he was supported by Sir John Gorst, M.P., Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P., Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., Colonel D. Gamble, C. 8., Colonel W. W. Pilkington, Colonel R. Pilkington ; Messrs. T. H. Pearson, B. B. Glover, J. Massey, and other leading Conservatives of the district. The Chairman referred to the national loss sustained by the calamity which had fallen upon the Royal Family, and to the loss felt nearer home, by the death of the late Mr. Edward Whitley, M.P. Mr. H. Seton-Karr, in.P. proposed "That this meeting whilst congratulating her Majesty's Government upon the eminent success which has attended their administra- tion at home and abroad., desires to record its approval of their just and statesmanlike policy in Ireland, and hereby expresses its unabated confidence in Lord Salis- bury and his Unionist colleagues:" (Applause.) He maintained that the legiative rec)rd of the Government had seldom been equalled and never been surpassed. They had pacified Ireland, reduced the national expen- diture, promoted most useful domestic and other reforms and had kept peace abroad. If they desired to maintain that pleasant state of affairs they must support and return Unionists candidates at the next election. For their own interests, and for the interests of thecountry, he asked them to support the present Unionist Govern- ment. (A pplause. ) Colonel Richard Pilkington., a Liberal 'Unionist, seconded the resolution, and justified the action of the Liberal Unionists in supporting the Unionist Govern- ment. He asked them to stand shoulder to shoulder in resisting the shameful and cowardly surrender to Irish agitators, and to support to the utmost of their power the complete supremacy of the Imperial Parliament throughout every corner of the United Kingdom. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Sir John Gorst, on rising to respond, was received with cheers. He said tke support accorded by them to her Majesty's Government would be sought from the people of the country in a short time, and the question was will that support be endorsed by the people of the kingdom? Even their opponents could .find little to complain about in the past record of the Government. But the electors would decide to support that party whom they considered the most likely to meet their wishes in the future. The masses of the country were anxious for social reforms which were undoubtedly needed. The Unionist Government and the Unionist party were desirous of devoting their energies to the con- sideration of such questions in the next Parliament, but if the people of this country returned to power a Parlia- ment pledged to spend a considerable part of its time in the discussion of organic changes, they could depend up- on it that there would be very little time left for the social legislation upon which their hearts were set. The choice of the people was a simple one. Were they pre- pared to embark upon a number of constitutional and organic changes, separating kingdoms,disendowing and disestablishing churches, and readjusting the represent- ation of the people, while there were so many reforms of a social character pressing for consideration? If they were so, then it was good-bye for years to come to all social legislation. He maintained that there was no reason why the Unionist party should be distrusted, and said their past character was worthy of the support and confidence of the working classes. The social position of ths people in England, Scotland, and Ireland was capable of very great amelioration and improvement without violence, without anarchy, with- out revolution, and without any violent alterations in the laws and property and the conditions under which they lived. He entreated the people of this kingdom when the next election came round, to return to power a Parliament which should address itself to the real com- mon sense improvement of the condition of the people, and let all those organic radical changes which might be very fine in theory, but would not put a shilling into any man's pocket or an ounce of bread into the stomach of any child, wait until more important matters have been considered and have been dealt with. (Loud cheers.) Major M`Tear proposed a vote of confidence in Mr. Seton-Karr, pledging the meeting to use every effort to secure his return at the next election.—Mr. F. Foram seconded the motion, which was supported by Council- lor Massey, and carried.—Ar. Seton-Karr, M.P., briefly responded. Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., moved a hearty vote of thanks to Sir John Gorst, MP., for his attendance. Colonel D. Gamble, C. 8., seconded, and the resolution was adopted with applause. A singilar compliment to the chairman concluded the proceedings. SIR JOHN GORS I' AND THE CHEMICAL WORKERS. After addressing the Unionist demonstration in the Volunteer Hall, on Tuesday night, Sir John Gorst, received a deputation of chemical and copper workers. The proceedings were private, but the representatives of of the press were informed that the deputation consisted of Mr. P. J. King, president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, and aboat a dozen workmen. The conditions under which the men laboured and the excessively long hours—in some cases amounting to an

-- average of 84 hours per week—were laid fully before the hon. gentlemen. His aid in the effort to remedy their grievances was:soulrht,and Sir John Clerst promised to use his influence in having the circumstances of the chemi- cal and copper workers brought more directly under the notice of the Royal Commission on Labour.—The deputation gave three hearty cheers for the honourable gentleman.

Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion which the Chairman had so ably put before them. He was sure they all supported the Chairman most heartily,and were imbued with the deepest sympathy and sorrow for those in bereavement. The motion was passed unanimously by all the mem- bers standing up in their places.

div.head: BURNS ANNIVERSARY DINNER.
div.p: BURNS ANNIVERSARY DINNER.

The anniversary of the birth of the poet Burns was celebrated on Monday evening, by a dinner at the Patten Arms Hotel. Councillor Fleming, the president of the local Burns Society, occupied the chair,and Major Mackie the vice-chair. There were also among the company Messrs. Thomas Morris, A. Mackie, W. E. Ewart, J. Carruthers, B. Shearer, C. Lyons, E. J.Robertson,F. Lane, W.Fletcher, G.Riley, F. Dinwiddie, J.Finlayson, and the Rev.W. E.Glenn. After dinner the toasting was commenced with the proposing of "The Clergy of all Denominations," the Rev. W. E. Glenn responding. Mr. T. Morris then gave the toast of "The Army, Navy, and Volunteer Forces." The Vice-chairman responded. The President proposed the toast of the memory of Burns. 1u the course of his remarks he said that at' a poet and songster Burns was unsurpassed, and he was equal to Shakespeare, Byron, and Milton. The Vice-chairman and Mr. Shearer sup- ported the toast. The latter, referring to a denial by the Chairman that Scotchmen were mean, said he was not sure that all thorough Scotch- men were not mean, and thought the fact that Burns was only allowed ten years after publication for his first book, £2O, was the essence of meanness.—The electing of officers then took place. Councillor Fleming was re-elected president of the society, Mr. Fletcher treasurer, and Mr. Shearer secretary. Mr. C. Lyons was also added to the committee.—Major Mackie pro- posed" The town and trade of Warrington," Alderman Francomb responded, and indulged in some reminiscen- ces of Warrington as a pretty little old-fashioned market town. Ald. Wright and Mr. Morris also responded. The latter said 2,000 tons of manufactured iron a week was the average output in Warrington for the past ten years. Warrington also contained the largest merchant iron works in the kingdom. That was something to be proud of. Americans when they saw the works in Warrington bent their knees. They were astonished, and stated that they had no idea that there were works better equipped and larger than their own, which they con- sidered A.l. The health of the president was drunk, as also the toast of the Press, and the proceedings con- cluded with "Auld Lang Syria."

THE PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR RUNCORN. As the proposal of the Board of Commissioners to erect a Technical Institute at Runcorn has aroused much interest, we publish the report of Mr. John Bowden, C. 8., of Manchester, whose No. 1 scheme has been adopted:—" In accordance with your in- structions on the 16th inst., I have prepared two alterna- tive sketch plans No. land No. 2, which I send herewith, by which I hope you will find that I have endeavoured to provide recreation for the several classes suggested in your repott. You will observe that both plans contem- plate a large room and class-rooms which might eventu- ally be used as a secondary school. I am of opinion that the site in Waterloo-road is suitable, and you will observe that there will be ample space left for extension without unduly crowding. The whole of the premises I propose should be heated by hot Water, the smoke flue from the boiler being formed so as to act as a ventilating shaft for the whole of the buildings. The plans give the following accommodation :—Ground floor: In plan No. 1 the entrance is dircet from Vi'aterloo- road, on the right is the master's room, 15 feet by 12 feet, behind which aro the lavatories and W.C. for males. The lecture hall or day school is 30 feet by 25 feet, with class room 25 feet by 20 feet, separated by a moveable partition which when not in use makes a room 50 feet by 26 feet, giving accommodation for from 200 to 300 persons. The class rooms for building construction and machine construction are each 25 feet by 20 feet, with a museum or model room 20 feet by 20 ft., and a preparation room. First floor : The lavatory and W.C. for females is entered from the landing. Oppo- site the staircase is a large room 301 t. by 25ft. for teach- ing elementary drawing,and connected with it is a class room 25ft. by 20ft. for study from life and advanced drawing; another room is also provided which might be used as a class room and model room. A laboratory 25ft. by 20ft., and a room for lectures or experimental science 20ft. by 201t.,is provided with a preparation or masters ante-room. The cookery room 251 t. by 201 t. will be fitted with a kitchen range and gas cooking sto ves.—Base- went. Here is situated the heating apparat us, also the work rooms for building trades and mechanics. The building covers about 490 square yards. In plan No. 2 the accommodation is similar to the foregoing, but the entrance is from the side, so that the full width of the front facing Waterloo-road is occupied by the school or Lecture Hall on the ground floor and the art room on the first floor. The building covers an area of about 500 square yards. I am of opinion that the cost will be about £3,500 if economically constructed."—The plans show a brick building of not unpleasing design, but of a plain and unpretentious character. It is to be situated at the bottom corner of the plot of land near the Town Hall, but at such a distance from that building as not to overlook it or to interfere with it in any way. The entrance is in Waterloo-road, and is approached by a flight of steps which add dignity to the building.

div.head: PRINCE GEORGE TO BE MARRIED.
div.p: PRINCE GEORGE TO BE MARRIED.

-- The" World " says that the immediate result of the Duke of Clarence's death, will be the retirement of Prince George from the navy, and his speedy marriage. It is certain that a strong effort will be made in high quarters to arrange for his betrothal to the you nger daughter of the Empress Frederick.

div.head: GENERAL ELECTION.
div.p: THE GENERAL ELECTION.
A SIGNIFICANT FACT.

-- The " Northern Daily Telegraph " states that on Wed- nesday night the leaders of the Conservative party in the Darwen Division were engaged in canvassing the voters on behalf of Lord Cranborne, the member for the division and the.eldest son of the Prime Minister. The circumstance has caused much comment locally, and is regarded as certain evidence of an almost immediate dissolution.

div.head: DEATH OF DR. CARPENTER.
div.p: DEATH OF DR. CARPENTER.

Dr. Carpenter, the eminent sanitarian, and late lec- turer at St. Thomas's Hospital, who was also a vice- president of the British Medical Association, died at Ventnor, on Wednesday, at the age of 67. Dr. Carpenter was a native of Northatnptonshire, but for many years resided at Croydon, where he took a prominent part in public affairs, and was a member of the Croydon County Council. Dr. Carpenter, who was a Liberal, contested Reigate in 1885 and North Bristol in 1886, but was un- successful on both occasions.

div.head: " COWD BEEF AN' A COB."
div.p: " COWD BEEF AN' A COB."
WOT LICKS UM?

One Setterdy neet eawr " Owd Scholar," 1 Coom into th' " Owd Heawse " fer his gill ; Wen sum on U 9 thowt he wur splashy,' Wile others believt he wur ill. " Then he wipet his owd meawth an' wur thankful, Au' played wi' his fork an' his knife; Neaw an' then breykin' eawt i' fresh places, An' vowin' we'd just savet his life. An' to -show be wur thorowly grateful, He poo'd fro his pocket a" Bob," To trayt aw his friends to a toothfal, An' pay fer th' " Cowd Beef an' a Cob!" Well, we aw bed a glass, an' we wished him A wife ez wud polish his shoon ; Keep his heause weel i' order, an' allus Ha' summut nice cookin' boon. div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE
DUKE OF CLARENCE. THE CHAIRMAN ON THE FREEBORN BRITON.

-- - For the purpose of passing a vote of condolence with the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales, on the death of the Duke of Clarence and Avondale, a special meeting of Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held on Monday morning, at the Town Hall. Mr. H. J. sGrice (chairman) pre- sided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., H. White, J. W. Lightburn, W. Timmins, R. Abel, H. Coward, D. Bisbrown, W. R. Wass, S. Tay- lor, W. Hankiuson, J. Dobson, and E. Marshall (secretary). The Chairman said the members would agree that it was the proper course to take to call a special meeting in regard to the national loss that had occurred, and be moved the following addresses :—"To the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty. May it please your Majesty. We your Majesty's loyal sunjects, the chairman and members of the Board of Improvement Commissioners for the district of Runcorn in meeting assembled res- pectfully approach your Majesty and beg leave to ex- press the profound regret with which we received the intelligence of the death of His Royal Highness, Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale, and we hereby tender to your Majesty the respectful expression of our heartfelt and earnest sympathy in the great sor- row and bereavement which has fallen upon your Royal house. We sincerely pray that your Majesty may be sustained in this hour of trial, and we assure your Majesty that we sincerely join in the nation's grief on the untimely death of the late Prince." "To their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales. May it please your Royal Highnesses, we, the chairman and members of the Board of Improvement Commissioners for the district of Runcorn, in meeting assembled,beg to offer to your Royal Highnesses our deep and heartfelt sympathy in the great loss you have sus- tained through the death of your eldest con, his Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence and Avondale. We beg to express how very deeply we deplore the early death of your son and how sincere and heartfelt is the sympathy we feel for your Royal Highnesses in your great bereave- ment. We would also express our earnest sympathy with her Serene Highness the Princess Victoria Mary of Teck• under the great affliction which has befallen her. We grieve for the bright career which has beenso prematurely closed and we would gratefully acknowledge the services which have already been rendered by the deceased Prince for the advancement of the welfare of the people of this realm. We earnestly pray that your Royal Highnesses may be strength- ened and comforted under your great afiliction."— The Chairman said there was no question that every ' member agreed with the sentiments expressed in those , addresses. He had lived a long while and he always felt proud of one thing, that he was born an Englishman. It was two thirds of the battle of life to an inhabitant of this sub-lunary sphere to be born an Englishman. Paul said he was free-born, but Englishmen were born to freedom. They were all aware of the sad affliction that had befallen the Royal family, and he was sure every man—every loyal subject of her Majesty—felt it as much as though the deceased had been a member of his own family. He did so himself from the fact that her Majesty had not only been the Queen but also something like a mother. In her home life the Queen stood as a pattern , to every parent in the realm ; and to a good many of them that remembered her coronation, and all the inci- dents that had transpired during the time she had held so high a position—they might congratulate themselves upsn having lived in a very eventful period. But it was unnecessary to narrate or go through or bring to mind any of the many incidents that had occurred during the reign of Queen Victoria, they were all as well acquainted with English history as he was ; but it had been a great and glorious privilege to live in such a reign ; and he had no doubt that the members would pass these addresses standing up.

EXTRAORDINARY DEATH IN A. TRAP NEAR RUNCORN. Considerable excitement was caut,ed amongst the people of Runcorn on Sunday by a rumour that a man had been found murdered in a trap on the highway ,r)s.r Hallwoodi Farm: kiutton,:but in- quiries revealed thit, although the Circumstances were (surrounded by some mystery, no capital °Renee had ,been committed. It appeared that about ball-past six that morning, Gilbert Parker, a milk seller for Mr. Lowe of Sutton Hall Farm, was driving along the road when he saw a horse and trap standing by the hedgeside, and a young man lying in the bottom of the trap with his head on the splash board. He called Mr. Baguley from Hallwood,and together they examined the man and found he was quite dead. P.C: Fryer was at once informed of the occurrence, and he, identified the body as that of George Roberts, son of John Roberts, cab proprietor, Frodsham. at ten o'cloclet on Saturday night he drove Dr. Carruthers from Frod- sham to his residence at Halton Castle, where he arrived about half-past ten. He left apparently quite well, and afterwards called at the Castle Hotel, where he had a glass of beer and a cigar, and did not remain more than ten minutes. He was not afterwards seen alive. INQUEST. The Coroner, Mr. J. E. Wersley, held an inquest on the body at Aston Arms Sutton,on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Acton was foreman of the jury, and Mr. Superinten- dent Large represented the police.—John Roberts, cab proprietor, Frodsham,said deceased was his sonand was 32 years of age. Ile had always enjoyed good health. He last saw him alive at ten o'clock on Saturday night. Arthur Foster said he was agent for brewers at the Halton Castle Hotel. The deceased came to the hotel about a quarter or ten minutes to eleven on Saturday night. He was sober. He did not remain at the hotel more than ten or fifteen minutes at the outside. He had a glass of beer and a cigar.—The Coroner said this was the last person who saw the deceased.—Supt. Large: It was said that a trap was seen coming from your house about 12 o'clock; is that true.—No sir. My own trap had been at Runcorn and came back between eleven and twelve o'clock. Gilbert Parker, a milk seller for Mr. Lowe, farmer, of Sutton Hall, deposed that he saw the trap near Hallwood Farm, about half-past six as he was fetching the milk. He thought the driver had got out for some purpose. He returned past the same spot about half-an-hour latar. The trap was still standing there, and he thought it strange and got out to see what was the matter. He saw the deceased hanging out, with his legs in the trap. He called Mr. Bagufey from the farm, and together they liftedhim up. He was quite dead. Dr. McDougall, said he had made a post mortsin ex- amination of the body of the deceased. He found two superficial scratches on the right arm and a mark on the forehead which was probably caused by falling against the splash board. The cause of death was suffocation, consequent, in his opinion, on a fit of a convulsive character. There was nothing abnormal about it. The internal organs were not in the most healthy condition. The Coroner said this was a case which required com- plete and satisfactory investigation, and he thought that such an investigation had been made. The doctor's evidence was perfectly satisfactory.—The jury returned a verdict of" Found dead," adding that death was pro- bably due to a convulsive fit.

div.head: MA.KERFIELD PLOUGHING SOCIETY.
div.p: MA.KERFIELD PLOUGHING SOCIETY.

The twenty-sixth annual meeting of the Maker- field Ploughing Society tooleplace, on Thursday, on Wicken Edge Farm, in the occupation of Mr. Balharry, Newton-le-Willows. Soon after the com- mericement of operations rain began to fall, which rendered the ground very heavy, but on the whole the quality of the work turned out was fairly up to the average. There were 42 entries and 36 competitors put in an appearance. The judges were for the first and third classes, Mr. Ledson, Fazackerly ; Mr. Turton, Hale ; Mr. Swinton Arbury, Winwick. Seco id class and diggers : —Mr. Dean, Roby Mills • Mr. Carswell, Lyme Farm, Disley • Mr. Sherratt, Caldy, Birkenhead. Turn outs, Mr. •Il'oardman, Kenyon Hall, and Mr. Fairhurst,

_ Prescot. At the conclusion of the match the annual dinner was held at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, Mr. I. W. Legh, M.P., presiding, supported by Messrs. W. Bethany, J. E. Pardey, R. Stuart, G. F. Clarke, J. Crompton, F. Frost (secretary), Sm. After dinner Mr. Legh gave the toast of the Queen which was duly honoured. In giving a toast of the " Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal family" Mr. Legh said under the circurnstrnces it was impossible for him not to refer to the unfortunate circumstances which fiad cast a gloom over every class in this country. They had the satisfaction of knowing, however, that the calamity which had overtaken the Royal family wag one that had the sympathy of every class of the community. The toast was duly honoured. Mr. Legh regretted to have to announce that he had to take himself away. The duties of a member of Parliament were such that they had to fulfil their engagements whatever might be the result. In giving the toast of "Success to the Maker- field Ploughing Society," he said he noticed that when people had anything to say about agriculture they alway took upon themselves to give advice whether they knew anything about it or not. If he took the liberty of giv- ire, them advice on agriculture, he should be presuming, iefact, to use a vulgar phrase, he would be" teaching his grandfather." If he were to advise them to cultivate anything it would be a good un- derstanding with their landlords, and if there were any present, he would advise the landlords to cultivate a good understanding with their tenants ; that was sound advise, and he thought he should not be found fault with in giving it. (Applause.) Mr. Legh then left the meeting and Mr. Balharry took his place, and proceeded to distribute the prizes as follows : First Class.—Single furrow ploughs: 1, John Bent,

SERIOUS CONDITION OF MR. SPURGEON.

MENTONE, THURSDAY, 11 a.m.—A bulletin issued this morning says Mr. Spurgeon's condition still continues critical. No improvement in the serious symptoms can he recorded since yesterday. He remains in a drowsy state, but is:cOnscious when addressed. Mr. Spurgeon's serious state causes the gravest anxiety to the friends who are with him.
MR. GLADSTONE.

, M. and Mrs. Gladstone, accompanied by several f fiends, made an excursion on Thursday from San Rap- hael to Flyeles by rail, and on arriving at the latter station'were met toy the municipality and a large number of citizens, a band in attendance meanwhile playing the British National Anthem. Replying to an address, Mr. Gladstone said he was deeply touched by the sympathy I manifested towards him in France.

div.head: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: THE OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.

Tle—" Times" says :—We understand that at the '--i— -openingof the session on the 9th February, the Earl of Dudley will propose the address i n the House of Lords. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, Mr. and Mrs. Henry Gladstone, and Mr. and Mrs. Stuart Rendei, will arrive in London on Saturday next. A letter, has, however, been sent out by the Duke of Devonshire to Liberal Umonist members inviting them to meet at Devonshire House on the morning of Febru- ary Bth to elect a leader in his place in the House of Commons. Most of the members of the Cabinet were engaged throughout Wednesday at their respective offices.

Warrington 776 ... 501 St. Helens Widnes Division Newton Division In 1880 Warrington returned the late Mr, UoMnonEs with a majority of 52(3; and, as the feeling in favour of Liberal principles is likely, by the time of the General Election, to reach the high-water mark of 1880, why should there not be a repetition of the success of 1880 ? If the Liberals of Warrington strive as mightily as they did on that occasion, they will most assuredly retarn Dr. HOUSTON by a large majority. As to St. Helens with a majority against them of 217 only, it is a matter of course to say that Mr. , /CENNEnv, Q.C., will be returned, if Liberals who have hitherto abstained from voting are brought to the poll. In the Newton Division the struggle Will unquestionably be a hard one; but since the last General Election the Liberals have won in a ounty Council contest; and they can win in the Parliamentary contest if, as the phrase goes, they it Put everything in." And so with the Widnes Oivision. More than half of the Tory majority °I 1885 was wiped out in 1886. The electors have simply to continuo the purifying process, and Widnes will be amongst the Lancashire constitu- ences to send aid for the first time to Mr. GLAD- STONE. The pros- Peet is therefore anything but gloomy, and it has °tightened considerably since Saturday last. Rossendale is inspiring; and its stimulus may ninan victory all along the line.

div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
S.A.—lt is contrary to our rule to insert letters in reply to communications which have appeared in a contemporary.—H. H. Dutton, and " One Interested."—Crowded out this week.
Rossendale Vale is full of curious nooks, And evidently has enough of "Brooks."
-- A hard-fought contest, but the Liberal's in: SD give three cheers for !Iladen's maiden win.

The Conservatives of Penketh had a dance on Saturday night. It would have been all right if the Unionist at Rossend ale was absolutely sure of winning. As it was, it was like dancing on the grave of the last of the Liberal Unionists.

People who desiro a perfect portrait of the Princess Mary of Tack should spend a shilling on the latest issue of Cassell's " Cabinet Portrait Gallery." It is a beautiful face beautifully photo- graphed. The number contains, besides, equally good portraits of Sir William Thompson and Miss Julia Neilson, with a brief biography of each subject.

"Advertising " is the title of a new publication admirably edited as to the first number by Mr. J. H. 03b3rne. It abounds in useful hints and information for advertisers. The following is the last sentence of an article on "Where to spend your money" :—" A man cannot partake of food with his mouth shut—no more can he benefit by a withdrawn advertisement. Briefly, no advertise- ment, no customers."

As we have no liking for the proverb which says " God sends meat, but the Devil sends cooks," we are pleased to learn that as many as 130 ladies were present, recently, at an evening class for cookery in connection with the Ashton-in-Maker- field Technical Instruction scheme. Good cooking may be made to mean economy, comfort, and even health. Shakespeare spoke a pertinent word on the subject when he folid—" Cooks sharpen with cloyless sauce the appetite."

Parliament meets on the 9th February; and the usual letters to supporters have been issuee by party leaders, urging members to be present. Mr. Gladstone is suggestive, when he says:—" Besides other matters of importance, we may hope to learn whether, and in what manner, it is the intention of the present majority of the House of Commons to grant local government to Ireland." This is the note of battle ; there will be wigs on the'green.

Electors are beginning to turn their thoughts to the County Council elections which take place early in March. In the Newton district, the Tories are seeking 'a candidate with a view to a change in the representation ; and the Liberals ought to be astir, and ready for the fray. Having beaten Mr. Pearson, they are equal, if they so mind, to beating any candidate the Tories may think fit to nominate.

Warringfon returns three County Councillors. Mr. join) White, however, does not seek re- election and has given way to Mr. John Fairclough, who will be glad to obtain the seat, if he be not called upon to fight for it. Mr. F. A. Roberts was urged at a meeting of the 'Warrington Liberal Council to allow himself to be nominated again, and he finally consented. With regard to Mr. F. Monks it is understood that he, too, is willing to act again ; and, as this will practically he" as you were "from a political point of view, it is not unlikely that the election will again pass over without a contest.

Nature abhors Conservative conferences because Nature abhors a vacuum. This week there have been two vacuous gatherings; there has been a meetino. at Bolton of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Conservative Associations; and a con- fereine at Altrincham of the Lancashire and Cheshire Conservative Working-men's Federation. These titles are both very fine and large,but, judg- ing from the report of the proceedings, they simply serve to give " a local habitation and a name to airy nothing." The Tories have nothing to offer, and they offer nothing.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Hawkins quashed the convictions be- fore the mag,istrates,against Salvationists of East- bourn. This decision should be a lesson to local authorities to be careful how they interfere with the right of meeting. It would seem as if the police of Chelsea had something to learn ; for they continue to interfere with the open-air meet- ings of the Socialists, at what is known as World's End. Let the Socialists by all means meet and discuss their grievances. It is better to let the steam blow off than sit on the safety-valve.

Two brothers who were twins, ten years of age, were drowned at Haydock, on Saturday, through going on ponds when the ice was unsafe. One of the little fellows lost his life through pluckily try- ing to save his brother. A similar but sadder case still occurred at Northwich, on Monday. Not only were two brothers drowned—one endeavour- ing to rescue the other—but a third school-boy perished in trying to give aid, while a fourth had a very narrow escape. In such cases it may, in- deed, be said— One woe cloth tread upon another's heels, So fast they follow.

To be or not to be ? That is the question which is being asked. touching the revived rumour as to Sir Gilbert Greenall being converted into a lord. There does not seem to be any room to doubt that the proposal has been under consideration; but it would mean a bye-election in Warrington, :ind— well, anything may happen at a bye-election after It)ssendale. Can tbe that Mr. Maden's return will cause Sir Gilbert to have to "wait a little longer" for the " good time coming "P If so, he will remember Rossendale.

With regard to the statement that the mem- ber for Warrington has not as yet had a peerage offered to him, that may be perfectly true, even when, under the rose, he may " know all about it." When the offer is formally made, the deed may be said to be done. The Queen is a grAt stickler for the proprieties in these matters, and it is on record that one gentleman missed an other- wise certain honour through making public what was understood to hemn store for him. Sir Gilbert will have been warned to be " mum," if a• peer- age is afoot. If not great as a apsaior, he can show himsif great at keeping his mouth shut.

Some years ago a certain clergyman,whose church had been under discussion, said "the penny papers were the curse of the country." The General Pur- poses Committee of the Warrington Corporation would appear to take a similar view of things, for they have passed two res,ltitions which strike at the publicity of Corporation proceedings. Accord- ing to one resolution, the newspapers are not, for the future, to be furnished with copies of the Council Summons and Agenda of business until the day of the meeting. This is to prevent an account of the business of Committees being pub- lished in the press on the Saturday before the Council meeting., as has hitherto been customary. It is an absurd regulation. It may put reporters to some inconvenience on a busy day ; but, as every Town Councillor and Alderman will have a copy, it is a matter of course to say that the news will be got, if not in the usual way.

The other resolution reads as follows :—" No officer or servant shall, unless required by law, or without the sanction of the Mayor, or Chairman of the Committee concerned, communicate to the public the proceedings of any meeting of a Com- mittee, or sub-Committee, nor shall lie, without the authority of the Committee having charge of tin matter, so communicate any information of the contents of any document relating to the busi- ness of the Corporation, nor shall he, without such authority, enter into any public correspondence with reference to the business of the Corpora- tion."

div.p: DIE AILWAY HOTEL, WIDNES. Thomas Laws was granted permission to sell at this hotel under the license lately held by the late llrs.Ander- son, by the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday.

WATERLOO-ROAD SCHOOLS, WIDNES. On Thursday evening, an entertainment in connection with the juvenile branch of St. Mary's Temperance Society was held at the above schools. The Rev. G. H. Garrett, R.D., presided, ST. PATJLS CHIIRCH, WIDNES. . _ .

Special sermons on behalf of the Pastoral Aid Society were preached in this church, on Sunday,by the Rev. J. Wright Williams, formerly vicar of Widnes. There were large congregations at both the morning and even- ing service.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LE.CTITIZE AT RONCOKIN.
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LE.CTITIZE AT RONCOKIN.

The second ol the series of lectures on the history of Florence, by the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw, M.A., was delivered on Monday evening in Bethesda Lecture Hall. The subject was" Dante," and the lecturer enlisted the attention and interest of his auditors.
PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-at. Warrnizon.—Advt.
WESTON BIBLI AND MUTUAL LUPROVEMENT CLASS.

On Monday night, the annual tea meeting of the above class was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. After tea a programme of recitations, &c., was gone through by the members. Speeches were made by Mr. James Ford (the president of the class), Mr. John Ball, Mr. T. Hazlehurst, and others. THE GEMS OF THE OPERA COMPANY AT RUNCORN.

Monday evening next will be remembered as one of the events of the concert season in Runcorn. Mr. J. W Temperley has engaged the company described above to give a concert in the Public Hall, and the programme to Le submitted is one calculated not only to charm every lover ot music but all those in search of a pleasant, enjoyable, and elevating evening.

- - ROBBING A FBLLOW-LODGER AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, Martin M'Coskie was charged with stealing a shirt and a pair of boots, the property of Anthony Lennant. Both men are Poles and lodged toge- ther at 27, Cromwell-st., and on Saturday afternoon the prisoner was seen to put on prosecutor's shoes. After he had left the house for Seacombe the shirt was also missed, and when he returned on Monday he had neither shoes nor shirt with him. He was remanded for further inquiries to be made.

div.head: MOTHER'S AWFUL THREAT.
div.p: A MOTHER'S AWFUL THREAT.

Catherine Kelly, of no fixed abode, who had been in the town several nays, was in Halton-road on Wednesday evening under the influence of drink and acting in a most unbecoming manner. She threatened to throw two young children of whom she was in charge into the canal, but the timely interference of P.C. Dutton prevented her from carrying out her intention, and she was sent to gaol forseven days next morning on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. tier children were placed in the custody of the relieving officer.
THE OLD PEOPLIeS TREAT AT WIDNES.

A meeting of the General Committee, who had the above matter in hand, was held on Wednesday night, for the purpose of considering the best method of dis- posing of the balance, after all expenses connected with the treat had been paid. The total sum collected amounted to £9O, and the total expendit,re to £36, but as there were upwards of 100 old people who were unable to be preseat at the treat, it was decided to give them the same as the others,and to devote the remainder to relieving the needy widows and orphans in the town.
HoIST ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Wbile employed discharging a flat containing lime- stone on the canal bank, at Widnes, on Wednesday afternoon Thomas Entwistle was very seriously injured. The limestone was shovelled into tubs, whichwere placed by means of a hoist on what is called the low level,—a platform 14 feet high. Entwistle Was in charge of the hoist,and the catches of one oithe tubs becoming unfas- tened, whilst being raised, tip tub overturned, and the contents, 35 cwt. of limestone, fell upon him. He was severely cut about the arms and hands, and was also seriously injured inteinally.

A. RUNCORN WOMAN CONVICTED OF THEFT AT WIDNES. ' Before Messrs. H. Gaskell, jun. and F. S. Timmis, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Catherine Thomas, a respectably dressed married woman, of Penketh-lane, Runcorn, was charged with stealing eight silk handker- chiefs, value 305., the property of Henry Chapman, draper, Widnes-road, Widnes. —On the Bth Sept. last, the handkerchiefs were missed from a glass case on the counter, and no trace was seen of them until Monday afternoon, when she offered two of the missing handker- chiefs in pledge at Mr. Imison's shop, in Churcii-st., Runcorn. She told the assistant that she had received them from a navvy, but he did not consider her ex- planation satisfactory, and informed the police.—Mr. Kno.wles contended that there was not evidence suffi- cient for a conviction, hut the magistrates considered the case proved, and imposed a fine of 205., or 14 days' imprisonment.
THE LATE MRS. WALTER TIMMINS OF RUNCOUN.

At a special meeting of Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners on Monday last, called to pass a vote of condo- lence with the Royal family on the death of the Duke of Clarence, the Chairman (Mr. H. J Grice) made a sym- patheti.: reference to the deaF Ii of Mrs. Walter Timmins. Every member of the Board, lie said, was well known to his colleagues, and when any misfortune, any bereave- ment, betel one every member felt it very strongly. He was sure that in expressing his own sympathy with Mr. Timmins in the recent loss he had suffered in the death of his wife he should be expressing the feelings of every member of the Board. (Hear, hear.) They were deeply grieved to hear the sad news, and they hoped that this stroke of Providence might be something better than it looked in the first instance, because they understood that all these things worked for good.—The members unani- mously acquiesced without a formal vote, and Mr. Tim- mins said he thanked them for their kindly sympathy. His heart was too full to say; the shock was so sudden and so recent.

FAIINWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL. At the last examination for the certificates of the Col- lege of Preceptors,l6 students from the Farnworth Gram- mar School were successful. The examination includes English, Latin, French, mathematics, electricity, and chemistry, and in the higher classes is a severe test of proficiency. By passing this examination, two of the Grammar School boys have also passed the preliminary examinations of the Incorporated Law Society and the Institute of Chartered Accountants' six have passed thee preliminary examinations of the Medical Council and Pharmaceutical Society, and four have passed the en- trance examination to the Victoria University. The fol- lowing have obtained certificates :—First-class, C. It. Lewis and F. C. Riley second-class, W. Denny, W. Nickson, S. G. Owens, J. Swale. and J. Williams ; third- class, F. E. Barlow, T. A. A_ WOMAN BOOT STEALER AT RUNCORN.

Edon, Mr. Thomas and Mr. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Mary Jones of Frodsham, pleaded guilty of having on the 21st November, last, stolen three pairs of boots, the property of William Gittens, of Lowlands-road ; and on the 22nd January stolen a pair of boots, from the shop of Thomas Cook, Church-street. She was sentenced to a month's impris- onment on each charge, the sentence to run concurrently. Umnr.ELLAs DF:COVERID.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Wairington.--.Adat. THE 11\ FLUENZI /N NORTHW,ICII.

_ In Northwich and district the influenza prevails to a most alarming extent. Sufferers are to be num- bered by the hundreds, and all the doctors have their hands full. Some 300 men connected with the Wilmington Chemical Works are affected. The epidemic is raging in every part of the district,and amongst all classes. UMBRELLAS RECOTBRED.—J. and W. DUTTON', Sankey-st., Warrington.— Advt. - DROWNED IN SANKEY Bnocor.

On Friday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest,at the Ship Inn, Newton Common, touching the death of Mary Ann Tracey, 15 years of age, daughter of Patrick Tracey, of Stone-street, Parr, who was drowned in the Sankey Brook, St. Ilelens, as previously recorded. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned." GAS FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-et., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: CLERICAL SECRETA.RYSIDP.
div.p: A CLERICAL SECRETA.RYSIDP.

The Rev. Canon Dodd, M.A., vicar of Stratton, has resigned the secretaryship of the Frodsham Ruri- decanal Conference, which he has held for some years. Canon Dodd will be succeeded by the Rev. George D. Wray, vicar of Dalton, near Runcorn. a grandson of the late Rev. C. D. Wray, rector of St. Thomas's, Ardwick, and Canon of Manchester. THE FIDLER'S FERRY TUNNEL. Mr. Deacon, water engineer to the Liverpool Cor- poration, has reported that excellent progress is being made with the Fidler's Ferry Tunnel, a com- pleted length of 57 feet having been added during the week ending the 23rd inst. This makes a total of 469 feet from the centre of the Lancashire shaft.

div.head: ACCIDENT .AT NBWTON BRIDGE STATION.
div.p: ACCIDENT .AT NBWTON BRIDGE STATION.

On &unday night, on the arrival of the passenger train due at Newton Bridge Station at 9.35, the guard of the train, John Long, belonging to Patti- croft, was lifting a box of bullion from the van to a luggage truck, when he slipped, and the box fell on his leg, breaking his thigh. Dr. Watkins was sent for, and on reaching the station, he temporarily set the broken bone, and the injured man was taken on by the train to the Infirmary at Manchester. UMBRELLAS RECOVERS:B.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankepst., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.

_ On Thursday night a large and influential meet- ing of landowners and manufacturers was held at Edgworth, when a deputation representing com- mercial and agricultural interests was appointed to wait upon the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company with a view to the construction of a line from 13.oddlesden to Ilolcombe, or from Entwistle to Bury, which will open a rich mineral and manu- facturing district. The Darwen district will be largely benefited, and Bolton station rolieved of the congested traffic likely to result from the Ship Canal.

div.head: DEATH OF A RUNCORN NONAGRNARIAN.
div.p: DEATH OF A RUNCORN NONAGRNARIAN.

, Ann Cooper, of 3, Cholmondeley-st.. Runcorn, passed away on Wednesday at the advanced age of 93 years. Born at Brirtington. Mrs. Cooper had lived in Runcorn since childhood,and the house in which she had died had been her abode for no less a period than 70 years. To the last the old lady retained her intellectual and physical faculties to a remark- able degree,and her memory of Runcorn went back to the time when the town was little more than a riverside village, much resorted to by those in search of health and quietude. lier death was due to natural decay. THE NAVVIES AND LABOUDERS' UNION.

Another important point in Trades Union law is about to come on for .argument before the County Court at Manchester. The district of the Navvies' and Labourers' Union has a membership of some 5,000 or 6,000 men. Some discontented branches, headed by the district secretary, Mr. Leonard Hall, well known as a speaker at, outdoor meetings, at Warrington, have seceded from the Union. They refused to give up the books and money, and for this Mr. Hall and some of the branch secretaries ' were summoned to the Salfsrd Police Court last week by Mr. John Ward,the president of the Union. The summonses were supported by Mr. M. Thompson counsel of the Union, and Mr. Hall was ordered to give up the furniture and books, Including the bank book. The point reserved for argument before the County Court Judge, is whether or not a special levy made by a district secretary can be claimed by the Union. The seceders maintain that it belongs to the district branches. The amount involved is about .£l3O. It is stated that about 1,000 Lancashire members of the Union have withdrawn from it on account of the dispute, but we learn from Mr. Price, the secretary for the Warrington district branch, that it has decided to stand by the Union to a man.
KITCHEN' R ANGEE.9.—Garlati4 Builders Ironmonger, War rington.— Advt. SINGTJLAR WIFE DESERTION CASES AT Sr. HELENS.

The magistrates at St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, were occupied for several hours in hearing a singular case of wife desertion. The complainant was Edith Louisa Ridgeway, who sought itn order of maintenance from her husband, Thomas Ridge- way, a signalman in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and residing at , 38, Brook-st., St. Helens. Mr. J. P. Mearns ap- peared for the wife, and Mr. 11. 1,. Riley defended. The case was before the court about six months ago, and the defence set up was that the com- plainant had committed adultery with a rail- way guard named Parr, who had since disap- peared. In view of threatened divorce proceedings by the husband, the case was adjourned for Six months, and was reheard on Monday. ' It was stated that the divorce case was at present under the consideration of the counsel. It was ack- nowledged by the complainant that the guard Parr had made a confession to an inspector of the com- pany that he had committed adultery with her, and that, in consequence, Parr was dismissed from his situation. Be had now disappeared,and his where- abouts could not be ascertained. The complainant, however, emphatically denied the allegations that she had misconducted herself. Witnesses were called for the defence to show that the woman had re- peatedly travelled by the trains of which Parr was in charge,and that they had been seen talking to- gether. The Bench retired, and on their return in- timated that they did not consider the evidence of adultery was sufficient,though there had been great imprudence. They ordered the defendant to con- tribute Bs. per week towards the maintenance of his wife, but that, of course, would be affected by any future proceedings Ridgeway might take. RICOYERED.—J. and W. InTrroN. Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUNCORN.

The old people of Runcorn had their annual treat in Runcorn Public hall, on Wednesday evening. The limit fixed was 60 years of age but this was not too strictly adhered to. and rich and poor were alike welcome to join in the festive occasion. Of tie 600 invitations issued 450 were resp-mded to, and the sight of so many people with hoary heads, and wrinkled faces—and every wrinkle a line of beauty—was one never to be forgotten. Their physical wants were supplied in the shape of a hot- pot—but savoury and generous in its proportions of the ingredients, followed by mince tarts, &c., while tea,dear to the heart of the aged, was not for- gistten, and was dispensed with no stinting band. Fruit was also distributed, and packets of tea and tobacco were there in plenty,and to be had for mere indication of choice. Those who were not able to be present were provided for at their homes, and those who were well enough to be present but could not travel along the dirty and sloppy streets consequent upon a heavy downpour of rain,were fetched in con- veyances kindly lent by Mr. Jackson and Mr. Peter Brereton. After full justice had been done to the good things provided, an entertainment was given in which the central figure wasMr.Jno.Allen,whose comic songs and sketches convulsed the audience with laughter. The following local vocalists also dis- coursed sweet music—Misses Simkin, Heathering- ton, Jones, and BirkettAlessrs. u.Morris, J.Birkett, Gates, C. Pow nail, T. Clegg, and J. Littler. Mr. J. Woods performed a cornet solo, and Miss Nina Har- rison gave a violin solo. Mr. 11. J.(3rice, the Chair- man of Commissioners, presided, and delivered an appropriate address.

The Golden Horn has sunk near Vera Cruz, the captain and three of the crew being drowned. The ship Holkar, which has just arrived in the Mersey, reports having encountered very heavy weather off the Azores. The private hill promoted by the Eastbourne Salva- tionists with the object of securing the repeal of the clauses in the Local Act which have caused the Sunday disturbances was passed on Tuesday on the standing orders by the Parliamentary examiner.

AT RUNCORN, &c. "By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The special correspondent of a Liverpool contem- porary in the Rossendale division observed just , before the election;—" Mr. Shores, of Widnes, who is assisting Mr. Wigley, the chief Liberal agent in Rossendale, has been doing a lion's share of the work now proceeding, and the great experience, urbanity, and tact he has brought to bear upon many of the minutim of the contest, upon which, after all, so much depends, have earned for him the warm approbation of his collaborateurs and the heads of the Liberal party generally."
That Runcorn and Widnes are remarkably free from the influenza scourge, for which we all ought to be duly thankful.

That congratulations have showered upon Hough- ton, the Runcorn Football Club's fall back, this week. His selection fot international honours has given great satisfaction to all the followers of the game, and it is hoped that he will display his best form against the Irishmen.
That the Aged People's Treat at Runcorn was as Mat a success as usual, and rhe old folk appeared to enjoy themselves immensely at both the dinner table and at the entertainment afterwards.

That it Is pleasing to know that the dispute be- tween Runcorn Guardians and Mr. H. a Linaker, has been settled without recourse to a court of law, which at one time seemed probable, and all un- pleasantness is now ended and ought to be for- gotten.
That Dr. Olieeffe and his colleagues had a mar- vellous escape from drowning in the Sankey Canal. The gentlemen have not yet recovered from the shock and the result of the immersion.
That it is stradge a canal should intersect the road in this way, and have no means provided to warn people at night that the bridge was open. More will he heard about the affair.

-- That the police busine.ss at Widnes and Runcorn has been very slack this year, and there has been a remarkable reduction in the number of drunken cases compared with other similar periods. Is it that the people are becoming converted to teetotalism,or that money is scarce ?

div.head: FUNERAL OF AN OLD RITNCORN LADY.
div.p: FUNERAL OF AN OLD RITNCORN LADY.

There was interred, at Runcorn Cemetery, on Tuesday morning, the mortal remains of Mrs. Ann Hignett, widow of the late Mr. John Hignett, formerly of the Elms, Higher Runcorn. 31rs. Hignett, who had attained the advanced age of 90 years, had resided in Southport since the death of her husband, over twenty years ago, and her body was brought by train on Tuesday morning. At the station it was transferred to the hearse of Messrs. Tarwood Bros., which was drawn by four Belgian horses, and following were three coaches containing the mourners, viz. :—Mrs. Heald, Miss Ockleston, Messrs. John Newton,W. Ockles- ton, John Ockleston, Major Hazlehurst, G. Ilazlehurst, F. Ockleston, G. J. Knight, arid A. F. Brundrit. The deceased lady was borne to her last resting place by Samuel Booth, Joseph Hulme, Thomas Dixon, Samuel Tomlinson, Samuel Worrall, and John Barrow—all workmen from Messrs.Ocklaston's tannery. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. Joseph Holden, curate of the Parish Church. The following wreaths were placed upon the grave :—ln loving memory of our darling mother, Pollie ; with deep sympathy from Fanny ; B. and E. Crook, Miss Burgess, Mrs. Charles Hatlehurst, Miss Ellen Ockleston, Mrs. Haigh Gill, Mr. John and Miss Coop. Miss Barnes, and Miss Pemberton, Mrs. Ockleston, Mrs. Mathieson, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Hutchinson and family, Mr. Thomas Ockleston, Mr. and Mrs. W. Baldwin,John and Allen Newton ; in loving remembrance of our dear mistress from Ann and Charlotte.—Messrs. Kelk Bros., of Southport, were the undertakers.

div.head: WIDNES EDUCATIONAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES EDUCATIONAL ASSOCIATION.

ADDRESS BY THE REV. J. HOLLOWELL. A public meeting under the auspices of this re- cently formed Association was held in the Conserva- tive Club Assembly Room on Monday evening,under the presidency of Mr. S. B. Stringer, of Warrington. There was a good attendance. The Rev. J. Hollowell,of Rochdale, delivered an address on the Education Ques- tion. lie said he had not come to Widnes to 'indulge in local personalities. This was a national question, and education ought to be carried on by the nation and not by individuals or churches. Before 1870 the education was carried on by the Church; but there was no progress made. If the nation had not taken the matter in hand, where would they be to-day ? Although 20 years had passed since the Education Act came into force,England was still behind other countries in educational matters. The income of the day schools in England during the current year would be about seven millions, which the ratepayers would find. The people provided the money to carry on the education of the country, and, therefore, they had a right to have a voice in the control of the schools. For many years voluntary contributions had been decreasing, while the cost of education has gone up. They were told that the Board Schools tended to increase the cost of educa- tion. That might be so, hut they provided a better article for the money. The voluntary schools had also increased their cost; in 1869 the cost amounted to 255. sd. per scholar, and in 1837 to 365. 4id. per scholar. In 1889 there were 32 schools in Cheshire that were not receiving a farthing voluntary subscrip- tions. livers were really no voluntary schools, only in the sense that the clergy had the management of them while the public had nothing to do with them. With regard to the Bible in the Board Schools, he could not help thinking that the Vicar of NVidnes was very much mistaken on this point. It was trut there was no Church catechism, or any other catechism taught in the Board Schools, but the Bible was read in most of the schools, which was a lunch better authority than any catechism. 'The speaker then quoted severe,' items from a catechism, published by "The Church Extension Society," which taught the real presence, confession of sins to a priest, and washing away of sin by baptism. The speaker said he preferred the New Testament to such teaching as that. Ile had been connected with many Board Schools, and the Bible was taught in its entirety. There was not a Board School in Lancashire where the Bible was excluded, and not one under the London School Board, and one of the London schools was worth a couple of hundred of those where the Bible was not read. The lecturer then dealt with the position of the teachers in the denominational schools, and said he was glad that they wore new determined to emancipate themselves. (Applause.) On the proposition of the Rev. It. G.fluelies, seconded by Mr. Jackson, and supported by Mr. S. Owen, a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Hollowell. A similar com- pliment was also paid to the chairman on the motion of 1 Mr. R. Lewis, seconded by Mr. Davies.

div.head: TERRIBLE FATALITY AT WI DN ES.
div.p: TERRIBLE FATALITY AT WI DN ES.

-- A young man named Wm. Lynch, aged 17 years met with a terrible death at IVidnes, on Wednes- day. He was employed as a labourer at the works of Messrs Norman, earthenware manufacturers, Widnes Marsh, and on Wednesday was engaged in conjunction with another youth named Nicholas Walsh, dipping earthenware pipes in a tank of ! boiling tar and oil. Lynch was standing on a raised platform, from which be slipped into the !tank. His companion at once rescued him, and !everything possible was done for him, but he was terribly burned, and died in great agony at the Accident Hospital the same nigi It. THE INQUEST.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on : the body of the deceased at the Widnes Accident Hos- pital yesterday (Frirday) afternoon. The evidence showed that the deceased was working near the tank, and it is supposed was knocked into it by the windlass of the hand crane he WAS working at. Alter a lengthy discussion, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death," but added the following rider "We consider there was neglect on the part of the employers in not providing proper protection and more room for the de- ceased to work in, and we suggest that the tank be pro- tected along a portion of the crane side, and that the crane ought to be moved two feet further back so as to give more room." Mr. A. Norman, who appeared for the firm, promised that the wishes of the iury should be im- mediately carried out,

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.

The annual ordinary general meeting of this Company was held at the'Bank premises, Warring- ton, yesterday. The Chairman, Mr. J. C. Parr, pre- sided, and the other directors present were Colonel Gamble, C. 8., Messrs. P. Stubs, Edward Greenall, T. H. Dixon, A. Turner, F. Parr, J. Dun, and Sir T. G. Frost.

THE CHAIRMAN'S REMARKS, The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said that the year just passed had happily been exempt from any Such sensational and disquieting incident as that one which last year threatened to paralyse com- mercial credit, and to cause widespread disaster, and even ruin, which would have involved the innocent with the guilty, the honest trader with the dishonest specula- tor, but which was averted by the courage and presence of mind of the governor of the Bank of England and others. Still, though this crisis was averted, and the danger escaped, they left in the public mind a feeiing of distrust and uneasiness which was not so soon overcome, and, from the excess of recklessness of one gigantic institution they were now threatened with what he felt inclined to call an excess of caution and susceptibility which, if indulged in, might have the effect of hampering legitimate enterprise and causing inconvenience and stagnation in various quarters without materially adding to the stability or the strength of the institutions concerned. It might be quite right that the Chancellor of the Exchequer should call atten- tion to the desirability of banks maintaining large avail- able reserves, but the limit of these reserves, and how and to what extent they should be accumulated and maintained should be left for the banks themselves and their shareholders, with public opinion at their back, to limit and determine. The suggestion of Government interference in a case of this kind would appear to be as unwise as it was unnecessary, and would tend to lower the high standard of banking responsibilty without add- ing to the security of the public at large. It would be a satisfaction to their shareholders to hear with reference to the Baring guarantee that Mr. Lidderda'e still class- tained the opinion that" in the absence of serious politi- cal complications in South America, and with careful management, there is not likely to be any call upon the guarantors." That question of reserves had brought tp another suggestion which was now exercising the commercial mind, and apparently occupying the attention of their highest financial authority. He alluded to the proposal to issue £1 notes. Whether that would effect the object in view he did not feel competent to express a decided opinion, but he was inclined to think it would not to any appreciable and tangible extent, and, as an old-fashioned banker, he apprehended many inconveniences and many drawbacks should the suggestion be carried into practical effect,and he hoped their authorities would satisfy themselves very fully that the advantages they anticipated would be realised before they subjected them to the disadvantages which in his opinion could not fail to ensue. Slaving remarked that the past year had been eventful in more ways than one, he went on to refer to the new issue of shares. By the issue of 2,500 new shares in terms of resolution passed on 24th July, and confirmed on 21st August last, the subscribed capital had been increased from £3,000,000 to £3,250,000, the paid up capital from £600,000 to £650,000 and the reserve fund from £370,000 to £377,400. 'Me year had also seen the successful carrvin, out of the arrangement whereby the old-estab- lished tank of Messrs. Fuller, Banbury, Nix, and Com- pany was incorporated with their bank, and he congra- tulated them upon the fact that their anticipations of the success and advantage which it would bring about hid been fully bdrne out. Be also congratulated them upon the accession to their Board of Directors of the two representatives of the London bank, Mr. Nix and Mr. Banbury. The assistance they had received from those two gentlemen had been of the greatest possible service in enabling them to keep all their old business together and at the same time in much facilit- ating the transference of the London business of the bank to the new head registered offices of the Company, 77, Lombard-st., London. The Chairman next referred in feeling terms to the great loss sustained by the death of two of the directors, Mr. T. P. Parr, and Mr. H. Woodcock. He concluded by saying that the business of the bank continued to be in every way satisfactory. The number of accounts went on steadily increasing and the total turn-over of the bank was largely in excess of what it had been in previous years. The net profits for the past year amounted to £164,191 7s. 10d. (Applause.) Mr. TURNER seconded the adoption of the report, which was agreed to. - -

" THE DIVIDEND. On the motion of Colonel Gamble it was decided to declare a dividend at the rate of 19 per cent, per annum free of income tax. Coknel Gamble added that this dividend now involved the distribution of nearly £5,000 more than formerly, owing to their increased capital,

WANDERER.—Percy Quinn, a small boy, was charged with having been found sleeping in the market shed at a quarter-past five that morning.—P.C. Critchley said that at the time named be heard some one snoring near a lot of potato hampers, and found the lad in one of them. The boy told him that he had not been home since Wednesday week . —lnspector Spinks said that the boy had been taken home by the police from 30 to 40 times during the past year.—The lad was detained in custody for the remainder of the day and ordered to have six strokes of the birch rod. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Gre enall) and Aldermen Francomb and Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Knockton, 27. Erwood-street, for being drunk and disorderly in Scot- land-road on Saturday night, and assaulting Thomas Harrop, was fined 54. John Mannion, in Scotland- road, on Saturday night, ss. DRUNK.—Peter Quinn, drunk in Bewsey-s t., on the 15th inst. was fined ss. DOGS etortizmn.—Wm. Blanchard, 13, Glasshouse row, for having a dog at large unmuzzled, was fined ss. including costs.—Thos. Bowers, fitter, 76. Knutsford- road, was fined the like amount,—Timothy Brannan, labourer, 10, Hall-street, said the dog had gone into another man's house, and he found it there, and this man had the muzzle. The defendant was dismissed, and a police officer was sent with nim to the other man's house for the muzzle.—John Hughes, provision dealer, 346,Knutsford-road ; Thos. Leigh, forgeman, 12, Jones's Buildings ; Wm. Leslie, tanner, 13, Mersey-street, Tabitha Sherratt, 63, Leonard-street, and John Wild- ings, furniture dealer, 73, Buttermarket-street, were each fined ss. including costs, for having their dogs at large unmuzzled. BEGGING.—James Harrington, engineer' of Liverpool, was charged with begging in Bewsey-road on Saturday afternoon. He was dismissed on promising to leave the town at once. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—John Ashton, aged 14, son of Abraham Ashton, linclworth Heath, Cheshire, was fined the costs 3s. 6d., for cruelly treating a horse in Bewsey-

street. SNOWBALLING IN THE STREETS.—WiIIiam Smith, haw- ker, 26, Haydock-street and Richard Warburton, 97, Tanners-lane, both young men, for throwing snowballs in Winwick-street, on Sunday week, to the annoyance of passengers, were fined 2s. 6cl. each.—Thomas Forster and James Allen, boys, the former of 19, Fennell-st., and the latter of 4, Egerton-st., were charged with like offences in Howley-St. The constable who proved the case said they snowballed him. They were fined is. each.— Albert Haliwell, a boy, of 13, Appleton-street, was charged with a like offence, and tined is. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE.—John Frane, canal labourer, 4, Back Atherton-street, and Andrew Johnson, fustian cutter. 23, Dutton-street, for having chimneys on fire were fined, the former 2s. 6d. and the latter is. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. G. J. Guest. THEFTS BY LADS.—Two lads, named Thomas Farring- ton, and John Didgett, were charged with having stolen an overcoat from an office, at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Coy.'s works, on the 20th inst. It appeared that the window of the office had been broken, and Farrington thereby opened an entrance, while Didgett watched from the outside. Farrington was sent to gaol for a month, the other prisoner being fined ss. DRUNKENNESS.—JUIia Ann Shield was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting P. C. Cooper, and was sent to gaol for a month.—Ann Quinn, for having been drunk and disorderly, was also sent to gaol for a month. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough and Alderman Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIiza Smith, 52nd appear- ance, drunk and disorderly, the previous night, in Tanner's-lane, was discharged on her promising to return to the Workhouse out of which she had come. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Captain Ridgway. CHARGE OF NON-MAINTENANCE.— rhe adjourned case of Matthew Flannaghan, charged under a warrant with absconding on the 31st ult., and leaving his wife charge- able to the Union was called. Mr. B. Shearer said the defendant did not appear, but he had started work, and would pay what was due, and was now supporting his wife. The case was therefore withdrawn. DRUNK.—John Timmis, drunk in St. James-street, the previous night, was fined 2s. 6d. Smoot, CASES—The following cases were dealt with : —Samuel Beckett, forgeman, 25 Warburton-at.. fined 2s. 61. ; Samuel Smith, forgeman, 44 Watkin-st., adjourned, Joseph Clare, Back Stamford-St., Sc, ; John Clare, labourer, Back Stamford-st., adjourned, John Mannion, labourer, Ashton's Yard, 2s. 6d. ; Thomas Waterworth, labourer, Old Road, 5g.; Elizabeth Hollo- well, 20 Litton's Row, 2s. Ba. ; Wm. Quinn, labourer, Pilkington's Yard, 2s. 61. ; Mary Towey, 36 Oliver-st., ss. ; John Plunkett, labourer, Old Road, 53. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man Wright, and Dr. Gornall. As OBSTREPEROUS COUPLE.—Sarah Marsh, 4 Hall-st., a woman of loose character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bewsey-st. the previous night, and Thomas O'Niell,a; soldier,was charged with obstruct-] log P.C. 31 in the execution of his duty. They were also charged with assaulting Kate Ann Jones aged 17. but who in stature was a little girl. The girl, her size being , so diminutive for her age, caused much amusement by ' saying, in her evidence, that she had lived in Warring- ton 18 years.—Alderman Harrison : Lived here 18 years, and only 17 years old! (Renewed laughter.) Witness: My mother lived here before ever I was born. (More laughter. )—The male defendant, who had to leave War- rington on Tuesday, was handed over to the military authorities to be dealt with. The female defendant was sent to jail for a month's hard labour. NON-MAINTENANCE OF HIS FATHETI.—Wm. Harper, forgeman, 32, Swan-st., Wigan, was charged by Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with leaving his father, 'Joseph Harper, chargeable to the Union. Mr. Shearer said the defendant could earn £2 a week.—The defendant said he only earned about 18s. a week at pre- sent as on account of the new American tariff work was slack.—Mr. Shearer, in reply to the chairman, admitted that the defendant had not earned so much as £2 a week since Christmas.—An order was made for allowance by defendant Of 3s.a week. CHARGE OF NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—Patriek and Cathe- rine Bartley, husband and wife, of 4, Hall-st., were charged with wilfully neglecting their children to the injury of their health. Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the ' Board of Guardians, applied for an adjournment as the woman did not appear, and it was stated she had ab- sconded. A warrant was issued for her apprehension, and the case was adjousned for her appearance. CRT/ELTY TO A floase.— Thos. Mack, carter, of Thel- wall, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state at Warrington, on the 20th inst., and Henry Cooke, farmer,of Thelwall,W3.3 charged with causing the same to be so worked. Inspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.C.A., prosecuted, and Mr. Shawcross, M.R.C.V., gave evidence on behalf of the defendants, but they had to pay the costs. ASSAULT.—John Whittaker, 18, Cockhedge-lane, was , fined 10s. and costs for an unprovoked assault on Thos. Starkey, in the Market Place, on the 23rd inst.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), W. Long, H, Neild, H. Talbot, J. Marston, and C. Marston. ASLEEP ON HIS LURRY.—James Seed, carter, for being asleep on his lurry on the highway, at Seven Oaks, on the 22nd ult., was fined 55., including costs. DELIVERING BREAD WITHOUT WEIGHTS.—F. W. Hall- wood, baker, Buttermarket-5t., Warrington, was sum- moned on a charge of delivering bread at Preston Brook, without having a beam and scales upon his cart cc that the bread could be weighed by the purchaser. The de- fendant did not appear, and the magistrates fined him I.os. and costs. POACHING.—Thomas Phipps, canal labourer, was charged with trespassing on the 31st ult, on land in the occupation of Mr. Ball, at Acton Grange.—The defen- dant did not appear.—Mr. Forshaw appeared for the prosecution, on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., owner of the land, and said that owing to the proximity of the Ship Canal it was often very difficult to catch these trespassers. Men went about and took a "pot shot" at a hare or other game, and it was almost im- possible to catch them.—P.C. Shatwell deposed to seeing the defendant shoot a rabbit, and then push it into the pocket of another man who was with him.—The defen- dant had disappeared from the district. He was fined OS., and costs, 18s. 6d.
