THEFT OF A CIGAR. John McManus, forge labourer, was charged at the borough police court, on Monday morning, with stealing a cigar from the shop of William Beswick, tobacconist, 72, Sankey-street on Saturday night. He went to the shop, drunk, and got a twopenny cigsr, but ran out without paying for it. A man named William Ashton pursued the prisoner, who fell down near the Farmers' Stores. Constable Cooper, apprehended him lying help- lessly drunk with the cigar upon him. He had nothing to say in self-defence, and was fined 10s. including costs. CHARGE OF ASSAHLT ON A CHILD. At the Borough Magistrates' Court on Thursday, Reuben Dudley, aged 20 years, son of Kate Dudley, a widow, was charged with committing, on the 18th inst., a criminal assault upon Elizabeth McCabe aged six years, daughter of Patrick McCabe. The defendant had recently been in the Northwich workhouse, and came to Warrington about three weeks since, and was lodging with his mother in the same house as the McCabes. The prisoner was in the habit of taking the little girl out for a walk, and it was on his doing so on one occasion that the alleged offence was perpetrated. The prisoner was committed for trial to the Liverpool Assizes. THEFTS AT THE BARRACKS. Two young men, named Murray and O'Connell, both of whom have been accepted within the last few weeks as recruits at the barracks were charged at Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with having stolen some groceries—jam, butter and bacon—the property of Mr. E. Hawthorne, of Winwick-st. A quantity of provisions had been taken to the barracks by the prosecutor in a pony cart, and a quantity was stolen from the cart. Murray was caught carrying away several pots of jam, and he was made to take them back. Afterwards part of the stolen articles were found in the chimney of the room in which the two prisoners were located, and some in O'Connell's bag. A Sergeant from the barracks said there had been several thefts of articles of clothing there, and he could not give the two prisoners very much of a character. O'Connell was sent to gaol for a month, and Murray for six weeks. A JUVENILE COAT STEALER. At the borough police court, on Thursday, Fred Farn- brough, aged 12, son of Thomas Farnbrough, 8, Helsby- street, was charged with stealing on the 22nd, 25th,and 26th inst.. three reefer jackets tram the Mount School, Manchester-road. The Chief Constable said a lad named Bertie Mason, son of Thos. Mason, went to the Mount schools on the 22nd inst., and put his overcoat in the lobby. At 12 o'clock the coat had disappeared. Detec- tive-Sergt. Monoglia.n was informed, and ascertained that the prisoner had pledged the coat for 23. A little girl, the daughter of Wm. Woods. went to the school on the 25th inst., and put her jacket in the lobby, but it was missing at 12 o'clock. On the 26th inst. the same thing happened as to the coat of a boy named Houston. All the garments had been pledged by the prisoner at the same place.—Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, said the boy was constantly playing truant. The Chief Constable said the lad smoked cigarettes, and went to the cocoa rooms regularly. Ile was ordered to be kept in the cells until Saturday, at 10 a.m, and receive 12 strokes of the birch rod. DRUNK AND ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—X FEMALE RUFFIAN. At the borough police court, on Monday, Joseph Warburton, hawker, Tanner's-lane, was charged with , being drunk and disorderly and with assaulting P. S. Taylor while in the execution of his duty, on Saturday night last, and Harriet Warburton, his sister, of Che- shire yard, was charged with assaulting P. S. Taylor, and attempting to rescue her brother from him on the same occasion ._Sergeant Taylor,apprehended the defen- dant on finding him with his coat off wanting to fight in Cheshire Cheese yard, Winwick-st., and was assaulted by him. The female prisoner told her brother with a foul oath to kick witness's guts out, and tried to pull his stick from him ; and to rescue her brother, being very violent. Witness had his lamp kicked out, was kicked in the eye, and had a piece of hair pulled out by the roots. Quite a crowd collected. He got the male pris- oner into Scotland-road, and he continued kicking, and Sergeant Craythorne and some other soldier came to witness's assistance. The male prisoner was sent to jail for a month's hard labour, and Harriet was fined ss. MORE THIEVISH JUVENILES. At the Borough Magistrates' Court,'on Monday, Joseph Frangleton, 29 Crossley-st., and Isaac Smith,26 Hopwood- st., boys, were charged with stealing a Cardigan jacket from the stall of William Craddock, in the Market Place, on tht afternoon of the 6th inst. It appeared Frangleton got under Mr. Craddock's stall, and stole the jacket. Smith and two boys named Arthur Lomas and William Clarke met Frangleton near the stalFputting the jacket underneath his arm. He said to Clarke " I shall go and pledge it. Smith said to Frangleton " You have stolen it." Smith, Lomas, and Clarke watched him go into Morton's and Tunstall's pawnshops and pledge it at the latter place. Smith took the ticket and redeemed the jacket and sold it to Smith, who a fortnight later sold it Clarke for 23.—P.C. Cooper deposed to Frangleton stat- ing at the Police Station, that Lomas, Smith, and another lad watched whilo he stole the jacket.—Frangle- ton was semtenced to receive six strokes of the birch rod to-day, and to be detained in custody till six o'clock the following evening, and then to have six strokes more, and Smith, a much bigger boy, was fined 109. including costs, Lomas being disallowed expenses,as a witness, the bench considering that he had been cognisant of the felony.—The Chief Constable said there was no imputa- tion upon Clarke. WIFE ASSAULT.—AN INSOLENT CHARACTER. At the Borough Magistrates' Court, yesterday, George Thompson Patrick, labourer, Green-st., was charged with assaulting his wife, Mary Ann Patrick, on the 27th inst. The complainant said the defendant assaulted her and her son while they were talking quietly together at dinner. She was sobbing in giving her evidence, and the defendant in a loud stentorian voice exclaimed, " Stop your crying." Alderman Harrison said he had better behave himself.—The defendant : I can behave myself as well as you.—The complainant said she did not wish to press the case.—The defendant afterwards swore several times in court.—The Chief Constable : Take your hands out of your pockets —The defendant : I shall put them where I like. You can't compel me to to take them out.—Alderman Harrison: You are very irepudent.—The defendant: I am impudent. I was brought up impudent; and perhaps you are no better than you ought to be. Alder- man Harrison : I shall not submit to your in- solence.—The defendant : I have to stand everybody's insolence, and you will have to do the same.—Alderman Harrison later on remarked to the defendant : You treat it with indifference.—The defendant : Perhaps you know everything.—Alderman Harrison told the complainant that he was afraid she made a mistake in not pressing the case.—The complainant said she would press pro- ceedings if he assulted her again.—Alderman Harrison said the Bench would have allowed the case to be with- drawn but for the defendant's insolence,but they thought that gave very little promise of his behaving better to his wife, and he would he sent to prion for 14 days. —The defendant: Thank vou, sir. You are a gentleman. —Alderman Harrison Perhaps you will come out a wiser man.—The defendant :It won't make any differ- ence to me.—Alderman Harrison No, I don't suppose it will.

REPORTED RECALL OF 'AIR. EGAN. SANTIAGO, WEDNIISDAY.—The Chilian Government has expressed willingness to accept the mediation of Spain or Brazil, but among the public there is a general opinion in favour of arbitration by the Supreme Court of the United ,States. American citizens here publicly demand the cancelling of the exequrtoe of the United States Consul at Valparaiso. If the report of American origin be true, the President has decided to recall Mr. , Egan without delay.

FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. WERNETH V. WinNes.—This match, at Werneth, on Saturday, proved to be very even and exciting. During the first half, after about 20 minutes' play, Widnes scored an unimproved try. During the second half Werneth had hard lines in not scoring, the ball being kicked dead in the nick of time. Widnes, two points ; Werneth, nothing. WARRINGTON "A" v. MANCHEISTER " A."—At War- rington. Having lost the toss, Manchester started the contest, but Barnes and Warburton showing up promin- ently, frustrated their efforts to break away. A splen- did bit of passing between Lally and Antrobus to Barnes, who scudded down the field right to the line, ended in a minor. Warrington continued to press, and while the game was careering about the half-way flag, Lally, An- trobus, Barnes, and Potts, emulating their previous dis- play, enabled the latter to dodge to the visitors' 25, Bailey, Buckley, Hampson, and Knowles followed up the advaatage, but Knowles relieved the Mancunians' lines, only to see Davies, Forster, Molyneux, and Barnes re- turn the leather, and a second minor was conceded. Al- though Barnes replied to the drop out by a run, the ball was rushed by the Manchester men into the home terri- tory. The stay was cf short duration, for Lally and Westall transferred the scene of operations to the other end. Wilkinson was the first to clear the danger, but Hamblett replied with a tall punt. Again Manchester were to the front, and a long cross dribble tested the defence of Warrington. The visitors now pressed, but Antrobus getting beautifully away threw to Barnes, whe ran into his opponents lines, this being supplemented by Buckley's dashing dribble. A little later the Mancunians rushed the leather out of danger, but after Potts had made a fine run, Barnes, by a grand dodging run, was only pulled up on the line, a minor being given. It was again Warrington's turn to pass, but Manchester, who showed a splendid defence in this half, kept their anta- gonists at bay, Kipping eventually getting clear to mid- field. Davies, by a run and kick, returned the ball, Knowles again coming to the relief of his side. Some grand passing by the home backs followed, and off a tall kick by Potts, Lally secured, and was within an ace of scoring. Success came at laSt, when Westall got a splendidly executed try by dribbling over, Barnes con- verting. Soon after half-time a fine bit of play of Bel- amy, Wilkinson and Russell was cheered, Barnes retali- ating with a grand dribble. Bailey, Buckley, Warburton, and Knowles then rushed to the line, and for the next five minutes the defence was severely taxed. Pagden brought about a slight relief, but Antrobus removing play to the visitors' quarters, Knowles rushed up in the nick of time and saved disaster. Knowles replied to the drop out, and Wincey mulling badly, Molyneux scored. Manchester began to show signs of distress, and al- though Knowles came to the rescue of his side, a swerv- ing run by Potts, followed by a fins run by Barnes, who was stopped on the line, caused the visitors a lot of trouble. The home forwards were playing very well, , giving the backs plenty of work, and after Hamblett had I, found touch near the line, Antrobus got a pretty try. Again the forwards, led by Hampson, Davies, Forster, and Warburton, rushed through the defence of the visitors, and a pretty bit of passing by Westall, Barnes, and Potts ended in the last-named getting a try, which he converted. An effort by Russell, Pagden, and Bent- ley was nullified by Molyneux, Barnes, Bailey, and Hampson, and Wincey making another bad mistake let in Davies. After this Manchester got the ball away to the further end of the ground, a minor only resulting, and the game ended—Warrington 2-3-6 to 0-0-1. _SWINTON V. RUNCORN. These clubs played their return match at Runcorn on Saturday, before some 4,000 spectators, in beautiful weather. Both clubs are strong, and it was anticipated that the victory would only be achieved after a keen 1 struggle. The result, however, showed that the Run- corn combination was superior to that of their rivals in every department, and the home team, after having the best of the play, won by 11 points to none. Houghton was unable to play at full back for Runcorn, whilst Marsh who is in Scotland, was abseht on the Swinton side. The winning forwards packed better, screwed I well, and generally carried the tight scrimmages, while they:were very quick on the ball. Then the home half backs over-played their rivals and fed their three-quar- ter backs admirably, who in turn were rarely at fault I in taking passes and gaining: ground. On the other 1 hand, the Swinton three-quarter backs, with the for- wards and halves outplayed, had few opportunitiesl given them. Valentine played centre three-quarter vice Marsh, but was by no means so effective as when 1 on the wing, and was well checked by Crompton. Winterbottom and Pearson made several good runs, but the tackling of the home players was too effective to admit of scoring. Of the visiting forwards, Halle:el, Hall and Walker were the most prominent, while Paul at full back saved his lines upon several occasions in fine style. Valentine kicked off for Swinton, and May mak- ing a poor return let in the visitors. After several scrimmages within the home quarter a fine passing run was made by Faulkner, Abrams, Crompton Pendlebury, Williams, and Robinson, the last-named player being sent into touch near the Swinton goal line. After a I scrimmage Crompton got possession, and upon being tackled passed to Abrams, who ran round his opponents and scored a try for Runcorn, the some player failing at goal. The drop-out kick was well returned by Cromp ton, and Swinton was soon again placed on the defen- sive, Crompton and Pendlebury being conspicuous with a good run, which was well stopped by Paul close on the goal line, and Bumby relieved the pressure with a short I run. Further ground was gained with a good dribble to the home quarter ; but play was quickly transferred to the other end of the field, when Abrams got the ball from a scrimmage, and after dodging his opponents passed to Crompton, who ran over the Swinton goal line and scored the second try for Runcorn behind the posts, the same player failing from the place. The Swintonians then played up better, and carried play by short stages to the Runcorn quarter, Brockbank, Bumby, and Valen- tine being conspicuous for short runs; but the home players kept their lines intact, and a fine combined dribble by Runcorn took the ball to the centre, when Davies gained further ground with a good run. Pearson then got possession, and upon being smartly tackled passed the ball in mistake to Hampson and Hampson running through the Swinton players passed to Massey who scored an easy try for Runcorn under the cross- bar, Crompton again failing from the easiest of places. Half time was then called, with the score three tries (six points) in favour of Runcorn. After changing ends Faulkner resumed the game. Winterbottom returned the ball to the centre flag, and Valentine getting posses- sion made a strong run and passed to Pearson, who upon being tackled threw forward, losing a favourable opportunity of scoring. Swinton for a time had some- what the best of the play, but could not quite break through the defence of the home players, Crompton once being compelled to touch down. The drop Out kick being well returned by Paul, Runcorn was again placed on the defensive ; but relief was brought with a fine run between Crompton, Pendlebury, Davies, and Abrams, and the home forwards, following up well pushed the ball strongly to the Swinton goal line, Paul saying in fine style and punting into touch at the centre flag. Runcorn, however, were playing splendidly toge- ther, and severely pressed their opponents, Paul being compelled to touch down. Soon afterwards Crompton picked up in the centre while on full speed, and easily dodging Valentine and Paul, scored a magnificent try under the posts, May kicking a goal from the place. " No side" was then called, with the score—Runcorn, one goal, three tries (11 point q) to Swinton nothing. The following were the teams :—Swinton : A. G. Paul, full back ; W. Pearson, J. Valentine, and W. Winterbottom, three-quarter backs ; W. Bumby and IL Brockbank, half backs ; T. Rothwell, S. Hall, T. Hallam, W.'Evans, G. 11. Murray, G. Sharples, W. Walker, A. Walsh, and J. Parkinson, forwards. Runcorn: H. May, fullback; G. Pendlebury, J. H. Crompton, and T. H. Davies, three-quarter backs ; S. Abrams and G. Robinson, half backs ; W. Faulkner, R. Rees, P. Riley, R. Dolan, A. Hampson, G. Lee, 0. Hughes, H. Williams, and D. Massey, forwards. Referee, Mr. T. Hunter, Manchester Rangers; touch judges, Mr. J. Sherlock and Mr. T. Banks.
WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER.

Warrington's first visit to the classic enclosure at Whalley Range was attended by anything but favourable results. It was only four weeks ago since Warrington met Manchester at Wilderspool, and on that occasion the city representatives were defeated by a goal and two tries to nil. However, on Saturday, in the return match the Warringtonians were not favoured with that amount of luck usually experienced by the modern footballer, and after having fixed the game in the Manchester quarters fully 45 minutes out of the 60 played, only minor points were scored, and a draw recorded. There would be nearly 3,000 present when the kick off was effected, and amongst this number was a fair sample of Warrington enthusiasts, who, though lacking in num- bers, made up for any deficiency in the shouting business. The ground was heavy going, and only two 30's were played. At 2.45 Turner started, and Bellamy and Heesom exchanged, the latter piloting back to Manchestor quar- ter flag, enabling Nevins and Jolley to give the visitors the task of attackiag. A miskick by James Bate was taken up by Mullineux, and the oval being taken to Webster, that player was forced to save. From the first scrimmage the Warrington backs were in the ascendant, and James and John Bate passing beautifully, the latter was safely held a yard from the line. D. C. Woeds cleared the impending danger, only to find Fair Turner steering the oval back again, and from some loose play Jolley got clear, but again the coveted yard could not be got. Steel and Mullineux, the latter with his strict attentions towards the visiting half backs, gained ground, but another splendid bout of passing by the Bates, Ileesom and Evans was applauded to the echo. Evans again had the ill luck to be held ran the verge of

scoring. From a kick by Heesom, Carson was held five yards from the line, and Turner, Ashton' Teare and Berry each in turn became prominent. Nevins was grassed when almost over by Steel, whilst Webster missed a low pass and a certain score. And so tho game continued, a series of hard lines for the visitors, Holmes on one occasion dribbling over and gaining an apparent try, but only a minor point was allowed, much to the chagrin ot the Warringtonians. Turner responded to the drop out, but Woods, who, it may be mentioned, made his first appearance since he broke his collar-bone when playing against Bradford, got clear of Webster, and when the homesters had predicted a tangible score, the lengthy Warrington three-quarter took after his man, and half-a-dozen strides sufficed for the Manchester hopes to be upset. However, this smart run, was the means of forcing more vigour into the Manchester play, and a fine dribble headed by Hulse, Steel, and Cameron, found Boscow employment, for the first time. The home backs now passed well but if their defence had been substantial, they found that Warrington did not lack in this respect. Wincey made an effort, but Evans was all there, whilst Boscow and Heesom accounted for Steel a minute later. A kick by way of penalty, was taken by Fair Turner, and the quarter-flag was reached, but C. Woods punted back, Evans being collared on the line. The homesters, headed by Nevins and Donohue, soon had the oval out of danger, and then a fine run and pass by Jolley to Heesoin saw the latter throwing to Evans, for that player to be well tackled when scoring seemed a cer- tainty. Another runby James Bate from a pass by his companion was duly applauded, whilst a similar passing bout between the visiting backs saw Evans again held on the line. Woods dribbled away, but the Warrington forwards, aided by the grand combination of the backs, soon had the oval back on the Manchester lines, and Gerson was compelled to save. Boscow put in a couple of fine kicks from the drop-out, and when half time was called the game was on the home lines, Warrington having aotched two minors. On resuming, Evans obliged with a sterling run to the Manchester 25, but James Bate did not seem to realise hispesition, other- wise a score would assuredly have results I in the first minute. & brilliant display between the two Bates, Heesom, and Evans was foiled by Steele,and then Teare dribbled well. Again the Bates and Heesom shone with passing tactics, only to find the tackling sure. The oval was worked away on one occasion to Boscow, and a ponderous kick sent it to touch near the Manchester lines. A run by Evans and pass to Bury saw some short passing being participated in by Nevins, Thorniley, and Teare : and although the oval was but five yards from the line, a score was not forthcoming. Cameron relieved finely, and Woods supplemented the effort with a short run, but James Bate, Jolley and Dare had the oval back at its original quarters in a moment. Nevins rushed to the line, but Manchester, improving in their play, worked the oval to the other end, and Wincey was nearly in, the fine tackling of Boscow accounting for him. As rapid as had been the visit to the Warrington lines, so was the return, and Turner had exceptionally hard lines in an effort from the ruck. Wincey saved, whilst a fourth minor was forthcoming from the foot of Webster. Nevins made his mark in response to a kick by Woods, whilst a palpably wrong decision gave Man- chester a decided lift. Near the call of time, Smith, P. Steel, and Cameron dribbled to the Warrington line, and soon after the whistle announced " no side," the result being—Warrington, 4 minors; Manchester, nil. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back ; H. Webster, F. Heesom, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs ; Jas. T. Bate, and John T. Bate, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Holmes, J. Jollcy, J. T. Thornily, J. Berry, W. Nevins, H. Teare, and T. Donohue, forwards. Manches- ter : R. H. Carson, back ;D. C. Woods, W. B. Steel, and G. C. Wincey, three-quarter backs ; M. Mullineux, and C. Wood, half backs ;G. M. N. Cameron J. Tait, J. H. Smith. 11. It. Bellamy, P. Steel, R. L. Hulse, T. G. Howson. A. Taylor, and A. C. Broadbent, forwards. Referee, Mr. S. Simpson, Broughton Rangers.

Sr. HELENS EXCELSIOR T. SUTTON ROVERS.—This re- turn match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and the game ended in a win for the Excel- sior by three goals to one. LANCASHIRE ALLIANCE.—HAYDOCK V. PARK-LANE WAN- DERERS.—The first alliance match between these teams was played at Haydook, on Saturday, there being a fair crowd of spectators. Haydock soon scored two goals, but before half time Park-lane succeeded in equalising. In the second half the visitors had the best of the game, and scored two more goals, ultimately winning by four goals to two. ST.HELENS LOWE HOUSE GUILD V.ST.HELENS Y.M.C.A. —ACCIDENT TO A PLitrait.—The first meeting between these clubs took place on Saturday last. In the end the game was left drawn, no goals being scared. During the course of the game a sad accident occurred to a player named McLean. It appears he had got the ball in his own territory and dribbled to the centr e,when one of the Guild half backs charged him, and McLean fell heavily on his arm. It was at once seen that something was wrong, and with the assistance of two or three other players he was taken to Dr. Knowles, who found that the arm had been broken just below the elbow. After bandaging his arm, McLean was taken home, and he is now getting on as well as can be expected. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. AIGIIURTH VALE.—This match was played at Fulwood Park in nice weather, the visitors being short of their two full backs, substituting two of their Reserve team. Kicking off shortly after 3 p.m., Warrington playing with the sun to their backs, the home team at once assailed the visitors goal, but Phillips and Tickle defended splendidly. Eventually after about 15 minutes play Aigburth scored their first and only point. This reverse seemed to" liven up "the Warringtonians and playing a steady combined game, were soon dangerous, Ball, Aitkin and Powell having each a try to equalise. Ultimately from a corner one of the home backs kicked it through his own goal. Half time result, Warrington, 1; Aigburth, 1 goal. Restarting the hornesters went off with a rush, being pulled up by the opposing half backs. Aitkin raced away and with a splendid shot put Warrington on the winning side. From this the visitors had matters much their own way, and showing a good combined game they easily scored two more goals in quick succession, one from the foot of Ball and the other by Powell, thus running out winners of a good game by Warrington 4 goals; Aigburth Vale 1 goal. Phillips and Tickle played a good back game for Warrington, while Ball, Aitkin, and Powell did credit to the front rank. The home backs and goal-keeper saved their side a heavier defeat. Warrington team :—Messrs. Jones, Phillips, Tickle, Clayton, Jack Mather, Stanton, Ball, James Mather, Aitkin, T. Mather and Powell.
THE RECENT WA.RRINGTON AND LEEDS PARISH CHURCH FIASCO.

At the annual ineetieg of the Yorkshire Rugby Union, held at the Green Dragon Hotel, Leeds, on Monday evening, before a large attendance of members, the Warrington F.C. reported th Lt Leeds Parish Church had failed to ken) their engagement on January 12th at War- rington. The Parish Church team journeyed to Man- chester, but missed the connection for Warrington. They therefore wired to ask if they were to come forward, but the telegram did not arrive at Warrinaton till after the train had left Manchester, and it was too late to send any reply. The team did not goon, and the Warrington Clah complained that they had lost £7l in gate money, cost of bills, posting, kc. The Leeds Parish Church team, for whom Kilburn appeared, offered to play a match on a future date. The Leeds club offered to visit Warrington on April 16th, but as Brighouse Rangers are due at VVilderspool on that date, the Tykes will have to make the journey on a week day with their best pos- sible team.
MURDER OF SERVANT GIRLS IN AUSTRIA. SENSATIONAL EVIDENCE:

The trial of Frank and Rosaline Schneider, on eight dis- charges of murder, outrage, and robbery. committed upon servant girls between May 26 and July 7, 1891, was opened on Monday morning in the Vienna Courts of Jus- tice. The court was crowded to excess, the case having excited an enormous -amount of interest owing to the peculiarly horrible character of the crimes set forth ,in the indictment. Three of the girls who were decoyed into woods near New Lengbach, a suburb of Vienna, under specious promises of employment as domestic ser- vants in respectable families, were murdered and stripped of their clothes, their naked bodies being subsequently discovered among the brushwood. The other victims were outraged and robbed, but escaped with their lives. Schneider pleaded guilty to criminal assaults under two heads of the indictment, and to the charges of murder in one instance under the third head. With regard to the remaining charges, he endeavoured to throw the guilt upon his wife. The latter denied all participation in the crimes, and a violent scene between the prisoners occurred in court, each endeavouring to inculpate the other. VIENNA, TIIIIRSDAY.—Further evidence was given to- day in support of the charge of murder and outrage against the Schneider couple. The branch of the case which formed the subject of particular investigation was the murder of the girl Zoufar. 'the crime was commit- ted in July last, and the naked body of the victim was not discovered in the secluded portion of the Haspen Walde, where it had been concealed, until the 15th November. To-day's testimony tended to further in- criminate the female prisoner, who when pressed by the judge as to what part she had played, burst into tears, and made no further reply.

The welcome Wan-ge-iiTthe -weather allowed football to have full swing once more on Saturday, and a vast number of fixtures were brought off. Northumberland Proved their superiority over their Durham neighbours, and in the international trial match at Edinburgh the West of Scotland beat the Eastern representatives some- what easily. The team that is to do duty for Scotland against Wales at Cardiff in a few days was afterwards chosen.

The match between Warrington and Manchester was not one of the most interesting gairies,and the only real excitment was when " Fair "Turner got over the line and just missed scoring owing to the prompt action of one of his opponents. The two Bates gave an admir- able half back display for the visitors, whose forwards also held their own. Turner, Jolly, Boscow, and Evans all did capital work for Warrington, their following up being a strong feature. The Manchester halves were not nearly so smart as those on the other side, but D. C. Woods was often conspicuous among three-quarters. Percy Steel, Smith, Carneron,and Tait, were about the best of the scrimmagers, the dribbling of the former being good.

The departure of Marsh for Scotland is sure to have itseffect on the play of Swinton, in proof of which we may point to their exprience at Runcorn. They lost no fewer than eleven points and were quite unable to penetrate the defence of the Cheshire cracks. The pass- ing of the Runcorn back division was of a very high order, and apparently did not suffer because of the absence of 11.ughton. The back play of Paul left a good deal to be desired. Following on their reverse at Hali- fax the Swintonians are doing none too well just now.

There was a g,ood gate at the meeting of St. Helens Recreation and Oldham, and an excellent exhibition of football. The " Rees" came out victorious, Unsworth dropping s clever goal which turned the tide in their favour. St. Helens gave Birkenhead Wanderers a very hard game, but just failed to hold their own.

For a one-sided game that between Cleckheaton and Crompton is worth notice. The Yorkshire club won by as many as 39 points to nothing. Therm have been many famous battles between Bradford and Wakefield Trinity, and whenever the two rivals are seen in opposi- tion feeling runs very high. Play was so rough on Saturday that a couple of players were ordered off the field. Bradford, who were without Hawcridge, had to acknowledge defeat by two tries to nil, which was al- together unexpected. t

Houghton (Cheshire), full backs ; R. E. Lock- wood (Yorkshire), J. Marsh (Lancashire), and G. C. Hubbard (Kent), three-quarter backs ; E. W. Taylor (Northumberland) and A. The first round of ihe'c-o-m—oWti-tio-n for the F. A. cup is n4w complete and the second round is to come off to- day (Saturday). At several of the ties there were tre- menduous crowds, fully 18,000 spectators paying for admission at Sheffield. 13,000 at Sunderland v. Notts, and 12,000 at Everton. The poorest muster was at the match between Sunderland Albion and St. George's, but this was owing to the other tie in the town being so much more attractive.

In every case where ties were replayed farm may be , said to have been confirmed. Sunderland again demon- strated their infinitely greater skill over Notts, and it is generally admitted that they will need reckoning with in future rounds, although Accrington may give them some trouble this week end. The Reds will !raw; the advan- tage of ground, and they are sure to make the most of its Sunderland Albion were easy victors against St. George's but they will find Notts Forest of vastly different metal. Stoke repeated their performance against the Casuals, the amateurs shaping no better on the soft and spongy turf than they did on the slippery surface when in the Potteries previously. All the southern representative have now disappeared from the competition.

About the best performance of the afternoon was that of the North End against lronopolis. In the " or- dinary" of a week ago each side scored a couple of goals, and this led the " Nops" to believe that they had a good chance of pulling off the tie. But they reckoned without their host. The Prestonians came out in grand style, and won with ridiculous ease by six to none. Several of the Ironopolis players were gnilty of very shady tricks. It is not a little straßge that in the next round the North End have to journey to Middlesbrough, and will thus have met the two clubs of the tcwn in the competition. Wolverhampton were so much strengthened by the presence of 'Popham in the centre that they knocked out Crewe Alexandra by four goals to one, and are now ready for Sheffield United.

A big disappointment was in store for Everton, and here again public form received confirmation. They were visited by Burnley for the third time within a month, and for the third time failed to score a triumph over the Turf Moorites. Burnley won the exhibition match of eight days ago by four goals to two, and now they won the actual tie by three to one. That clearly stamps them as the better team. In Hilman they have a marvellous goalkeeper, and their all-round defence was of a sounder stamp than that of Everton. Geary again did duty for the home side, but he was of little use. The back play of Howarth was poor in the ex- treme, and Williams ought to have done better in goal. The blow to the Everton supporters was a very heavy one.

general election the constituencies which elected Lib- erals in 1885 would return to their allegiance. Mr. H. Campbell-Bannerman, M. P., delivered a political address at the Reform Club, in Manchester, on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. H. Madee,the newly elected member for Rossendale was present, and the speakers also included Mr. R. 'Lire, M.P. and Mr. W. Mather, M.P. Mr. Edwin Guthrie presided. WARRINGTON LIBERALS AND THE ELECTION. A considerable number of the members of the Warring- ton Liberal Association 'waited the result of the poll in the club rooms, Bewsey-st., on Saturday night. Arrange- ments had been made with ths Post Office to have the message transmitted after official hours. The result was made known half-an-hour after midnight, and the over- whelming majority, far greater than the most ardent of the company had ventured to anticipate, was received with enthusiastic cheers.

GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The scene on Saturday night in front of the Mechanics' Institute, Bacup, whore the counting took place,was one which has never been equalled in Rossendale. There gatherei an immense throng of spectators. They extended as far as the eye could reach, and were huddled together in dense masses close up to the door. The ballot-boxes were a long time reaching Bacup from the outlyingi, polling stations, it being nearly half-past nine before the last of them weilhanded in. The High Sheriff was in personal attAdance, and was assisted by ten counters. Mr. Davitt represented Mr. lifaclen, who was unable to he present, but Sir Thomas Brooks was on the spot in person. The public-houses re- mained open by special licence till a quarter to mid- night, and the streets were very animated and somewhat noisy. It was close upon midnight when the 'tloor of the counting room was opened, and the High Sheriff announced to the representatives of the Press who were in attendance from all parts of the country the following result : Mr. Maden (L) . . 6,066 Sir T. Brooks (L U)

Majority... . 1,225 There was immediately a desperate, wild stampede for the telephone and telegraphs, and the news was sent flying all over the country. The High Sheriff proceeded to declare the result from a window to the crowd below. There were frantic cheers when it was known that Mr. Maden had won, and these were kept up for hours after- wards, as the tide of humanity rolled away into the different glens and hamlets in the constituency. At the close of the counting, the Rev. It. fleyworth, on behalf of Mr. Maden, moved a vote of thanks to the High Sheriff, and this was seconded by Sir Thomas Brooks, who acknowledged the fairness shown by his opponents during the contest. The voting in 1885 and 1886 was as follows :
1885. Hartington (L) Ecroyd (C) 4,228 Majority 1886. Ilartington (U) 5,399 3,949 Newbigging.(L)

Majority 1,450 CONGRANUIATIONS TO THE NEWLY-ELECTED MEMBER. Although the Bacup Post Office was only open a couple of hours, Mr. Maden received a shoal of telegrams on Sunday morning. One of the first to arrive at Bacup was from Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., who handed in a telegram in Ireland, dated 12.42, or within an hour of the declaration of the poll. Mr. Sullivan's message was, " Hurrah, hurrah, hurrah." The Workington Liberals were sixteen minutes in advance of Mr. Sullivan's. The message read, "Sir Wilfred Lawson's constituents send hearty congratulations on victory." Mr. Schnadhorst telegraphed, "Most hearty congratulations. Rossendale is the crowning mercy of the campaign." From the National Liberal Club came the brief message," Bravo." The Daily Telegraph" of Wednesday contains the following despatch, received from a St. Raphael corres- pondent on Tuesday:—" Mr. Gladstone is delighted with the result of the Rossendale election." div.head: FOUR WIDNES GENTLEMEN PRECIPITATED INTO SANKEY CANAL.
div.p: FOUR WIDNES GENTLEMEN PRECIPI- TATED INTO SANKEY CANAL.

NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING. On Tuesday night the inhabitants of Sankey Bridges were thrown into a state of considerable excitement by the news of a startling and alarming misadventure which was experienced by four Widnes gentlemen, and their narrow escape from drowning in the Sankey Canal. Dr. O'Keeffe, Medical Officer of Health for Widnes, Mr. D. Wright, Chairman of the Health Committee of the Widnes Local Board, Mr. G. Neil, a member of the same committee, and Mr. .J. S. Sinclair, Surveyor to the Board, on Tues- day visited Warrington for the purpose of investi- gating the arrangements being _ carried out at the Infectious Diseases Hospital in Aikin-st. They had come to Warrington in a conveyance belonging to Mr. Neil, and left the Nag's Head at half-past five to return home, Dr. O'Keeffe taking the reins. As the trap reached the side of the Sankey Canal, about a quarter to six o'clock, it happened that the bridge was open, and as the night was very dark, though there were two lighted lamps upon the vehicle, and two street lamps, also lighted, about six yards trom the canal, the occupants of the conveyance did not perceive that the bridge was not closed, it being open at the time for the passage of a flat. The usual precaution of throwing two iron bars across the side of the canal in front of the road tc prevent accident, had, moreover, not been observed. The consequence was that the four gentlemen, with the horse and trap, were precipitated into the water. Dr. O'Keeffe went to the bottom of the canal on the other si(4e of it, with the conveyance on the top of him, and though he is a swimmer, and tried to swim to the side, he had considerable'tlifficultyin extrica- ting himself, the more so because the horse was struggl- ing to release itself and making his position still more embarrassing, the animal kicking him several times on the legs. The doctor, however, notwithstanding that he is an elderly man, made such determined exertions that he freed himself. The flat passing through the canal at the time, was being drawn by a horse, and the man in charge of the horse fortunately had the presence of mind to run back with the rope and hitch it to a post,and thus &rest the craft in its progress, or it would have run down the four men-in the water, and they would almost to a certainty have all perished. As it was they clung to the side of the bridge, and made use of the conveyance as it lay submerged, to stand upon, and by that means were saved from drowning. The man at the canal-house and other employes of the London and North Western Railway Company, to whom the canal belongs, together with some men who were coming home from the works close by, united their efforts to save the four gentlemen, and all of them were brought to the bank, Dr. O'Keeffe being the last to be landed. The horse, however, was drowned. The scene while the lives of the endangered gentlemen hung in the balance,was, as may be imagined, a most exciting one; and soon after they had been rescued, a crowd of hundreds of persons who had heard the news of the accident, had collected on the spot. The four gentlemen immediately, all of them, especially Dr. O'Keeffe, being considerably shaken and exhausted, walked to the Black Horse Inn, hard by, where the host, Mr. George Roughley, treated them with every consideration. They were placed before a good fire, and brandy was promptly supplied to them. The host provided a change of clothing for each of them, but they all thankfully declined to avail themselves of this kindness ercept the doctor, though he would only consent to change his coat and stockings. Mr. Roughley requested the driver of a bus which was passing to Warrington, to send a cab, to take the gentlemen home, and in about 20 minutes one arrived from Mr. Edward Connor's establishment in Sankey-st., and they were driven to Widnes.' The horse and trap were got out about half-past nine,the latter, strange to say,being very little damaged. The depth of the canal at that part where the bridge crosses is about seven feet. It may be men- tioned that it was fortunate that the oversight of the ron bars not being thrown across had been committed, as had the contrary been the case,the conveyance would have collided with them with great force, the trap have been smashed, and the occupants probably killed or drowned through the violence with which they would have been hurled to the ground or into the canal. It may be stated that one night only a few months ago the Rev. A. Moore was bicycling at Sankey Bridges, and, intending to cross the .canal, but not seeing that the bridge was open and his passage barred, came into forcible collision with the bars, and had his machine destroyed. This circumstance and the more startling occurrence of Tuesday demonstrate the fact that it is imperatively necessary that the Railway Company should adopt some method of precaution by which such accidents, and perhaps even a terribly fatal catastrophe may be averted in the future. We regret to learn that the four gentlemen were on Thursday so far suffering from their immersion as to be confined to bed.

NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS C RICKET AND BOWLING CLUB. The annual general meeting of the members of this alub was held at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Friday evening. Mr. B. B. Glover presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. The minutes of the last general meeting were read by Mr. Cook, secretary, and duly confirmed. Mr. Hindlef, treasurer, submitted the balance sheet, and statement of accounta, which showed the receipts from all sources, including a balance of £3 2s. Id., and£s3 Is. subscriptions for extension of pavilion, to be £169 12s. 2d., and expenditure £166 9s. 5d., leaving a balance of £3 2s. 9d. There were no outstanding amounts, and this was the third year in succession that such a happy state of things had been accomplished.—Mr. Hindley pointed out that the annual concert had not vet been held ; had it taken place they would have had -the best balance that the club had ever experienced. The balance shtet was. unanimously adopted. To the list of club patrons were added the names of Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, and Mr. James Smith, Brookside, Newton. Mr. B. B. Glover was re-appointed president for the entuing year. The whole of the vice-presidents were re-elected, the names of Mr. T. S.Fairclough and Mr. B. Stuart being added to the list. Mr. W. Hindley was re-appointed treasurer, and Messrs. Cook and Singleton, secretaries. The following were appointed to serve upon the General Committee: Messrs. J. Bateman, F. Brierley, W. Dud- ' geon, T. Harrison, G. Harrison, W. Price, A. Syme, H. sweetlove, T. Wilkinson, J. Williamson, and Dr. H. Watkins. Mr. W. Hindley was appointed captain of the first team, a position he accepted on condition that he be relieved next year. The following appointments were also made :—Bowl- ring captains, Messrs. C. H. Bodmer, E. Fairclough, J- Liptrott, and T. Fairclough. Auditors :—Messrs. J. H. Lane and J. Rimmer. Ground committee :—Messrs. F. Brierley, W. Longton, J. Sankey, and T. Wilkinson. The question of groundsman was left over to be dealt with by the committee. It was unanimously decided ' that the club should again become members of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire County Bowling Association.—Mr.W. Urquhart, an old member of the club, sent in his resig- nation, which was accepted with regret, and the secre- tary was instructed to write Mr. Urquhart to this effect, and to thank him for his past services to the club. Mr. Singleton brougbit up the question of subscrip- tions to the tennis club, and moved that the subscrip- tion be reduced Ca, 10s. per member, to include the pri- vileges of cricket, bowling, and tennis.—Mr. Hindley seconded .—Mr. Stuart moved as an amendment that the subscription be as at present, viz., 155., for tennis mem- bers. Mr. W. Longton seconded, and the amendment was carried by a large majority. Messrs. W. Longton and R. J. Berry were appointed tennis captains. The President intimated his intention of giving a cricket bat for the best batting average in the first eleven, end Mr. J. Rimtner promised a ball for the best bowling average in the second eleven. Several new members *ere proposed for the coming season. A good list of matches has already been arranged for the coming season, amongst others being Wavertree, Leigh Haigh, Spital, Stanley, Earlestown, Ashton, Prescot, and Flint. A vote of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

PoLrrEsEss.—ln cases of what old-fashioned school-ma'ams " call "manners," cultivate civility and good-nature. Be polite to the rudest boor you meet. Your own politeness may often be met with !light or rudeness. That need not trouble you. If you are guilty of impertinence, and receive tit for tat, then, indeed, you may wince, not other- wise. The feeling often seems to be: "Such an one has been insolent to me; I will show him that I will not submit to suoh treatment—that I can be ?8 Careless of his feelings as he is of mine." This Ls very foolish. You only lower yourself, and, very Probably, produce no effect upon him; because ill- bred People are generally endowed with feelings about as delicate and sensitive as the hide of an elderly rhinoceros. Besides, if his insolence is 7a6alce prepense, and he wants to sting you, bow better could you baffle him than by showing your iisual suavity and polite consideration of him, thus Proving yourself unwounded? THE MORAL SENSE IN YOUTH.—The training of the conscience, or moral sense, is the most delicate and important of all the duties devolved upon the teachers p 1 or youth. The mete disposition to follow right and avoid wrong, however sincere and earnest St may be, is not all that is required. The reason Must be brought to bear upon and direct this dis- Position—in other words, the conscience must he taught to discriminate intelligently. It would be rio exercise of this sentiment to bid the pupil abstain from vicious acts because they are practised °lll3' by the mean and despicable, and are sure to bring down odium on the perpetrators. That ,I:vould be an sppeal to the pride, not to the moral "ense• The argument must be addressed directly to the conscience itself. CONVERSATION.—In the management of conver- 'lation avoid disputes. Arguments, as they are --.t.isus.lly conducted, seldom end in anything else. 11 We have not the requisite patience, good feeling, sod politeness to prevent this, let us defer arguing ,a,ltogether. The attitude of a seeker after truth is e only one in which to argue, whereas most a.lgaments are pursued simply to uphold an opinion 'treacly formed and to overthrow an antagonist. I:he habit of talking too much and consuming the „"me that should in fairness be given to another is 4 very common blot on conversation; so is that of interruption, and of obtruding matter known only t° two or three into a large circle. Good taste and good feeling alike forbid these. • Stear•Ts.—We must regard every matter as an intrusted secret which we believe the person con- 'eriled would wish to be considered as such. Nay, further, we must consider all things as secrets in- f....till, sted which would bring scandal upon another if .""iri, and which it is not our certain duty to discuss, ;V that In the presence of the accused. The rine rule of doing as we would be done by is "yes better put to the test than in matters of good 141 d evil speaking. We may argue with ourselves 1 ' ,WPoll the manner In which we would wish to be , 'reated in many circumstances; but everybody recoils instinctively from the thought of being .' 'lPoken ill of in his absence. TIM following rules are necessary to acquire :wealth :—Be honest. If Satan tempts you to de- fraud your neighbour, it is only that he may rob Y.°ll of your ill-gotton gain in the end. Be tem- perate. Liquor has made more paupers than all Other vices combined. Be industrious. Improve *akh day as if you expected to die on the to-mor- row. Indolence, debt and disease are brothers. Let Your word be your bond. Good credit is a fortune to begin with. Limit your expenses by tecessity and comfort, leaving a good margin for , Mance saved. Invest your funds carefully and intelligently. Beware of the brilliant bubbles that , r blown up to tempt ingenious speculators. Ive your personal attention to your business. To do this, keep brain and body healthful. ' ,_ Wu° art thou that braggest of thy life of idle- ;'"ess ; complacently showest thy bright gilt equip- -Iges ; sumptuous cushions; appliances for folding ...of the hands to sleep? Looking up, looking down, ' Iround, behind or before, discernest thou, if it be 'slot in Mayfair alone, any idle hero' saint, god, or 'w ven devil? Not a vestige of one. In the heavens, , • Lii the earth, in the waters under the earth, is none ' wke unto thee. Thou art an original figure in this rreation ; a denizen in Mayfair alone, in this ex- aoroinary century, or half-century alone I One tn rethuiTtn:tisr there is in the world—the idle man.— Carlyle. a this greatest blessing an individual can have in znea. i:World is a sound, healthy, well-balanced con- Which can be obtained only from sound, by Parents. On the other hand, the greatest f isfortune that can befall one, is to inherit a body -,esble, ill-balance& and predisposed to disease. language can describe the advantages and dia- 'advantages which, from this one source, must kttend these two persons through life. Whether We consult the interests of the individual or of the -, wornmunity at large, there is no knowledge in a - Worldly point of view, so important or so valuable .44 that of the hews of inheritance. ' „AN old historian says about the Roman armies :Inat marched through a country, burning and estroying every living thing, "They make a wilitude and they call it peace." And So men do , With their consciences. They stifle them, sear ~._"sm, forcibly silence them, somehow or other; : Zod then, when there is a dead stillness in the heart, broken by no voice of either approbation or `,.',lstrie, but doleful, like the unnatural quiet of a , r serted city, then they say, "It is peace," and • Ze. Man's uncontrolled passions and unbridled :Sefrires dwell'Ssolitary in the fortress of his own :I.P.trit / You may almost attain to that. —Alexander ~(If aclaren. u_CRARLES DELMONICO, of the famous Now York Ziitkurant, used to eat only the simplest of food, :V. he always drank with his meals. His cellars linere stocked with the richest and heaviest of wines, 4 ' via ilis kitchen produced the greatest feats of tWa,strY ever known. But his dinners generally 11;e-stilted of a few raw oysters, a bit of roast beef, tf or three plainly cooked vegetables, and a pint , all his own cheapest claret. His nephew, who now 1 s) Os the big restaurant, can be found at twelve or siole o'clock almost any night taking his supper in mills oyster-saloon or chop-house rather than eat his own table. pi,4l Li young people should be taught the full jinille of money—how to save and how to spend it. Is "(irn to a heritage of wealth, they should be billight that its possession brings greater responsi- gs„tties, and its proper management when they 14.'w oli will bring even a heavier tax on their theehtel or moral powers and faculties than would sh earning of a livelihood. If born to labour, they 1e„0411d be taught that work is not disgraceful so • a$ they labours well; and that then- earnings 'ild not be squandered, but inv-sted wisely in , ttf,, ,—enee to the future. .eo th/ e.' If we analyse those 44a,r4cters, so much admired by them, we shall %ll' that the rare quality of moral courage is a th,,Picuous ingredient in the composition of them, it Ta true greatness cannot consist without it, that ore Pre-eminently both the foundation and the he ament of a beautiful and steadfast character, treirire young men should try and clearly ascer- %Liz What it is, how it should atiect their actions, they may strive to infuse it into their lives. 400 Much work to do ! THE HOURS OF WARRINGTON SIIOP ASSISTANTS.
Sir.--1 am instructed by the Association mentioned below to request you to be kind enough to publish the following in the next issue of the " Examiner." lam Sir, yours truly,
EDWARD MOORE, Hon. See., 4, Market-st., Warrington, Jan. 26, 1892.

At a meeting of the Evangelical NonconfArmist Min- isters' Association held on Monday Jan. 25th, it was unanimously resolved that the Secretary be instructed to write a letter to the Local Press expressing the earn- est hope that the tradesmen and shopkeepers of War- rington may be able to see their way to grant the weekly half-holiday now desired by their employes.

div.head: " ST&NDING TO CLERGY."
div.p: " ST&NDING TO CLERGY."

Sir,—Mr. Robert Foulkes objects so strongly to what he appears to consider the modern High Church prac- tice of "standing to clergy," that I think he will be inte- rested in the following account taken from a book re- cently published :—" The Sabbath of Puritan New Eng- land "

In Puritan New England, 200 years ago, in many chdrches the congregation" rose reverently when the parson, dressed in black skull cap and Geneva cloak, en- tered the door ; and they stood in token of respect, until after he had eatered the pulpit and was seated." In the last century it was the custom in many of the New England churches for the entire congregation to stand at the end of the service while the minister " des- cended from his lofty pulpit, opened the door of his wife's pew, and led her with stately dignity to the church perch."—Yours faithfully, J. S.

div.head: "THE AORRORS OF SPORE"
div.p: "THE AORRORS OF SPORE"

Sir,—Your leader on " The Horrors of Sport" in your issue of the 16th inst. was most timely and most com- mendable. Such views will have the solid support of all humane people. It is a barbarous and fiendish thing that men and women should so sink their gentler and diviner nature as to find pleasure in the suffering of the dumb creation. Though I belhve that in unany—in the large majority of cases, kind Nature reduces suffering in the animal world to an unavoidable minimum, yet that is no justification for such conduct as goes under the name of sport. I would trust no man or woman who was cruel to animals any further than I could see them. 'lt is a wonderful world we have beside us—this dumb, suffering, mutely-beseeching life, working for us,watch- ing for us, and providing us with pleasure, with food, feeding our curiosity, and supplying materials for philo- sophical and scientific speculation. So it appeared to good Cardinal Newman, and filled him with awe and wonder. What right have we to defaceonaim, and villainously destroy God's handiwork? The duty of kindness to animals needs inculcating in every Christian home in the land. Let the new gospel begin there. Let us boycott the cruel, for they really deserve it. May I ask the kind attention of your readers to the wants of the little birds this severe weather. A few moistened crusts, thLt is all they require. Perhaps some Almighty Hand feeds us, as we feed the starving spar- rows.. Who knows ?—Yours,,Stc.
OLOING-B.

div.head: MR. KIERNAN NAIL 3 DOWN A TORY
div.p: MR. KIERNAN NAIL 3 DOWN A TORY
COUNTERFEIT.

Sir,—You recently published a paragrah 4‘ in connec- tion with the opposition to the purchase of the Old Barracks at Bank Quay," which is distinctly libelous as far as I am concerned ; but as I believe you were actuated by the most disinterested motives, I am deter-

mined to take no further action in the matter, except in asking you to publish this letter. The paragraph states, " Several gentlemen made much of the :fact that the Radical landlord of the Patten Arms might probably profit by proximity to the New Cattle Maxlset, and one of this choice party said he wouldn't put anything in the way of that damned Fenian." I must tell you lam not a Fenian. lam not now, nor have I at any time been a member of any society that was bound together by an Oath, taken publicly or in secret. Ever since I came to England in 1881, I have helped in the regeneration of my country, and in conjunction with fifteen-sixteenths of the Irish people here, I may say our labour has not been in vain. I have been in the movement for Mome Rule since its conception, and in fact, I may say of it, that, in conjunction with several patriotic men besides, I have been its sponsor. I need hardly say that I hope to con- tinue until Irishmen have obtained everything that is fair, right, and just—and, the crowning point of all, a Parliament in Dublin. When the Grand Old 'Man of the Liberal party has done this, there will be .nothing for me to live for, except to forget the past and look for- ward to the future. Small-minded men will -forget their bigotry and intolerance, and will do noble deeds when noble deeds ought to be done. I forgive most willingly the few " Municipal Fathers " for their denunciations, and tell them now that I fear no harm they can do me, or my family, and, as I have been severely punished in the past for my opinions, I intend to go on as I have begun—a thorough Home Ruler and a sufferer for a holy cause.—Yours truly, _ _ .
T. B. KIERNAN.
P.S.—The Fenians were and are a chivalrous patriotic society, whose motto, I can imagine, is a fair fight with their opponents for justice for their countrymen—T.B.K.
THE PUBLIC HALL AT EARLESTOWN.
Sir,—On reading the proceedings at the last meeting

of Commissioners, I notice that they have se/led the c ontract for the building of the Public Hall. As it is no , use" crying over spilt milk," I think the Eatlestown -portion of the Commissioners should spend some more of the ratepayers' money, and treat them to a Demon- stration over the Laying of the Foundation Stone. Should they adopt the suggestion, I beg to submit the following programme for the occasion :- 1. A Procession, headed by the Bellman with his organ, playing "That's the way the money goes, pop goes the weasel !" 2. Address by the Chairman, showing the meanness and folly of the Newton ratepayers, when they say that the site is more suited for a " Destructor " than for a Public Hall. 3. Tune on the organ, played Allegro Vivaee,by the Bellman, "We may be happy yet !" 4. Address by the Deputy Chairman on " thrift 'in relation to the spending of public money. 5. 'rune on the organ—" Tommy, make rootn for your uncle !" 6. A special vote of thanks to the two Earlestown Commissioners who made the laudable but unavailing attempt to put a vent peg in the spigot-hole when the leakage was taking place in the bung-hole ! 7, Chorus by the ratepayers—" Thay fowt, but wur byeten '!" 8. The Surveyor to mount the stone and return thanks for the officials, for the kind and ample manner in which their wants (including a suit a clothes for the Surveyor) have been attended to. 9. Tune on the crg,an—" I dreamt I dwelt in marble halls !" 10.—Finally, the youngest member on the Commission to make his maiden speech by closing the proceedings with his best " A—men 1" Perhaps " Turn O'Pegs," or, failing him, " Pluto," might lend a hand, by composing a " Hode " for the occasion. I would also further suggest that a tablet should be shown over the principal entrance, with the following inscription :—" Tills faithful representation of "Noah's Ark " is erected as a standing memorial of how to build square rooms on triangular spaces." " Alack, and Well-a-day !" "Our Surveyor wants a bigger suit of clothes !"
RIGDUM.
January 26,1892.

div.head: EARLESTOWN PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN PUBLIC HALL.

Sir,—l think most of your readers will agree with me that it is rare occurrence for a public body to find itself in such a condition of utter helplessness as that of the Newton Commissioners. Their position will excite pity rather than contempt, for as a body they are quite in- capable of satisfactorily performing the duties with j

which theylhave been entrusted. Anyone endowed with ; ttu average amount of common-sense would have thought that, when a vacancy occurred, the Commissioners wouid have selected a colleague who would have raised the intellectual standard of. the Board, a man whom the ratepayers would have been proud to acknowledge as their representative. Such a man might have been found, for instance, in Mr. Borron, whose gentlemanly conduct, business capacity, and tried experience as a Commissioner, would have been a decided acquisition to the Board, and gratefully accepted by the ratepayers. This, however, would not suit the purposes of some of the Commissioners, so the strings are pulled, and Mr. Ratcliffe is instigated to propose the election of Mr. Thompson. In his own sphere Mr. Thompson is a decent, worthy man ,but as a Commissioner he will be of very little service to the ratepayers. Supposing that, at one of the Board's meetings,a resolution, on any subject, should be proposed by Mr. Emmett,and seconded by Mr. Ormand, do your readers think Mr. Thompson would venture to oppose it? It is scarcely likely. Now, sir, in my opinion, Mr. Ratcliffe's action in this matter should be exposed in every possible manner. For a considerable period I have been one of his most ardent supporters, and it is with deep regret that I am now ' compelled to withdraw my support. My contention is that the present building is quite capable of meeting the requirements of the present gene- ration. At least two-thirds of the ratepayers will derive no benefit whatever from the Public Hail, and I ask is it fair, or is it honest, that these two-thirds should be saddled with an additonal rate, solely to benefit the remaining third, and not have even a voice in the matter. Hereto- fore Mr. Emmett has proved himself such a businesslike man that I am extremely surprised to find him an ally of Mr. Radcliffe. I can assure Mr. Emmett that this matter will be probed to the bottom, and a stronger reason than the one he has given will have to be supplied. After the opposition they have met with, will the Corn- missicrnets persevere in their wild-goose scheme? and if so, will the ratepayers stand quietly by., and allow them to do so ? Apologising for trespassing so far on your space.—l am, sir, yours, Ire., FAIRPLAY.
THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON.-A

WORD TO WORKING-MEN. Sir,—ln my last note published in your issue of January 16th, touched Amon the working-man's just demand of "One man one vote-;" and we will not rest until we obtain this natural heritage. Why should s. d. be estimated f high.r value than human be- ings ? Is not the £ s. d. hewn by working-men from the mine, and digged from the land? Yea, at the 'terrible cost of the loss of many thousands of limbs and lives every year. Yes, and should we escape these fates 'we cannot always escape another fate—that semi-hell. the Bastile, though tens of thousands have helped by brain and muscle to make England one of the wealthiest nations in existence. Once in a lifetime is quite enough for the writer to live in such a place. Let the reader try to experience living in such a place—living, did I say—ah ! it is a purgatorial dying, and followed by "Rattle bis bones over the stones, He's only a pauper whom nobody owns." " Dig a big hole, drop the wretch in, Out of my sight, and out of my din" says the man of £ s. d.' whose love of money has steeled his heart, blinded his mental vision, and dulled his hearing to all but the jingling siund of cash in his purse and till. It is utterly impossible for either the rich or the poor to be high-toned and noble-souled, or truly realise the highest joys of existence, until those at the head of the affairs of the nation rightly comprehend and wisely carry out the principle that a nation's true wealth, greatness, and abiding glory lie not in her cash, pomp, or armies, but in her righteous laws justly administered, and her well fed, well clothed, well housed, and thoroughly cul- tuied citizens. But such is far from being the case at present. Jahn Ruskin wisely says :—" Look intri the history of any civilised nations analyse, with reference to this one cause of crime and misery, the lives and thoughts of their nobles, priests, merchants, and men of luxurious life. Every other temptation is at least concentrated in this ; pride and lust, and envy, and anger all give up their strength to avarice. The sin of the world is essentially the sin of Judas. Men do not disbelieve their Christ, but they sell Rim." Mr. Robert Pierpoint, our Conservative candidate, has set himself against us working-men, and utterly failed to show any just reason for resolving to fight against us, if returned as the member for this town of Warrington. If Mr. Pierpoint was not our enemy, he would not think of opposing the payment of members and the proposal which at the Trades Congress held at Newcastle- upon-Tyne, on Thursday, September 10th, 1891, was greeted with "Agreed ! agreed ;" thus demonstrating the fact that that vast host of the most trusted, and in- telligent sons of toil are now determined to secure our ancient birthright, direct representation of the woiking- clam es. All working-men should vote only for those candidates who pledge themselves to vote for the payment of all- members of Parliament. Mr. Pierpoint cannot therefore be worthy of the votes of the working-men of Warring- ton, for he has already taken up arms against the truest interest of the working-classes. He that is not for us is against us, and an enemy to the truest interest of the nation.—Yours, Sze.,

div.head: WORKING-MAN.
div.p: A WORKING-MAN.
EVOLUTION IN EICTREMIS ; EXTREME UNCTION, BY W. IL B.

The ability of men to compromise between conflicting beliefs is very remarkable—remarkable, at least, if we sup- pose them to put their conflicting beliefs side by side not so remarkable It we recognise the fact that they do not put them side by side."—Herbert Spencer.

Sir,—My friend Mr. Butler—l account any man my friend who tries to amend me by candid criticism my friend—l say,is unfortunate. He is unhappy in not being able to sever himself from the bad habit of making un- verified and unverifiable assertions. Now it is unwise to do this, where you can be asked for proof and verifica- tion. It is extremely easy to assert that your opponent has given himself away when you do not burden your- self with proof.

- He is unhappy also in the fact that the only bit of valid criticism of my last letter hangs upon one word— and that a typographical error which escaped my 1 correction :—unbiassed for unba-sed. This last was what I had in mind to write, and Mr. Butler might have gathered as much from the context, had he not been over-hasty in claiming cheap and meretricious victories. Unhappy in himself, he is also likely to be the cause of unhappinness to others. I dread to contemplate the state of mind Herbert Spencer will he in when he hears of Mr. B. and the terrible onslaught he has made upon the Spencerian Philosophy! Nothing less than the entire recasting of" First Principles." can be look:Al for- ward to as the outcome of this " breaking in two."

Our critic still evinces a great remign-an-c.e—to the practical application of the findings of science as mate- rial for the formation of a judgment on some most important religious problems. I can quite understand his hesitancy in this ;it is natural. His predilection for pure or unapplied science, might find more fitting place 'in the Field Club or the Literary and Philosophical ' Society. I distinctly object to the filling of the pages of ' a newspaper with bald extracts from scientific text- books, having no direct application to the teaching and conduct cf our people. On the principle of " a place for everything, everything in place," let us here, in these pages, discuss something of vital and immediate concern to ourselves and our fellows. And here I would earnestly commend to the consideration of all who are interested in the relig- ious teaching of the young, the problem so closely in- volved in the question I have offered to discuss with Mr. Butler :—ls it right and reasonable to teach a child in one school, that which we know must needs be un- learned in another? In other words—why sow weeds with the certainty of having to pluck them up again? it is surely a sinful waste of the teacher's time and the child's brain-space, to say nothing of the moral degra- dation involved in thus teaching that as " truth" which is now demonstrably untrue. Is there not plenty of , •necessary and much needed knowledge to teach the very young, rather than giving, a bad start in life as now by inculcating the crude imaginings of semi-barbarous nomads? In view of its general rejection by cultured adults ought we to continue to cram the infant mind with the scientifically discredited Adamic fables and the equally exploded aboriginal fiction of a hebdomad ,cofittlin creation? I say no! Dare Mr. Butler—or any one else—take up the cudgels as (I presume) a Sunday , School teacher, in defence of such a position? lam much pleased by Mr. Butler's tardy agreement to come , to the point, but am sorry, though not at all surprised, that he should propose to waste time and effort in vapouring on the general question of man's origin. Better far to confine ourselves to a definite branch of this wide subject—i.e. all the facts and the logical infer- ences from these facts, bearing upon the earliest appear- ance of our species. Finally I would ask if Mr. Butler has not " given himself away" in that bit of rant as to the " probabili- ties" being alead against the doctrine of the evolution of life, and wholly in favour of the spiritual origin of the same? If this be the way he is going to conduct the discussion, it will assuredly not need " a more formid- able opponent" than he has to make him bite the dust. The spiritual.or.igin of life stands. as regards proof, in just the same position as "abiogenesis "—aaavbere. But as to probability, abiogenesis is far ahead, While "the spiritual origin of life" is out of the running. This is evident when we reflect that every forward advance of science has been accompanied by a concomitant reces- sion of the "spiritual origin" of every thine', until COW it is forced to find sanctuary—along with its antithesis, abiogenesis—in the citadel of the Unknown. JOHN PEERS. ! GRAPPENHALL RATEPAYERS MEETING.— , OBJECTION TO THE POLL. Sir,—On Monday last, in obedience to the summons of the Overseers, the ratepayers of the pariah to the s number, I should say, of nearly 150. !tumbled i the

div.head: 14-AA [NEW RATURDNY, JANUARY 30, 1592.
div.p: THE 14-AA [NEW RATURDNY, JANUARY 30, 1592.

Schoolroom, to, quoting the notice, "consider the elec- tion of, and if necessary appoint an assistant Overseer." When the meeting was opened the Rate Book was asked for, but it was not forthcoming; it had not been brought to the meeting. Then Mr. Kaye, as Overseer, explained that he desired that the Overseers, with the assistance of some person whom they would select,should carry on the work of assistant Overseer until Eister. The ratepayers thought otherwise,and carried an amend- ment to the effect "That we proceed at once with the work for which we were summoned, viz., the appoint- ment of assistant Overseer." Then, on being defeated, a poll cf the parish was demanded by Mr. Kaye. Not a word was said about a poll until the motion favoured by Mr. Kaye was lost.

To show that the step was premature I may say that when a poll of the parish was demanded by Mr. Kaye, and the Chairman declared, "That if a poll is demanded, we have nothing to do but to agree to it, and therefore this meeting is at an end," not a single applicant had been nominated for the post. Again, this we know, that any ratepayer may demand a poll, yet I think as a rule, when it is done, it is done by an aggrieved candidate who has failed to secure the support of the vestry. The Act was certainly never in- tended to accommodate the caprice a any individual who might desire to be unpleasant, and who may be sufficiently factious to attempt to coerce the parish. A great many persons present asked that the usual forms approved by the Local Government ,Board should be sent to every ratepayer so that is case of a poll, it should be real. But this would not do. It meant expense, and it meant extra trouble. ,Butswhat about the desire to continue the work of the Assistant Overseer? A great number who were at the Lmeeting I find have concluded from the remarks made ,by the Overseer, that whatever we did at that meeting wonld be rendered null and void at Easter, and that we :should have another batch of applicants for an office that was not open, and to elect a person to a post which had been already filled. I confess I did not so under- stand the gentleman, nor would I think that he could seriously, harbour such a thought. At the meeting I par- ticularly called attention to the Alit of Parliament bear- ing on the appointment of Overseers. The 59 Geo. 2, 5..7., provides that" it shall be lawful for the in- habitants of any parish in the vestry assembled to nom- inate and elect any discreet person or persons to be As- sistant Overseer or Overseers of the poor of such parish, and every person or persons so appointed shall continue to be an Assistant Overseer of the poor until he, or they shall resign such office,or until his, or their appointment shall be revoked by the inhabitants in vestry assembled and no longer." The above seems repealed, for on the 17th June, 1886, the Local Government Board issued a general order bearing on Poor Rate collectors and assistant averseers. Article sth says, referring to those appointed to such offices as the above after the issue of the crder : " Every such officer shall continue to hold office until he shall die, or resign, or be dismissed by the Guardjans subject to the consent of the Local Government Board, provided, that the Guardians may, with the like consent, determine the appointment of any such officer, at any time before, or at the expiration of the first year of his services, by giving to the officer three months' previous notice in writing, signed by the Clerk, of such their intention." If Mr. Kaye correctly reported Mr. Sutton in his say- ing, " That it would all have to be gone over again at Easter," then perhaps one or both of them would kindly explain the above, also the passages in the letters received by the Local Government Board," Proceedings can at once be taken for the nomination of a new Assist- ant Overseer by the parish." " You as Overseer have no control in the matter; as to whether or not the assist- ant Overseer shall be appointed, or as to what particular person shall be appointed." sow, can Mr. Sutton ' in his capacity of Clerk to the Board of Guardians i refer to a case where the Local Government Board annulled such an appointment, without some charge being made against, or incapacity proved on.the part of, the person so elected ? • lam charged,' hear, with having packed the meeting. I will simply state that I never asked a person to attend it ; nor did I either directly or indirectly influence an individual to do so. Can the overseers say as much? ..
i-seriousl

To prevent any dispute about the appointment when it shall have been made' I am sending a copy of the letter underneath to the Rev. Canon Greenall as Chair- man of the vestry by virtue of his position, to J. Charl- ton-Parr, Esq., chairman of the meeting on Monday night, and to Lister Kaye, Esq., overseer. _ S. 11. JENKINS.

[Cary.] Whereas the law governing the appointment of assis- tant overseer, says:—" Appointment and tenure of office of assistant overseer. Page 11, section 3, Over- seers' Manual : "It is necessary that the nomination of an assistant overseer should be made by a vestry after due notice of the purpose for which the meeting is to be held," and as no such nominations were made on Mon- day last when the chairman declared the meeting at an end and most of the ratepay era left the room, I submit that the polling fixed for Monday next is both irregular and unconstitutional, and I obj ect to the poll. (Signed) STEPHEN HOSKIN JENKINS. Thelwall-view, Grappenhall.
