DANCE AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

On Saturday evening a dance, in aid of the funds or the Sankey Brass Band, was held in the Con- servative Club-room, Stocks-lane. Mr. J. Kent ably officiated as M.C. There were about 30 couples pre- sent. Dancing was commenced at seven o'clock, and continued with little intermission to eleven o'clock. Miss M. A. Pownall prepared and took charge of the refreshments. Mr. Wright Hardman, supplied the music, assisted by another gentleman. Mr. Hardman also played various selections between the dances.

div.head: ' CHILDREN'S CONCERT.
div.p: ' CHILDREN'S CONCERT.

On Tuesday evening the annual entertainment of the senior scholars attending the PenlKeth Wes- leyan Day school was given in the schoolroom, Mr. J. Watson, the schoolmaster,conducting. An excel- lent programme, consisting of songs, recitations, and dialogues; singing from the mantle). signs; wand and dumb-bell drill, spelling and mental arithmetic contests, &c., was gone through in a praiseworthy manner. Mrs. Wilson conducted lie girls' wand exercise. Miss E. H. Watson played the musical accompaniments to the various drills on the piano in an able manner. The proceeds of the entertainment are in aid of the school recrea- tion fund. The following were the results of the spelling and arithmetic contests :—Mental arithn tic 1, W. Shingsby ;2, D. Dobson; 3, W. Carman. Spelling; 1, Colin Cooke; 2, Florrie D Irl'ngton ; 3, Harriet Gleave. Mr. C. E. Parker presented the above children with prizes, kindly given by se ;7eral gentlemen. Mr. Parker also remarked that irom the report on the drawing examination recently re- ceived from her Majesty's Inspectors, he noticed the school had passed "excellent." The following boys had also received the Government" cards of ' merit " for excellence in drawing, viz., D. Dobson, John Watson, C. D. Cooke, and It. Cragg. In the pupil teachers' Bible history examination, out of 100 teachers examined, Miss E. 11. Watson was number 10 on the list, and Miss E. M. White number 14. The prize distribution concluded the programme, and a most pleasant evening was terminated by the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: ANNUA.T. LIBERAL TEA PARTY,
div.p: ANNUA.T. LIBERAL TEA PARTY,

Last evening week in c6nnection with the Penketh Liberal Association, the annual tea party and entertainment were held in the Wesleyan day school. Tea was on the tables at 6.30 p.m. and there was a large attendance, over 160 being present. Tea was prepared and the tables presided over by the following ladies, viz :—Mesdames Longshaw, White, Routledge, Goulding, and Misses Clarke,A. Griffiths, S. Pownall, A. Pownall, Hughes, Winn, Gandy, and Hurst. The tea was an excellent one and well pre- pared. After tea an entertainment was held, the chair being occupied by Mr. 11. Roberts. In the course of an able address, Mr. Roberts said he did not reckon much of a man who could not give a good sound reason for his political opinions. If there was one thing more than another that he could not understand it was that curious production ,of the 19th century, the Conservative working-man. Such a man did not need to give a reason for his political faith, the one, that he was" a Tory because his father was before him," being considered good enough. But how any working-man could, in the face of the legisla- tion of the oast 50 or 60 years, be a Conservative, passed his comprehension altogether. Mr. Roberts then gave a brief sketch of the chief political events of the last century, showing how most of the great reforms which have been made law in the past half century, emanated from the Liberal party. He also referred to the chief political questions which are agitating the public at the present time viz : Home Rule; direct veto of the liquor traffic, " one man, one vote " &c. (Applause.) An excellent programme, consisting of songs,readings, pianoforte solos, comic songs in character, &c., waS gone through in a praiseworthy manner, the various efforts meeting with much applause. Mr. and Mrs. Gorse of St. Helens, gave several valuable contributions to the evening's enjoyment. Mrs. Gatley ably accom- panied. At the conclusion of the programme the room was cleared and social games were indulged in till 11 o'clock, the evening being closed by tile singing of t he National Anthem.

MORE REPRESENTATION FOR MANCHESTER.

At the General Purpose Committee of the Manchester City Council on Thursday, upon the motion of Mr. Gunson who said they had been hoodwinked, it was re- solved that it be an instruction to the Parliamentary Sub-CoFrimittee to provide for the insertion of a clause in the new Bill enabling the Corporation to app)int eight of the 15 directors of the Canal Company.

div.head: NEW ROAD AT THELWALL.
div.p: THE NEW ROAD AT THELWALL.

The wall which is to strengthen the Thelw.all New- road is in course of construction. It is about six feet thick at the base,and one foot at the top. The road about here is of a very sandy character, and the Canal Com- pany thought it necessary to construct the wall to pre- vent the road giving way and slipping into the Canal cutting. NAVVIES AND THE FAIR SEX.

Jane Radnor, of London, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court yesterday charged with sleeping in a cart in Public Hall-st. on the previous night and with not giving a good account of herself .—Superintendent Large said they were much pestered with these women, who came after the Ship Canal navvies, and now that the weather was a little milder they slept anywhere.—The prisoner was committed for seven days. LETTING WORKS BY CONTRACT. It was stated some short time ago that the Executive Committee of the Board of Directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company had decided that, with a view to the speediest and most economical completion of the undertaking, as much as possible of the remaining works should be let by contract. In order to secure a free hand, the Committee gave three months' notice at the beginning of the year to a large number of members of the engineering staffs on the different sections. We now learn that the preliminary arrangements of the Committee have been made. Between Eastharn and the estuary of the river Weaver—nearly a third of the entire ength of the canal—the works are complete, except in so far as it is necessary to flatten the banks of parts of the lace section. This the Company will undertake. Between the Weaver and Runcorn the task to be acom- plished is of a very delicate character, involving opera- tions in the estuary. This short length will not be let by contract,but it is also to be undertaken by the Company. The cutting between Runcorn and Latchford has been divided into two nearly equal sections, of which the re- sident engineers are Mr. Abernethy and Mr. Brooke. These gentlemen are authorised to give every informa- tion to intending contractors who choose to visit the sections during the two or three weeks in which Mr. Leader Williams is occupied in preparing quantities. The contracts will be advertised in the early part cf February. A long stretch of the canal between Latch- ford and Warburton was nearly completed before the recent floods filled the channel with water. The work will be finished by the Company itself in the summer months without much difficulty. From Warburton to Manchester the entire work is to be let in two sections. The arrangements to be made are the same as those given above. Mr. Meade-King is the resident engineer on the section between Warburtoi and Barton, and Mr. Kyle of the section between Barton and Manchester. When the Committee have completed the system of let- ting all, or nearly all, works by contract, they will then be in possession of information which at present is sadly wanted—namely, the approximate cost of finishing the undertaking. WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL. REPORT ON THE NEW BILL.

A report has been presented to the Warrington Town Council by Mr. 3. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, and Mr. T. Longdin, borough surveyor, with regard to the new Bill of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. Having quoted from the Act they go on to state that " in the original Act, the Company took power to construct a dam across the bed of the River Mersey, in a south- westerly direction (with a lock therein), commoncing in the township of Warrington, and terminating in the township of Walton Inferior, in the Parish of R uncorn, on the left bank of that river. It was proposed to con- struct the dam immediately under, and in line of the new bridge now in course of construction over the river Mersey at Walton. This work will now be abandoned, and in lieu of it, the dam proposed by the new Bill will be constructed about 308 yards on the east of the new ' bridge, and 396 yards west of the centre of the arm con- necting the river or dock with the canal.

_ . The substituted dam will be an improvement upon the dam originally intended to be constructed. In addi- tion to a lock 125 feet long by 25 feet wide, there will be a sluice of the same width. By section 88, s. s. 16 of the Act of 1885, the Corporation secured power to require the Company to construct "a sluice or sluices at least 20 feet wide with a sill or sills level with the bed of the River Mersey." The sills of the new lock and sluice will be one foot below the bed of the River, and 9 feet below ordinary low water level in the river. The ordinary low water level of the canal will be six inches below ordinary low water level in the river. The level of the water in the lock, on a tide rising 21 feet over Old Dock sill, Liverpool, will be 18ft. 6in. The level of the water in the Old Quay Canal is about 18in. higher than the level of a 21400 t tide in the river. The lock will be capable of passing a vessel of 250 tons burden. The water impounded in the dock will be highly charged with sewage matter_ The outfall of the sewers of the Stockton Heath drainage district, and the drainage of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., Limited, now discharge into that portion of the river which will form the dock. The water in the dock will only be affected by the rise and fall of high tides flowing up the Canal from Eastham. The great importance of having proper and adequate means of flushing or chang- ing the waters in the dock is a matter upon which the Manchester Ship Canal Company should be pressed to make provision. The proposed sluice will only be avail- able in times of flood..

The company should be asked to proceed with the construction of the substituted dam, and works con- nected therewith, forthwith, so that it would be com- pleted and the lock ready for use by the time that por- tion of the canal between Eastham and Latchford is open for traffic. The preamble of the Bill further recites :—" And whereas the period limited by the Act of 1885 for the completion of the works by the Act authorised was seven years from the passing of that Act, which period was by The Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1891' extended until the 31st day of December, 1893,and it is expedient that the said period limited for the completion of the said dock should be extended until the 31t.t day of December, 1895." And section 21 is intended to carry out the extension of time for the construction of the dock. There is considerable ambiguity in the recital and the clause when read together. If that portion of the canal between Eastham and Latchford is open for traffic before the 31st December, 1892, then the clause and the recital will be consistent ; but as far as can be ascertained, it is not at all likely that the canal will be open for traffic for some time after the date named. The preamble should be amended so as to remove the ambiguity. If it should be thought that the object of the clause is in itself unobjectionable, the position of the borough in relation to the construction of the dock is in no way altered by the proposed Bill. In the Act of 1885, the Company were bound to con- struct a dock within three years after the opening of the Canal between Eastham and Latchford, and the new clause is a repetition of the one in the Act of 1885. With regard to the latter part of the clause, namely : " From and after the expiration of that period the power to construct the docks shall cease," it should be pointed out that in the Act of 1885, the whole of the works were to be completed within seven years from thepassing of the Act, and that the power to construct the works after that time should cease to he exercised. Too much meaning should not be attached to the words quoted, as a similar provision is inserted by Parliament in every Act in which power is taken for the compulsory acquisition of land. The period of seven years referred to would have expired on the 6th August, 1892; but by the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1891, that period was extended to the 31st December, 1893, so that, unless the clause in the Aet of 1885 is kept alive by the insertion of the clause in the present Bill, the power to cookruct the dock at Warrington will expire on the 31st Decem- ber, 1893. • Power should he obtained to enforce the construction of the dock within the time named. In any event, it will be necessary to present a petition against the Bill in order to secure such atnenchrtent thereof as may be necessary for the due protection of the interests of the Borough. The time for petitioning against the Bill in the House of Commons will expire about the 24th February.

A MEMORIAL FROM TRADERS. The following memial has been presented to the Corporation, signed by nearly all the leading manufac- turers and traders of the town, viz. 1—" We, the under- signed ratepayers of the borough of Warrington, beg to call ywur Worship's attention, and that of the Town Council, to the application to Parliament proposed by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, for permission to make certain modifications in their Act which,if allowed to be sanctioned, will, in the opinion of your memoria- ltsts, most seriously endanger the interests of the town. Your memorialists consider that the proposal to defer the construction of the Warrington Docks,or in any way to interfere with any of the rights and privi- leges which are secured to Warrington by the original Act of Parliament, should be strenuously opposed by the Corporation an behalf of the ratepayers and traders of the town, and all necessary ! steps should be taken to make such opposition effectual and conclusive. Without the docks, the Canal will be practically useless to Warrington, and any ciwtallinent of, or interference wiCh, the privileges already 4 secured would materially affect the interests of your memorialists and others engaged in the trade of the district." THE WALTON LOCKS.

The Rivers Committee of the Warrington Corporation are taking steps to urge upon the Ship Canal Company to construct the lock at Walton of not less dimensions than 200 feet long by 45 feet wide. div.p: BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE.
(MIXED.)

Br Tun( o' Dicic o' Bon's. Aw think id were Tennyson as wrooat "Each month, a birthday coming on, We drink, defying trouble; And sometimes two would come in one, And then we drank it double." Well,onybody as wants them excuses for drinkin'l hes hed a opportunity to drink id double this week, becose last Monda. were Bobby Burns's birthday, an' last neat were Ned Waugh's. Burns were 133 year owd, an' Waugh 75. Aw darsay some intelli- gent chap wod like to tell me as booath o' these poets are deead, an' aw should contradict him; aw think they've a scoore or two moore year to live yet, judgin' hi th' way fooak act. Look at o' th' Burns dinners every year, an' th' way as rich an' poor, English, Irish, Scotch, or Welsh, do o' as they Icon to honour him; well, to try to fratch o' Bobby is like tryin' to paint th' lily, an' gild refined gowd. , One con but say he were gradely jonnock o' through. As for Waugh—"the Lancashire Burns"—well, it's just th' same wi' him; aw knew him middlin' wee!, an' aw look back wi' pleasure to th' chats as aw hed wi* him. Id uobbut looks t'other week sin' aw sent him a tooathri birthday verses—when he reycht 73—but it's two year sin' to-day; there is a bit o' dispute as to wod his age wor, an' aw gi' th' followin' fro' one o'th' last letters aw geet fro' him: "With respect to the date of my birth, the certifi- cate of my baptism is dated in the year 1818, but my sister always asserted that I was born on the 29th of January, in the year before the year of my baptism. Of course, I cannot swear to the fact, althouyh I was Mere at the time, but I am inclined to think that mysister was right." * *
At th' end o' th' owd year aw said summat on th' subject of wages addled neaw an' say forty year back, an' aw wondered iv onybody could tell me why fooak were woes off neawadays nor they wor then.

Yo' know a good able-bodied bandloom weyver could nobbut mek fro' ten to twelve shillin' week; fleawr were sixpence a peawnd, sugar eight- pence or ninepence, tay eight shillin'. Neaw a goo I weyver con bring in double them wages, con ged five peawnd o' fleawr for sixpence, four peawnd o' sugar for eightpence, an' three peawnd o' good tay for eight shillin'..

" Oh," yo' say," it's eeasy enough to explain. They paid less nor hofe wod we do for heawse-rent, an' they kept off fleawr, an' tay an' sugar." Well, that's middlin' true; an' aw con say they used varra little gas, an' less coyl nor we use ; they dudn'd keep th' wife waitin' up on 'om till welly hofe past eleven at neet. But for two things they ne'er spent one quarter o' th: brass we spend neaw-a-days on finery, an' lilippen nobbut one tenth o' th' brass we wear i' Booze; yo' know many a werkin' chap—or lass—spends as mich as five or six peawnd on a new rig eawt, au' mony a four loom weyver sups thirty flat pints a week,, an' thad meks a hoyl one-therd or his wage. Aw think— tekkin' everything into consideration —as th' operative classes are nod as badly off as a lot o' th' Socialists try to mek etiwt,thougli they met be a bit better off. Ov coourse a lot on 'em are olez th' wo'st off when they're addlin' mooast, an' olez will be, but that's nowt to do wi' them as isn d nobbut it's mooastly these soort as bawl an' mek a noyse. But we'll hay a word or two later on.

Heaw is this for heigh ? " We have 180,000 people in Toronto, and yet , there are no street cars running on Sundays, no Sunday newspapers. and you cannot buy a banana or even a sweetmeat. You think that the people are inconvenienced by t his ? Not at all. All Pro- testants and Catholics alike unite in this thorough observance of the Sunday, and will uphold it to the end. The result is that the churches are crowded, and there is great religious prosperity. Is it law or sentiment? It is sentiment backed by law and authority. Our ex-Nfayor preaches in the Protest- s-it Churches ; our present Mayor presides at religious gatherings. The majority of the thirty- six aldermen are members of the church, and the same may be said of our School Board, so you see that it is not without reason that statistics show that Toronto is one of the least afflicted with crime of any city in the country." That's wod a Methodist minister o' Toronto hes bin tellin' th' focak o' Washington, an' aw dorn'd know heaw mony on 'em sung " What must it be to be there ?"

* So mich lies bin said i'th' pappers abeawt th' deeath o' th' young Prince till aw thowt there were no room for me to ged a word in—even edgeways. Aw nooatist wod took place at th' Miners' Confer- ence at Stoke, an' aw nooatist as " Nunquam " cor- roborates; well, nayther on 'em are serious, for nobody's ony woss for wod they said—except it's thersels'. Fooak say it's this meean, an' thad meean an' Vother meean, but they dorn'd know wod meean- ness meeans ; they should gooa to Darrun to learn —but aw'll tell yo''next week abeawt th' Nurses' Ball theere, an' yo' con judge for yor'sels'.

THE LIVERPOOL NAVAL EXHIBITION. The arrangements for the Liverpool Naval Ex- hibition, which will be opened in the Walker Art Gallery, at noon on Monday next, by Lord George Hamilton, M.P., First Lord of the Admiralty, are approaching completien,and, though much remains to be done in the way of finishing touches,the bulk of the heavy work is over. For the most part the cases containing models of steamers and of war vessels are now in position, and such large exhibits as the model of the Suez Canal in relief, the Deep Sea Mission to Seamen, the Mersey Docks, and the Bombay Docks are practically placed. A good deal remains to be done in the hanging of the pictures which illustrate" A Life on the Ocean Wave," but in the course of a day or t /fro this will be finished. An important part of the exhibition is, of course, that which is designed more for the amusement than the instruction of the visitors. To transform a broad cartway into a winter garden, and the an- nexes of it into artistically-appointed refreshment rooms is no easy task ; but this has been done, and the result has been very striking. The Museum and Fine Arts Committee have been equally successful in dealing with the smoking roorns,which are being finished in a Turkish style. Not an inch of room has been lost, and the wonder of the public Will be that so many objects of interest and of artistic beauty could be crowded into so limited a space.

WA.I.I.ItINGTON MEDICAL ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the Warrington Amalga- mated Friendly Societies' Medical Association was held last night week ;—The following Officers and Delegates representing the Lodges and Courts met in the room of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce,—Joseph Albinson, president. George Roughley, vice-president, Alban Stirrup, treasurer. Samuel Dunbobbin, Wm. Holmes, and W. Barlow, trustees, and Wm. Bibby, secretary ; Messrs. Thos. Wadsworth and John Burgess, auditors, Messrs. Peter Edgar, Peter Langley, Thos. Pemberton, Wm. Gilbert, Henry Kent, Robert Rudd. Robert Perdue James Fearnly, John Beswick, Wm. McCullam. Henry Lloyd, Wilkinson, Haigh, Mathew Massey' James Smith, John Tyson, James Bramhall, Wm, Drury, and James Boyle, delegates. The Secretary presented his annual balance sheet. This showed that the income for the year had been £5BO 29. Bd. and the expenditure £562 13s. 8:341., leaving a balance of £l7 Sc. llid.—The balance sheet was adopted unanimously.—The number of members was reported as 3,808. The work of the society, the committee reported, had gone on during the Year so well, that the committee felt that especial thanks and praise were due to their respected Dr. Kisby, and also Mr. Lake, for the highly efficient manner in which they had performed their duties. The committee pointed out the desirability of having a second medical officer, and that what was necessary to accomplish this object was the addition of some Friendly Society Lodges and Courts. Dr. J. ILKisby, resident medical officer,presented his annual report. This stated that compared with the previous year the number of prescriptions had been 385 less, but the visits to patients at their homes 190 more, and deaths 4 more. The surgical injuries were chiefly fractures. There had been only a small number of dangerous fever cases, principally typhoid fever. At the close of a very pleasant meeting, a unanimous vote of thanks was accorded to the officers, and as a special mark of esteem of the committee every officer was unanimously re-elected, the president and vice-president for their third year, the secre- tary for his 11th year,and the treasurer for his 13th . year.
TEE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
The Rev. J. P. Ferguscn, rector of Shenfleld Brentwood, died on Thursday night from bronchitis, following in- fluenza.
The death of Mr. William Brentnall, brewer and hotel keeper, took place at Mold, on Thursday morning from influenza.

The following bulletin was issued at noon on Thurs- day : " Lord Coleridge, who is recovering from an attacx of influenza, is not so well to-day." Professor Dill, coroner of Belfast, is seriously ill with influenza.

Mr. Charles John Radley, who presided over the High Court of Foresters in London in August last, died on Wednesday, at Brixton, from influenza. The official sanitary returns report 620 cases of in- fluenza in Copenhagen during the week ending 23rd inst., 30 of which terminated fatally. A Berlin correspondent telegraphs that the Empress Frederick was unableto congratulate her son in the cus- ternary manner on Wednesday,having a slight attack of iufluenza. Her Majesty was confined to her rooms. The Rev. H. W. Burrows, Canon of Rochester, died on Tuesday from congestion of the lungs, following in- fluenza. Mr. JoheMaconcliv, head surgeon of County Down Infiimary, died on Tuesday from influenza. A Munich telegram announces the death of the Dowager Duchess Maximilian from influenza. OFFICIAL RECOMMENDATIONS.

A meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee was held on Wednesday afternoon. Councillor J. Forster pre- siding.—Mr. Robertson read a communication from the Local Government Board suggesting precautions against the sprea lof influenza. He recommended that handbills be printed and circulated among the householders for their guidance in case of illness. He remarked that St. Helens had, happily, escaped the epidemic so far, and the death-rate was much lower than in many other towns. Some gce.d would be done by the circulation of the handbills towards preventing the disease. On the motion of Councillor Dr. Gaskell, seconded by Councillor Bennett, it was resolved that handbills be printed and circulated with the following information :—" Influenza is an infectious disease, the infection being carried from person to person. It is, therefore, necessary that the tollowing precautions be taken when influenza occurs :-1. Separation of the sick from the healthy should be carried out as far as practic- able. 2. Rooms and articles of clothings should be dis- infected. 3. Persons suffering should not expose them- selves in public places ; they should absolutely avoid at- tending large assemblages of people. 4. Those who are affected should carefully avid the great danger of a re- lapse by not exposing themselves to cold or damp bef ore complete recovery. They should not attempt to fight against it, but at once seek warmth, rest, and medical treatment. During the prevalence of an epidemic those , who have not suffered should observe the following : (1) Avoid exposure to cold or fatigue of any kind what- ever. (2) Attend to every measure which will assist in 1 maintaining good health—warmth, clothing, the avoid- ance of any unwholesome food, and especially avoid the excessive use of alcoholic stimulants. (3) Disinfection of zooms and clothing will be done free of charge by the health department of the corporation." DR. GORNALL'S REPORT.

The Medieal Officer of Health of Warrington (Dr. Gornall) has received and commented on the memo- randum from the Local Government Board. We are told that influenza is spread by infection from person to person, so that the first case of the dis- ease in a town is often a patient who has come from an infected place, and thus the disease spreads along the lines of human intercourse. One attack of influenza does not for any considerable length of time confer immunity from another attack. Persons suffering from influenza should not expose themselves in public places. The liability to contract influenza, and the danger of an attack if contracted, are increased by depressing conditions, such as exposure to cold, or to fatigue, whether mental or physical. Once attacked by influenza, all persons are warned not to fight against it, b,ut seek rest, warmth, and medical treatment, and to avoid premature exposure to cold and fatigue.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL lIVIPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The usual meeting of this society was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. A very interesting paper on " Diseases of Plants," was given by Mr. Gilanders, of High Legh. The subject was discussed by Messrs. Briggs, Brown, and Mort, an able reply to the criticisms of these gentlemen being given by Mr. Gilanders. Mr. H. S. Brown was in the chair.
SALE OF WORK AT THE EMMANUEL
CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

On Thursday afternoon a very successful Sale of Work was held in the rooms over A.rpley Station, in aid of the funds of the Emmanuel Church. Bold-st. The Vicar, the Rev. Edward T. Reed, in the course of some remarks, said their friends, particularly Mrs. 'John Allen, thought a sale of work should be held this year on the day of the congregational tea party, and it was therefore being held that after.- noon. They had obtained a room in which to hold their Bible class, and for other church purposes. The sale of work was being held in it that afternoon, and it afforded a good opportunity to show the room to their friends. They sympathised with Mrs. Allen in her sickness, which had prevented her doing what she wished to do for the sale, but they hoped it would be a success. Raving referred in complimentary terms to the earnest band of workers in connection with the church, the rev, gentleman declared the sale open, and said he trusted it would be very successful. (Applause.) The sale of the various goods was then proceeded with, the stalls being in charge of Mrs. Annie Gandy, and the Misses Fanny Mason, Eva Parsons, Beatrice Lees, Eva Lees, Eveline llu,ghes, and Mrs. John Allen. The sale was a successful one, all the goods being dis- posed of. In the evening a tea meeting and entertainment were held, about 200 sitting down at the tables, which were presided over by ladies of the congregation. Amongst those present at the alter meeting were the pastor, the Rev. E. T. Reed, the Rev. W. Bibby, Liscard • Rev. T. Jones, Eccles ; and the Rev. W. Storer, Birkenhead. An excellent programme of music, was rendered. It included songs by Mr. Taylor, Mr. Williams, Mr. J. F. Jack- son, Mr. W. Booth ; violin solo, Mr. Y. Taylor ; con- certina solos, Mr. Foster ; quartettes by Misses A. Landon and C. Ashley, and Messrs. 11. and W. Lan- don ; and glees and part songs by the choir. Mr.G. Riley was the pianist.

div.p: MARKETS. - MANCHESTER NAY AND STRAW FRIDAY—Hay tild to 61; clover 51ct to 71-d ; straw, wheat, 3d to 41d ; ditto, oat, 3d to 44 per stone of 141 b. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. Cotton keeps steady, futures have changed little since the opening, and 8,000 balre Is deemed an estimate large enough to cover transactions at_ Liverpool. Prices generally unchanged. Yarns are quoted at Tuesday's level. In cloth nothing better is noticeable. For the Levant just S. moderate trade gets &nein miscellane- ous goods, and some South American trade is also reported. CORK BUTTER, FRIDAY. Ordinary: Seconds, 123 s thirds, 106 s ; fourths, 90s. Mild cured firkins : Fine, 131 s ; mild. 114 s. In market : 39 firkins, 3 kegs, and 6 mild. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY. Sugar: Pieces quiet but. steady • stoved goods and crystals slow at late rates ; cane dull ; beet firm—January buyers /4 6d and sellers 148 81d ; May sold at 15s plus Id. Coffee firm on the spot; future° firm—Rio. March 57s ; Santos, 64s 3d. Tea quiet but steady. Rice firm. Jute slow but firm. Linseed oil, 183 1014 to 19s 3d. Turpentine. 248 6d. American petroleum 511-d to 51d spot. GLASGOW METAL, FRIDAY.— Scotch idle; business done at 43s cash and 43s 24 one month; closing buyers 43s oasis; sellers 43s 114 cash. Middlesbrough steady, with a smell business done at 36s 51d cash ; closing buyers 36s 4/c1 cash and 36s 61d one month ; sellers ld more. Hematite steady, with a small business done at 46s 7d to 46s 71d cash and 46s 9d, 46s 91d, 46s 81d, 468 91. and 46s 94 one month closing buyers 46s 61d cash and 46s 94 one month ; mile" 1d more. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. Fine grades of beef more firmly held. Pork very firmly held. In bacon a lair amount of business has been transacted, previous rates, however, not being in every instance obtained. Hem" Short cuts rule firm ; long cuts quietly steady. Shoulders : Square cuts In request, at full prices, but New Yc:k being more freely offered favour buyers slightly. Cheese strong In tone, with a good consumptive inquiry. Butter steady an unchanged. Lard slightly easier. Imports of fresh u"rn from Baltimore, 2,850 cwt. ; ditto from Newport New', cwt.; from New York. 346 cwts. ; from Philadelphia. 274 cwts. Imports of salted provisions :—Beef. 54 tierces ; 17 barrels ; 13 icon. 1.137 b .xes ; Hams, 746 boxes ; Cheese, 1.147 boxes ; Butter, 619 packages ; and Lard, 33 tons. servant" is told that he can only communicate information with the sanction of "the Mayor or Chairman of the Committee concerned," after which he is informed that he must have " the authority of the Committee," thus knocking the Mayor and Chairman on the head—so to speak. But the main point is that an unwarrantable attempt is being made to keep the ratepayers in the dark as long as possible as to what their repre- sentatives are doing. It is in this way that ser- vants become masters—that is, if the ratopayers will let them ; but that is a point which can, happily, be settled at the polling booths. It is to , be hoped for the credit of the Town Council that both these proposals will be rejected on Tuesday next. We shall be surprised to find any Liberal voting for secrecy in the transaction of public business. In St. Helens the Committee meetings themselves are fully opea to the press.

THE ILLNESS OF TEE POPE. It is stated that prayers are about to be offered in all the churches of Rome for the recovery of the Pope. MR. SPURGEON'S CONDITION. Yesterday's bulletin says Mr. Spurgeon's symptoms cause grave anxiety, though his strength.is well main- tained. THE FASTING MAN GIVES UP. The Italian, Succi, who attempted to fast for 52 days, gave up at noon yesterday, having fasted 43 days, 18 hours, and 45 minutes. PROPOSED UNION OF IRISH PARTIES. The" Freeman's Journal," "National Press," and Inde- pendent " again discuss the question :of the union of the parties, the " Freeman "suggesting that a union for the session should be formed. ALLEGED ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER. A Swansea correspondent says Mr. 11. Williams, land- lord of Wassail Stores, Swansea, and local secretary of the Coal Trimmers' Union, shot his wife with a revolver yesterday morning. Mrs. Williams was removed in a critical condition to the hospital. It is stated that the parties had lived unhappily for some years. Williams was subsequeutly charged with attempting to murder his wife, and was remanded. THE VIENNA MURDERS. VIENNA, FRIDAY EVENING.—The man Schneider and his wife were to-day found guilty of the murder of several servant girls, and sentenced to death.
